utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is IT-00-39-A, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask Mr. Krajisnik if he can hear me and follow the proceedings through the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I call for the appearances. The Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, members of the Court. Peter Kremer appearing with Barbara Goy, Katharina Margetts and Lourdes Galicia, our case manager, will be assisting us this morning and this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you. Now counsel for Mr. Krajisnik in the matter of -- MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: [Microphone not activated] Alan Dershowitz and Nathan Dershowitz appearing on the issue of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. The amicus curiae.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Colin Nicholls appearing with Mr. John Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is the appeals hearing in the case of the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. At the outset I will briefly summarise the appeals which are pending before the Appeals Chamber and the manner in which we will proceed today. The appeal deals with crimes committed in 35 municipalities in the Bosnian Serb republic between 1st July 1991 and 30 December 1992, and with the role allegedly played in these events by Momcilo Krajisnik who allegedly held several high-ranking positions within the SDS Main Board and was president of the Bosnian Serb Assembly at the time. Both Krajisnik and the Prosecutor have appealed the trial judgement rendered on 27 September 2006 by Trial Chamber I composed of Judge Orie presiding and Judges Canivell and Hanoteau. In addition, amicus curiae, who was appointed on 8 June 2007 to assist the Appeals Chamber by arguing in favour of Krajisnik's interests has filed an appeal against the trial judgement. The Trial Chamber found Krajisnik guilty pursuant to Article 7(1) of the statute of persecution as a crime against humanity, count 3; extermination as a crime against humanity, count 4; murder as a crime against humanity, count 5; deportation as a crime against humanity, count 7; and inhumane acts, forced transfer as a crime against humanity, count 8. It found him not guilty of the crime of genocide, count 1; complicity in genocide, count 2; and murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war, count 6. The Trial Chamber sentenced Momcilo Krajisnik to a single sentence of 27 years of imprisonment. The Trial Chamber in reaching its verdict and sentence found that Krajisnik participated in a joint criminal enterprise whose objective was to ethnically recompose the territories under the control of the Bosnian Serb republic by drastically reducing the proportion of Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croats through the commission of various crimes. Krajisnik, who chose and was authorised to represent himself at the appeals stage, filed his notice of appeal on 12 February 2007. On 28 February 2008, the Appeals Chamber authorised Krajisnik to retain the services of attorney Alan Dershowitz to prepare a supplementary brief on his behalf on the subject of joint criminal enterprise which was filed on 7 April 2008. The Prosecution filed its response brief on 12 March 2008 and responded to the supplementary brief of Mr. Dershowitz on 25 April 2008. The registrar received Krajisnik's reply on 16 May 2008. Let me now briefly summarise Krajisnik's grounds of appeal. In his appeal, Krajisnik claims that his right to a fair trial was infringed by the Trial Chamber and by the Registry, that he was not represented by competent counsel at trial, and that the Trial Chamber was biased. He raises numerous challenges to the factual findings of the Trial Chamber denying in particular that he possessed and abused de facto executive power and authority and that he was informed about the committed crimes but did not investigate or punish them. He further submits that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that he was a member of a joint criminal enterprise and that he supported and advocated the commission of crimes against Muslims and Croats. He also challenges the Trial Chamber's reliance on certain testimonies and its findings on the creation, objectives and functioning of the Bosnian Serb authorities. The supplementary brief of Mr. Dershowitz raises three grounds of appeal, arguing that joint criminal enterprise is not a legitimate theory of liability, that the Trial Chamber erred in not requiring substantial contribution of Krajisnik to the joint criminal enterprise, and that joint criminal enterprise as applied to Krajisnik is an inconsistent and incoherent theory of liability. I will now turn to the Prosecution's appeal. The Prosecution filed its notice of appeal on 26 October 2006 and its appeal brief on 27 November 2006. Krajisnik and amicus curiae both responded on 12 February 2007. Prosecution replied to Krajisnik's response on 27 February 2007 and to amicus curiae's response on 22nd February 2007. The Prosecution raises a single ground of appeal arguing that the Trial Chamber abused its discretion by imposing a manifestly inadequate sentence. It requests the original sentence be substituted by a sentence of life imprisonment. Finally, I will briefly summarise the amicus curiae's grounds of appeal. Amicus curiae filed a notice of appeal on 8 June 2007 and an appeal brief on 31 August 2007. Prosecution responded on 14 September 2007 and amicus curiae replied on 26 September 2007. Amicus curiae raises the following grounds of appeal. I will just list them. Krajisnik was not accorded a fair trial, the Trial Chamber failed to provide a reasoned opinion, the Trial Chamber's conclusions on joint criminal enterprise were erroneous in law and in fact, the Trial Chamber erred in law and in fact in its findings on the crimes of deportation and of forcible transfer, the Trial Chamber erred in fact in its assessment of Krajisnik's hierarchical position, the Trial Chamber erred in fact in concluding that Krajisnik possessed the requisite mens rea to be convicted, the Trial Chamber erred in law by allowing the Prosecution to breach Rule 90(h)(2) with impunity, the Trial Chamber's approach to Krajisnik's evidence was wholly unreasonable, the Trial Chamber impermissibly accumulated convictions, and finally, that the sentence of 27 years imposed by the Trial Chamber is excessive and disproportionate. During this appeals hearing, the parties may argue the grounds of appeal in the order they consider most suitable for their presentation. However, I would urge the parties not just to repeat verbatim or summarise extensively what is in the briefs as the Court is aware of the briefs' contents and has studied them. I also wish to note in the schedule order of 18 July 2008, the Appeals Chamber has invited the Prosecution to address specific issues during this hearing, issues that do not have to be restated here now. This invitation is made, I want to stress, without prejudice to any matter the parties or the Appeals Chamber may wish to raise and in no way constitutes an expression of an opinion on the merits of the appeals. I would now like to recall the criteria applicable to errors of fact in law alleged on appeal. The appeal is not a trial de novo and the appellants must not merely repeat the case from the trial level. Rather, in accordance with Article 25 of the Statute, the appellants must limit their arguments to alleged errors of law which invalidate the decision or alleged errors of fact occasioning a miscarriage of justice. Additionally, it should be recalled that the appellants have an obligation to provide precise references to materials supporting their arguments on appeal. This hearing will proceed according to the Scheduling Order issued on 18 July 2008. Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Dershowitz will present their submissions this morning for one hour and 30 minutes, following 15 minutes pause they will continue their submission for 30 minutes. Afterwards, the Prosecution will present its response for one hour and after a pause continue its response for another hour. Mr. Krajisnik will then reply for 30 minutes. Then we will move to the lunch pause, and in afternoon we will continue according to the schedule. I will not repeat all the schedule as stated in the Scheduling Order. It will be most helpful to the Appeals Chamber if the parties could present their submissions in a precise and clear manner. I wish to remind the parties that the Judges may interrupt them at any time to ask questions or they may prefer to ask questions following each party's submission. At this point, I would like that we go into private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to state that in light of yesterday's decision pursuant to Rule 115 of the Rules and the admission of the statements of George Mano and Stefan Karganovic, any reference to these statements and to any question regarding the inadequacy of the appellant's representation at trial during the hearing today will be heard in private session. These documents are confidential, and any reference to them should be made in private session. So we move to private session when necessary. And of course, I wish to remind the parties that at any time parties or counsel refer to confidential materials -- other confidential materials, they should advise they are going to do so in order that we may go to private session for that purpose. Well, we can revert to public session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Having said this about the manner in which we will proceed today, I would like now to invite the appellant to present submissions in support of his appeal. Please, Mr. Krajisnik, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone present in the courtroom. As you are aware, I testified before this court for 40 days, because at the time when I arrived to The Hague Tribunal and to the Detention Unit I was convinced that I was not guilty, and I never questioned my intention to be subjected to testimony and to cross-examination on any issue arising out of the indictment. You received some material that I drew in goodwill. It is in English, and it's a chart, as I called it, references. I wanted to help you in understanding the case, and I wanted to respond in kind to the very proper conduct of the Prosecution lately. Even though they are my opponents they provided a lot of documents to me which I attached as exhibits. I would be happy to answer any of your questions because I think that this is how we will reach the truth in the best possible way. As I have said, I testified before this Court deeply convinced that I would prove the truth. Unfortunately, the Trial Chamber did not believe that I spoke the truth and the judgement reflected that. You will see from all of the documents, and I'm telling you that everything that I said during my testimony was reinforced in my appeals brief and corroborated by various exhibits which prove that what I said was how it was. Thanks to you and God I was given an opportunity to represent myself, and I would like to thank the Appeals Chamber for that even though it's difficult to represent oneself. It is a hard task, but as a result of that I managed to understand well the trial judgement so as to be able to analyse it and link it. Once you link all of the events, you come to a conclusion which is different than what the trial judgement says. You will see in my appeals brief that I used a method to respond to each finding in the judgement then show why that finding is not true. So I urge you -- I urge you -- or, rather, I will be happy if you put any questions to me. I am accused here of the gravest crimes that exist. Listening to you just now, I was horrified. It was so difficult to listen to what you said because these crimes are so grave and much evil resulted from them. It is my personal opinion that from the very beginning of my political work I was committed to preserving peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina and reaching an acceptable political solution. Since you gave me an opening, I won't spend much time speaking about the appeal. I have to tell you about the sequence of events which clearly indicate that I could not have been and was not a member of any JCE. You have a lot of evidence showing that in January 1991 we had a session of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whose president I was, where we decided to come up with a platform about what the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina should be, because we could see that Yugoslavia was about to fall apart. It was decided at that time that Bosnia needs to be decentralised and reorganised to ensure that it had as few responsibilities as possible at the level of Yugoslavia. Mr. Izetbegovic, who was the president of Presidency, was greeted with applause. I was proud because I saw that we would preserve the peace. Let me digress. My entire family and my ancestors always warned that Bosnia was a specific area and that every even minor conflict was remembered for many years afterwards and that everything needed to be done to prevent any conflict from arising. This is why we were happy that we had found this solution. The next solution came about one month afterwards. For different unforeseen circumstances the other side came up with a declaration on sovereignty, presenting a completely different solution whereby Bosnia was to secede and to no longer remain part of Yugoslavia. That was a shock to us, and we, the Serbian side, vetoed this document. The constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina provided for this possibility to veto a proposal if it went against vital national interests. So we said let's put it to the council and discuss it there and then find a solution. One month later, as we discussed it at the council, all three sides accepted the proposal and one month later, one of the sides came up with this new solution that the declaration would be accepted if the Serbian side agreed to it. And then in April, there was regionalisation. It was a political response. It was a political response of the Serbian side to unconstitutional behaviour of the opposing side. Then negotiations started and in July there was a historical agreement, as we called it, of the two largest sides, the Muslim side and the Serbian side. It was a time of celebration. People were hugging each other. They were happy that there would be no war. You will find an exhibit among the documents, KU81, reflecting the event where I addressed the public saying that there would be no war, that we have to nurture good neighbour relations. And all we wanted was to preserve the peace. The agreement was supposed to be signed and implemented. It wasn't in the interest of the Muslim side. No. Somebody suggested to them, and they gave up on that agreement during the very TV show where it was about to be proclaimed. And then in September there was another Assembly session that I presided over, and Mr. Izetbegovic took the floor and he said that we would talk to each other for 100 years if necessary only to preserve the peace. Nobody would threaten anybody else. And once again everybody was happy. Now we are covering the time period from my indictment. Everybody was saying, sure, we will discuss. We will talk among ourselves only to preserve the peace. And then in October once again they tried to push the declaration, and then Serbian side vetoed it. I concluded the session Assembly and then after that they voted on this platform on the declaration of independence. This is when it all went downhill. Then they said the Serbian Democratic Party, and that was the majority party representing the Serbian people, they said, "You don't have the mandate to represent all Serbs. There are other people voicing other concerns." And what did we say then? We say we would interview the people. We announced a referendum, and we said that the Serbs would express their will as was provided in the constitution. In order to know who gave what answers, the ballots containing these questions were of different colour reflecting different ethnicity. What happened afterwards? A warning was issued by the Serbian side to the Muslim side to go back to the constitutionally provided order because that was the greatest conflict between two leading sides, the Serbian side and the Muslim side, even though the Croatian side was a completely equal partner. After the referendum, the people decided that Bosnia should remain in Yugoslavia. I'm now speaking of the Serbian side and minority of Muslims and Croats. It was a negligible percentage. Following that, all of the regions pretended to be in existence where in fact they were not, and there came a request that we should verify the regions. And we did not verify them all the way up until somebody asked the Serbian side to recognise the independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. It wasn't possible for them to recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina until the constitution was changed, and the constitution could not be changed without the Serbian side which had one-third of the votes, and they needed a two-third majority. Then they out-voted the Serbian representatives in the parliament in order to accept this request. I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the Serbian side said, "We, our deputies, will form Serbian Assembly, and their only task will be to start operating when the vital interests of the Serbian people are in danger." That was the main task of the Serbian Assembly. The Serbian deputies left the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I demanded that I continue to preside over the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly, and I worked until the war erupted leading both Assemblies. I did not want the war to begin. People used to say, "If he leaves," meaning me, "the war would begin." There was a psychological kind of war. Then the war began or, rather, in the beginning of 1992, the Muslim side said that they would start on the path of independence and that there would be no going back. At that time, the republic of Serbian people from Bosnia and Herzegovina was established, and the negotiations had already started on the new organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What happened then? Mr. Cutileiro got involved, and they came up with a solution. I have to reiterate that once we were given this solution we were all very happy. You have evidence indicating that on the 25th of March, at the -- or, rather, just before the conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Muslim side came and said we had pretended all along. We did not want to participate in negotiations. We did not want this. And the whole system crashed. On the 27th of March, we held the Assembly, and we voted on the constitution, saying that there would be a solution there for the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 26th of January, we held a session of the Assembly, and there were many very reasonable deputies there, and I used my influence over them to force them to go into the joint Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The agreement had been reached and -- or, rather, had the agreement been reached the Serbs would have recognised independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. It would not have been a question. The only question was whether the Serbs would rule themselves or somebody else would rule them. And why were the Serbs afraid? We asked the Muslims to remain in Yugoslavia. We asked them that because they were the majority nation. We were afraid. We did not want to be a minority. And they said, "We cannot remain in Yugoslavia." They said, "Why don't you remain with us in Bosnia? You would receive your own unit." We said we wanted to have a territorial continuity, and they said, "You cannot have territorial continuity but you can exchange lands with other sides and then you would gain the territory you wanted, and you would have your own unit where you would have absolute or relative majority." And then everything was clear, all the way up until the beginning of the war when the referendum of independence was held. It was then that the incident in Sarajevo took place where the groom's father was killed in Sarajevo and demonstrations broke out and the war erupted in Sarajevo. There were only two things or, rather, three things that I did during the war. I was president of the parliament and I was a negotiator, and I was never a member of any Presidency. I said here hundreds of times that I was not a member of Presidency. They said I wasn't a de jure member but they said that I was a de facto one. I wasn't that either. There is not a single document saying that Momcilo Krajisnik was member of the Presidency. Nor did I have any competencies within the Presidency. And when this happened, when the war erupted, the shells were falling and exploding all over Sarajevo, and I went from Ilidza to Sarajevo to meet with Mr. Izetbegovic to find a political solution for Sarajevo because that was the key so we could continue discussing. And we agreed on finding the solution. I went back to Zabrdje. I did not have any further contacts with him, and then this was abused once again, saying that Momcilo Krajisnik wanted Sarajevo to be divided. So once again I was not a member of any JCE. I did everything in my power to find a political solution, and five years later, I participated in Dayton talks. We managed to ensure peace there. It wasn't perfect, but let other new generations now find better solutions. They said that I was a member of the JCE and that I worked on supporting the SDS in creating their organs and other organs. Gentlemen, I was not a candidate of the leadership of Republika Srpska or, rather, the SDS when the multi-party elections were organised. It was just a coincidence that I became president of the Assembly when the political life in Bosnia and Herzegovina became quite active. I was not a member of any board. I did not participate in any pre-election campaign events. One year later when I did become a member of the Main Board of the SDS, I took part in only three sessions of the Main Board that were combined with the Deputies Club. I did not take part in a single Executive Board of the SDS meeting. I was not involved in the personnel policy of the party. I studied management and organisation, and I knew that I could only perform the tasks for which I had been officially appointed. I did not take part in the government cabinet session when it was established on the 12th of May. I did not take part in any meetings of any Crisis Staff except for once when they came to visit. It was the Crisis Staff of Ilijas. And now people are saying, "You assisted the SDS." Well, the SDS had deputies in the parliament, that's true, but during the war the SDS froze its activities. I'm now speaking of the facts only. They said that I knew of certain crimes. Gentlemen, you have my appeals brief before me [as interpreted], and I said in my testimony that the Main Staff never informed me. I never issued any orders of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. You have evidence before you indicating that they had never sent any report to me. The same goes for MUP, the Ministry of the Interior. They had never sent any reports to me. I said that during my testimony, and now I corroborated that by various documents that I submitted to you. I never received any reports by any Crisis Staff. The judgement says that I had been informed by the members of the so-called JCE. Gentlemen, you have documents indicating that Mr. Karadzic and I sat at a press conference where we were told that there were no civilians in any gaols. Mrs. Plavsic said publicly in an interview that there were no civilians in any gaols. Mr. Djeric said the same that there were no civilians in prisons. Mr. Stanisic sent a request to inform whether there were any civilians in the prison. Mr. Mandic in his interview to the OTP said that Momcilo Krajisnik was never close to him until he was replaced and now they are linking me to these people. I didn't even know Arkan until 1995. Slobodan Milosevic exerted pressure on us saying you have to do this, you have to do that. And now they're claiming that I was in some JCE together with him. Now that I'm saying this, I'm remembering the following: They said that I gave a contribution to the JCE. You have an exhibit there. On the 18th of March, Momcilo Krajisnik called to arms. That's what they're saying. I as a member of the negotiating team simply conveyed what we had agreed upon with the Muslim side on the previous day, and I simply said it's better if we draw maps out in the field rather than in an office, but several words were dropped from this text and it was wrongly quoted, taken out of context implying that I called to arms. I used the word "separation" several times. Let me now reiterate that the only meaning of the word "separation" was what we had agreed upon with Cutileiro. What was the compromise that we reached? Bosnia was to be an independent state and we were to separate along the ethnic lines, the territorial lines, and we were to have our own constituent unit. You cannot have your own unit without a demarcation. This was later done in Dayton. And had we done it earlier through Cutileiro's plan, many more people would still have been alive, and I would have avoided this fate, and many other -- many more other people fared much worse than I did. What is being imputed to me here in the appeal, and you've seen that was that I was informed of crimes. You can see it in the appeal here. Not a single municipality from which the Muslims have left, and that's Bosanski Novi, Petrovac, Kljuic, Prnjavor, and all the rest. None of these municipalities had informed anyone from the leadership about that, myself included. You have Pasic Radojko, other witnesses. They all said we did not inform leadership about the departure of the Muslims. I just knew about the departures of Serbs because 15.000 Serbs from Sarajevo arrived in Pale and they were all happy to have remained alive and no one said that that was not true and they said fine. One has to flee from the war. And then when peace comes, like in any other war, everyone will go back to their own homes. I did not submit a resignation as speaker of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina hoping every day that a solution would be found at some conference. Once a solution is found, we will all go back and we will continue as things happened through the centuries. That did not happen. Different arguments are being taken into account here, arguments to prove that Krajisnik knew of certain matters. I'm just going to say one thing by way of an illustration. They asked me, "Do you know that Sarajevo was shelled on the 14th of May?" And I said I don't know. And "Do you know that on the 10th of June there was supposed to be another shelling?" And I said I don't know. And then they said, "Do you know that a big group of Muslims on the 14th of May were in Pele and exchanged?" And I said I don't know. And then they said, "Well, you don't know anything. How can you not know when that happened 100 metres away from your office and that's where the Muslims were and Sarajevo was below Pale?" And I said I really don't know. That's the only answer I gave and you have it there. I was not in Pale. And finally, on the 14th and 15th I attended the Assembly, and I was in Belgrade, and I did not know that when I was responding. And on the 10th of June it is certain that the Chamber would have ruled differently if they knew on the 10th of June, rather, that this witness was not telling the truth, rather than on the 9th of June a decision was made, Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, Djeric, Krajisnik, Mladic, saying that the use of artillery had to be stopped vis-a-vis Sarajevo. And now somebody decides that Sarajevo would not be shelled on the 9th and on the 10th, all of a sudden Mladic says somebody -- Sarajevo is going to be shelled, and the person who says that has a good reason to say it because he is responsible for that. There are other facts that you will see too. You will see that I objected to each and every fact that was presented there and you will see that I did not say anything by way of giving a mere statement. All of this is evidence, hard evidence, and I hope that this is going to portray a different picture from what is reflected in the judgement. Not to go into other crimes, but I would like to assure you that I know that whenever there was some indication of a crime, whenever I attended meetings, instructions were immediately given to investigate this, to see what this was all about and to punish the perpetrators. You will see in each and every one of these remarks that that was the case. I'm going to give an illustration of the Assembly from the 24th until the 26th of July that took place in Jahorina. That's when the MPs came. This was the first Assembly outside Banja Luka. And you know what? People were saying MPs were talking about hundreds of crimes, about the fact that the state was not functioning and they said to me what have -- and then they said to me here what did you do -- do about this? And I said, Well, I don't know. I went to a conference. I gave you evidence here. On the 28th of July there was a meeting of the government and this was on the agenda, the resolutions of the Assembly. They took measures, they sent a team to Banja Luka to investigate all of this and Karadzic gave an order because he was the Supreme Commander to disband the so-called special units from Novi Grad that were creating problems, and Mladic said the paramilitaries should be disbanded. Whereas the minister of the MUP was sent to Birac and Mr. Dukic had come from there and he said that he had replaced all the Muslims. They were all the Muslims who were judges there. I did not know about that when I testified. I did find out in the meantime and I've presented all of this to you so that you could see. They tell me that I had to know about things that I was informed of from international media and other media. Believe me, Judges, whatever I heard -- I mean, I hadn't heard of any one of these pieces of information, rather, I did not believe all of these things. They said Momcilo Krajisnik's father committed suicide because he renounced his son because he had left with the Chetniks. I heard that people were saying that lions were eating children in the zoo and that they were showing cemeteries saying that this is where Muslims were buried and it was actually Serbs. You would not believe the anti-propaganda at the time. I had to ask the people only who were in charge of different matters. You're talking about JCE here and I said has anything come out of this and they said no, no, nothing, and they said that publicly. I just listened to what was going on to the Serbs. That is the other thing I heard about. I did not hear about anything else. What I'm trying to say now is I am being cautioned, I mean we've split up our time and, you know, these lawyers are dangerous people so I really have to stick to what we agreed upon. They told me I was a powerful man. I did not know why I was powerful. I did not issue a single order. I could not carry anything out, so what kind of power can that be? When I sat there as a witness and as I was watching the Judges and watching you today, I realised why I was powerful. The person who is down there looking at the people down there, and I was the president of the parliament and that's the person who gives people the floor and reaches conclusions and so on, that person seems omnipotent. And then if this person Momcilo Krajisnik even attended negotiations, then he is really important. And I'm going to end on this note while giving this example: Once this lady came Mrs. Plavsic was the head the commissioner's office from Pale and then I had this delegation from Pale coming in saying, "There was a shelling of Pale and we don't want her on the school board." And they said, "What do you mean?" "Well, we don't want to have a school because a shell is going to fall here and then the children will be killed. Are you going to be held responsible for that?" Well, who is going to be responsible if for 500 years there is no school? So then I said call your parents and see whether they want to send their children to school on their own responsibility. They called the parents and all the parents said that the children should be sent to school, and there was no shelling ever after that. And then they say people would not go to see Krajisnik if he were not powerful and if he did not resolve their problems. Let me just end on this note, what the Prosecution presented yesterday, these references here. I would like to assure you all of this is in the English language so I could not understand it very well, but on the basis of what I did manage to understand, not a single one of those things is the result of a joint criminal enterprise. I'm just going to give you two illustrations: In Pale -- well, Pale I know about. Crncalo was a witness. He did not know that he had signed an agreement on property, that he should safeguard Serb property and that the Serbs should safeguard his property. He did not know that he was going to Sarajevo voluntarily and he did not say one of the basic things. The Muslims did not leave Pale because somebody had expelled them. Rather, they left because 60 Serbs had been killed a while before that, so they left through a gorge, having received the word of the Muslims that nothing would happen. However, they killed them nevertheless. So they were scared. So they wanted to leave. You have proof of the fact that I did not know that the Muslims had left. The session on the 26th of July, you have a statement to the effect that Muslims are still there at Pale on that day because we all thought that that's the way it was, and -- but this was all the result of what the local authorities did. Another thing that I am going to end on, Bijeljina is the first element in the JCE. That's what they say. Gentlemen, on the 27th of March we have a session. That is only a question of three days. At this session we say we need peace. We have to preserve peace. This is our Assembly saying this. War is not a good thing. Again we will have to negotiate, and there was no plan whatsoever. What was stated publicly, and you have this by way of evidence, before this there was a conflict in Brod and before that in Kupres when the Serbs were attacked. In Bijeljina, there was no reason for the Serbs to attack the Muslims. The Serbs held power in their hands 100 per cent. That is to say they did not have to have a takeover. It was a conflict among people locally. No one knew about this. I was in parliament in my office, the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I did in the know that this was going on. I testified about that here and I asked the person over the telephone, I said, "You are interested in what you are liberating, but if you cannot help us do not do anything to unhelp us." I will have another occasion to address you. Once again, I thank you for your patience and I hope that I did not take too much time from my lawyers. I gave them a lot of time, but then I see that once I get talking, I even have to omit certain things without mentioning them. Thank you once again. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: May it please the Chamber, my name is Nathan Dershowitz and I appreciate the opportunity to share the argument with both the defendant and my brother Alan Dershowitz. The overall problem with the decision below is that it conflates three different concepts into one. The first is the political arguments, views and actions that had been taken to establish a separate Bosnian Serb republic within Bosnia-Herzegovina. We have heard extensive testimony just now, and if you read the record, what is crystal clear is that Mr. Krajisnik was the principal person responsible for seeking to implement the negotiator, the spokesperson, the leader in that sense of the activities in order to arrive at a peaceful solution. There were numerous problems, and I'll go through that in a moment, but you have to separate that which was said politically, that which was sought to be accomplished through negotiations and discussions with two other areas of concern. The second area of concern is the actual war that subsequently took place. There is a third area and technically the only area that should be of concern to this Tribunal and to the Chamber below, and that is by definition the war crimes which by definition are violations of laws or customs of war. So you have three separate categories, and the decision below, and I invite the Court recognising these distinctions to review the decision below because you will see that Mr. Krajisnik has been convicted on the basis of statements that he made that were political statements articulating views as a representative of a position that was being asserted that was totally, completely legitimate. A tribunal to adjudicate who is responsible for violations of international humanitarian law must make this distinction between these matters as clearly as humanly possible. I recognise that it is an extraordinarily difficult task, but it is an essential task. It is the essential task to distinguish between those who articulate politically acceptable views, even politically unacceptable views, and then those who engage in war and then those who engage in war crimes. Here the way the JCE was used eliminated the distinctions, and if you read the decision, you will see that the efforts to create a separate Serbian-Bosnian republic resulted in people being declared to be war criminals. The result in the instant case is in direct conflict with the report of the Secretary-General accompanying the statute and the language and objective of the statute. Though eschewing guilt by association, the Trial Chamber below's decision when carefully reviewed demonstrates that there was guilt by association for those who espoused a political view, those who carried out the war and those who committed war crimes. There is no question that Mr. Krajisnik was a strong, vocal advocate for protecting Serbian interests and sought to avoid Serbia being a powerless minority within a separate country of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is further no doubt from this record that he was a or the principal negotiator seeking to establish that position. What is seriously in doubt, what is not only unclear but inconsistent with the -- internally within the decision below, is any indication that Mr. Krajisnik had the common objective to carry out violations of the statute, the permanent removal by force of Bosnian and Muslim -- Croats and Muslims, and that they participated during the indictment period in any criminal acts to effectuate the common criminal goal. JCE and its lack of clarity as to what these elements are must be established to find culpability. This is the heart and soul of this case. It is a question as to whether you find people being war criminals who engage in political advocacy and were vocal in support of a position that they had every right to articulate. In fact, if their positions had been suppressed, that would be a violation of human rights. They had absolute right to articulate those views. They even had the right to exaggerate the efforts that they were seeking to -- that which they were seeking to secure in order to posture for purposes of carrying out their objectives, and that is completely lost by this decision below. The problem which started with the Tadic decision has now reached a point where the elements are so elastic and unclear that they virtually have no meaning. Moreover and equally dangerous and what is the heart and soul of this case is that the concepts now criminalise those who are engaging in legitimate protected behaviour that we should be encouraging, not discouraging. There are numerous fundamental problems with the Tadic decision, and I will not seek to relitigate those questions at the present time, but I think it's clear if you look at the precursor to Tadic and Tadic itself, the case that Judges Cassese and Mumba in Furundzija started, they had a very, very limited concept. In the preliminary case, the one that was decided in 1998, which was the first case to discuss a common -- a common enterprise or common objective, you had one person seeking to secure information through interrogation of a victim while at the same time another person with him was actually committing the -- the abuse, the physical violence, and the rape. A decision had been made that you can find the person who is seeking the information as part of this, that person was engaged in a common enterprise with the person who was actually committing the crime. There was an acquittal, by the way, on rape charge on that case. That concept of two people carrying out the act together, the actus reus in that situation is so far removed from the concept as it is presently applied that one could not recognise that concept in those earlier cases. The same thing is true in Tadic. The Court first made the preliminary determination that Tadic was a part of the group of people that actually committed the atrocities, but they could not point to him specifically as a person who shot someone. It does not take a grave extension of actual participation to find when five people go into a town and people are killed in that town by that group, by that group, that all five people are responsible. That again is so far removed from the way it is being used in this case that it is non-recognisable. The core problem --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down for the purposes of interpretation. Thank you. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: The core problem with Tadic is that there was a desire to look for theories in order to justify what was stated in that decision as being the legitimate objective, and that is a recognition that under international law all participants in serious violations of international law could and should be found responsible for the acts that they committed. The Tribunal went so far as to suggest that it not only had the right but it had an obligation to find a theory to justify that. More recent decisions by this Tribunal have recognised that it is inappropriate for the Tribunal to be the entity that establishes policy, but it is being blind to reality not to recognise that when you're dealing with levels of culpability, who is responsible, who is to be punished, that you are dealing in policy and that there is a continuum, a line has to be drawn on the continuum as to who we hold culpable. That is a policy decision that is -- normally occurs by a statutory grant of power. When you use phrases which are so elastic as have been used in this JCE, you have lost all concept of original accountability and knowledge that you are committing or potentially committing a crime. In this complex world with -- with complex historic and ethnic and religious clashes, it is essential that the core principles of international culpability be capable of being articulated before a person is charged and not after. The problem in the instant case is that not only were these principles not articulated before, but after reviewing the decision below and the positions of the Prosecutor, there is a lack of clarity on all basic elements of JCE. And more disturbing, once the elements were articulated in the decision with some degree of clarity, the facts contained in the opinion do not support the Chamber's conclusion of culpability. Let me be very specific. In paragraph 883, the Chamber below articulates the elements of JCE. What's interesting just as an aside is you can look at that articulation if you go through many of the decisions by Trial Chambers and by this Court, you will see different formulations of the same principles of JCE. If you review the Prosecutor's presentation, there are slightly different articulations of JCE, but the degree of modification becomes essential to an understanding. Had there been a statutory grant, you would look at the words of the statute, but when you have case law development, there is a tendency to expand and extrapolate constantly on the concepts. The first concept as stated by the Trial Chamber: "A joint criminal enterprise exists when a plurality of persons participate in the realisation of a common criminal objective." I would suggest that that language would seem to be relatively easy to apply in a factual context, but the reality is anything but in terms of this case. Let me deal with the two ends or the three ends of that problem. If you begin with the -- I guess it's the indictment itself. The indictment in this case is so over-broad as to be unbelievable in terms of its description. Let me read you paragraph 7. The indictment says: "Numerous individuals --" now bear in mind where the history of JCE began, with participants who we knew, participants who were present, participants who engaged in the activity but participants who may not have been actually the physical hitter but clearly a participant, holding someone or interrogating someone while someone else assaults them is clearly a participant. But let's see what's charged in this case as compared. It says: "Numerous individuals participated in this joint criminal enterprise. Each participant by act or omission contributed to achieving the objectives of the enterprise." And then it lists the defendants and it says, "they worked in concert." I think "worked in concert" is conspiracy law. No one wants to call it conspiracy because conspiracy is a substantive crime, and if you were to acknowledge that it's a conspiracy, you would clearly be violating the statutory provisions. But then it says: "With other members of the joint criminal enterprise including," then it lists a few names. It then says: "... and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership at the republic, regional and municipal levels, members of the SDS leadership of the republic, regional municipal levels, members of the Yugoslavian People's Army, the Yugoslav army, the army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," and it then says -- I'm skipping parts, "the Bosnian Serb Territorial Defence, the Bosnian Serb police, members of the Serbian and Bosnian Serb paramilitary forces, and volunteer units and military figures, political figures from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the republic of Serbia, and the Republic of Montenegro." I think I'm the only one not included in that general category. It is an overwhelmingly expansive category including everyone who in any way supported the Serbian point of view. Not the war, anyone who was supportive of a Serbian point of view. You then had in the decision a listing of names of people who were then added at the end of the case as the specific people who may have been members of the JCE. Then the concern that was addressed in the Brdjanin case and addressed by this Tribunal in its July 18th Scheduling Order then comes into effect. And what I mean is that's the other end of the equation with respect to the persons. And you have starting off a clear indication as to who are the members of the JCE. You had the question which the Tribunal resolved as to whether those who actually commit the crimes on the ground have to be members of the JCE, and the answer was "not necessarily," but you must show the link, the direct link between a member of the JCE and then the person who actually perpetrated the crime. So if you have three or four members of the JCE all agreeing and one undertakes the task of then retaining someone, hiring someone, persuading someone, securing someone to actually commit the crime on the ground, you have the necessary linkage. What has occurred in this case is absolutely the opposite conceptually, and that is you start off with a group of people, and I'll get to the common objective, but just the persons, a group of people, then anyone who engages in any activity suddenly becomes a member of the JCE, and then anyone who then directs anyone to commit a war crime is by definition made a member of the JCE. That's what occurred here. It is so far removed from what was contemplated by the Judges in Tadic that I suggest it is a totally different concept unrelated to the original concept, but if you allow it to expand as it does, you are engaging in charging people solely by guilt by association. My brother Alan will address in more detail the problem that relates to when you do that and how it applies in an international setting. But if you go then to the second element that's listed in the -- in the decision as necessary in order to prove that someone is a member of the JCE, you run into at least the same if not worse problems. It says: "The common objective, the first form of JCE exists --" let me just digress for one second, and that is they talk about the forms of JCE, I and III. The only one that's really discussed in this opinion is JCE I, and in the most recent submission, now the Prosecutors are claiming JCE III. When you cannot even tell which concept of JCE is in a 400-page decision and a finding of liability, you are obviously inviting a disaster, and that's what occurred in this situation. But going back to the quote it says: "The first form of JCE existed with a common objective amounts to or involves the commission of a crime provided for in the statute." I suggest that if you look at the indictment here, the decision suggests clearly that the joint criminal enterprise must be a stated statutory crime. The common objective has to be a state -- stated statutory crime. I should say that the Prosecutor in its submission, and I refer the Tribunal to paragraphs 35, 36, and 37, even on that simple item there is confusion. They cannot -- you cannot tell from the submissions that have been made here as to whether the objective has to be -- the objective, not the means, whether the objective has to be a statutory crime or whether the means can be the statutory crime. They float back and forth. But the way the decision is written, it is clear that the crime, that the objective must be a statutory crime, but the way the indictment reads here, it says: "The permanent removal by force or other means." That added language is very, very important for the present situation, because it is indisputable that Mr. Krajisnik, through his negotiations and other efforts, was seeking to work out a solution where there would be voluntary, consensual, constitutionally derived methods of transferring populations if the populations chose to. When you set up a separate entity within the context of Bosnia-Herzegovina, people will not be comfortable if there is a majority Muslim population in one area and a Serbian population in the other. There is a radical difference. One is a war crime, and one is a political solution, and the indictment here charges both the war crime and the political solution as being part of the common objective. In addition, if you look at the precursor provisions in the decision and if you listen to Mr. Krajisnik, there is again no doubt he was seeking a political solution to a highly charged setting in which there was a history, a history of whether one wants to talk about months, years or 500 years, there was an underlying history there. There was a lot of tension there. And when you were seeking a solution, he was seeking a non-criminal solution. Certainly not a war crimes solution. And to confuse the two, and again I plead with the Tribunal, read the decision recognising the three different categories. Look at the evidence that was cited throughout as to Mr. Krajisnik's personal involvement and you will see that every comment that he made was directed towards a determination that he was supportive of having some security for the Serbians that were living in Bosnia-Herzegovina. One suggestion early on was they become members of Yugoslavia, of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Another one is that there is a connection to Serbia, of the Serbs, and the Croatians to Croatia. And another one which was the political discussion that was taking place was that you then take within Bosnia-Herzegovina a subsection which then is a recognised unit but unit within the government, which is in fact what happened as a result of the Dayton Accords. The solution that he was politically advocating is what ultimately occurred later on, and you have a gap in the evidence, particularly a gap in the evidence with respect to the relevant period of time. And to the extent that you have him making assertions that if we have a conceptual agreement that we will have a boundary for Bosnia, for Serbia, the Serb republic, you have a political determination, it is more effective for purposes of a political solution if you actually start, once there was a declaration of independence by Bosnia and Serbia, to actually start having municipalities in place on the ground. That is a factually correct statement. It's a political position. It is a position that every negotiator will take, and there is nothing in that statement which leads one to believe that if he took that position, he is advocating he is part of a group seeking to have a -- a solution -- seeking to engage in the war crimes. Similarly, the decision suggests that all co-perpetrators must be acting pursuant to the common design and have the same criminal intent, and that is the heart and soul of the question. There is no evidence that he had the criminal intent to permanently remove by force the Muslim population. Yes, he had the intent, the objective, the goal of having a Serbian municipality of some type established legitimately by constitutional means as he has expressed throughout. The third element in the decision, which is also subject to extreme confusion, the decision says: "Participation of the accused, this is achieved by the accused's commission of a crime forming part of the common objective and provided for in the statute." So he had to be a part of the desire, the objective, a part of a -- a participant in the permanent removal by force. There is no evidence of that. It says: "Alternatively, instead of committing the intended crime as a principal perpetrator the accused's conduct may satisfy this element if it involves procuring or giving assistance to the execution of the crime forming part of the common objective." And I would request that the Tribunal inquire of the Prosecutors as to what evidence there is to satisfy this action which is required, and again you will see conclusory statements. Those conclusory statements are all based upon his personal political assertions of the political position which was acceptable, which is allowable, which is to be encouraged under the circumstances. The other core problem that occurs, and I invite the Tribunal -- I can go through many of the statements that are made by the Prosecutors. If you look at them carefully, as I have done, you will see a general statement, a citation to the decision. The decision citation will then be to something which doesn't quite say that, and what it does say is in the early period prior to the outbreak of the hostilities those were the political assertions that he was making in that context, and they have to be looked at with care. As I repeatedly have -- have asserted, you cannot, you cannot have a determination made that if someone is engaged in a politically acceptable conclusion and then others later carry out a similar objective but in a totally illegal way that the person who articulated the initial political position is responsible and has joined in in order to engage in the illegal activity that subsequently takes place. What I'd like to do at this point is turn the floor over to my esteemed colleague, brethren at the bar and brother to proceed unless there are any questions to be asked of me as to the part of the presentation that I have just made. Thank you very much. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you, Your Honours. May it please the Court, it is a great personal privilege and honour for my addressing this august body. It's been a lifetime dream of mine to be able to participate in the work of a great and distinguished international tribunal and I appreciate the Court's permitting me to participate in this argument, even in the limited presentation that I intend to make about joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please keep interpretation in mind. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: [Previous translation continues] ... acceptance that there is no mention of joint criminal enterprise in the statute that bestows the authority on this distinguished Court. This is in contrast to the Rome Statute, for example, which does provide for specific liability based on the act of working in concert with others to a joint goal. Now, if one looks at the report of the Secretary-General, which my brother referred to in another context, which is part of the legislative history of the statute that is the jurisdictional basis for this Court's work, it states that: "In the view of the Secretary-General, the application of the principle nullum crimen sine lege requires that the international tribunal should apply rules of international humanitarian law which are beyond any doubt part of customary law so that the problem of adherence to some but not all states to specific conventions does not arise." I don't think there is any dispute here today that the JCE concept is not, is not beyond any doubt part of customary international law. There is grave, grave doubt, grave doubt. The academic community is bitterly divided over this issue. We have cited articles which include within them citations to other articles which raise grave doubt about whether the entire concept of JCE is acceptable in international law. Now, we know, we recognise, we acknowledge that this Appellate Chamber has repeatedly said it would not revisit the issue of the appropriateness of JCE. Nonetheless, we feel an obligation to our client and to the law to persist in our objection. We believe that the idea of constructing a new basis of liability violates the very principle that the Secretary-General talked about. We believe that the defendant in this case could not have known during the period of indictment that he would be subject to a JCE indictment. Now, the Court, of course, has been very careful to say that joint criminal enterprise is not the creation of a new crime. It is simply the articulation of an acceptable principle of criminal liability. But functionally, of course, it is a new crime. It is like conspiracy. It is like RICO. It is like so many of the other constructs of joint liability, and it is like what appears in the Rome Statute, yet all of those are statutorily authorised crimes or statutorily authorised bases for criminal liability. This is the first time in our knowledge that what looks like a crime, sounds like a crime, has all the criteria of criminality, has been articulated by a Court in the absence of a clear statutory basis. Because we recognise that this Court has said it would not revisit the issue of joint criminal enterprise, we obviously have as our principal argument to make today to this Court while reserving the argument that I have just briefly articulated and that is expressed in our brief in further detail, we do argue that JCE, even if permissible as a matter of general law, and as my brother argued even if permissibly applicable to the other cases, like the interrogation rape case which, by the way, could have been resolved, without introducing JCE as any principle of law. A person who conducts an interrogation while other one is beating a suspect is a principal. There is absolutely no doubt that you can convict under ordinary principles of criminal law a person who is in such close intimate connection. I would say the same thing was probably true about the Tadic case. This case is very different, and we argue that JCE, even if proper, cannot be applied to Mr. Krajisnik's activities even under the Trial Court's findings of fact which we dispute and -- I'm sorry. I'm speaking too quickly and I will slow down. We dispute the findings of fact. We certainly agree with Mr. Krajisnik's presentation. We appreciate the Court's ruling yesterday which we only got literally at the close of business that we are entitled to interview Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and I can represent to this Court on the basis of a brief contact that I did have with Dr. Karadzic that he will in fact be providing very significant exculpatory evidence, that we will satisfy the Court's obligation to present that evidence within the appropriate period of time. I must also add something, and I'm sorry for this, but we did not get the Court's ruling on the Rule 115 judgement, 54-page ruling until the close of business yesterday on my Blackberry. We have not seen it. It has not yet been given to us in person and so we argue here under a burden of not knowing the content of the Rule 115 judgement. We understand the Court's restrictions on what we are to say publically and we will, of course, completely abide by that. Having said that, I must add again that without faulting anybody else it's the fault of communication and technology that we had a representation from the Prosecution's office --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. You're saying that you did not receive the decision, the Rule 115. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Should have been given to you actually. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It was sent on my Blackberry at about 7.00 p.m. last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's correct. It was signed about that time. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: And we had no access to it. We tried --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Do we have hard copies here? MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: -- as best we could. Thank you so much, and we will read it during the recess. The other document we did not receive, and again I don't fault anybody, is the Prosecution made a representation that they would within 48 hours of the argument present us with the list of material and response to the Court's order of the nexus issue that was discussed previously. I never received that and received on my Blackberry at about 9.30 last night a revised list. So we do not have the original list, but I will not allow that to interfere with the general argument that we're making here. I just want to reiterate that without accepting any of the findings below, particularly the findings that are disputed by our client, for purposes of this appeal, just for purposes of this appeal, even if everything found by the Trial Chamber is credited, every single fact credited, our position is that those facts do not give rise to appropriate joint criminal enterprise liability, and from this point on, I will assume the accuracy of the Trial Chamber's findings though we dispute them and will continue to dispute them for purposes of Rule 115. Now, I think it's very important to note that the trial findings below include a finding that Mr. Krajisnik was not a principal perpetrator. He was not a principal perpetrator. That is, he did not commit any of the actus reuses that are specified in the statute itself, in Article 7(1). It is also important to note that the Court made a finding, and this appears on page 402, that in relation to effective control, that the evidence does not demonstrate that Mr. Krajisnik himself had effective control over these bodies, meaning Bosnian Serb political and governmental organs, Bosnian Serb forces which participated in or facilitated the commission of crimes identified in the indictment. What the Court finds below, and it appears particularly in paragraph 1120 under the heading of Mr. Krajisnik's contributions, were that the accused's overall contribution to the JCE was to help establish and perpetrate the SDS party and state structures that were instrumental to the commission of the crimes and that he also deployed his political skills, both locally and internationally, to facilitate the implementation of the JCE's common objectives through the crimes envisioned by that objective. And it's very important, as my brother mentioned, that there is tremendous lack of clarity as to whether or not our client was convicted based on the first principle of JCE liability or the third principle. The Court seems to suggest that it was only based on the first category, yet the Prosecution in its reply to our brief says, citing several paragraphs, that it was based on category 3 as well. We've read those paragraphs. We do not see in those paragraphs any clear conclusion that category 3 JCE liability was found. The main issue that we think is lacking in this case is simply the absence of an actus reus. Before we get to mens rea, we respectfully challenge the Prosecution finally to tell us what is the actus reus that was required and was committed by the defendant in this case. What we have is a very important set of distinctions here. What did Mr. Krajisnik personally do that constituted the actus reus as distinguished from the mens rea of the crime. We know, because the opinion say so and because the indictment says so and because the Prosecution has said so, that he did not personally commit war crimes. That could be one possible actus reus, the commission of war crimes. We know that he is not charged with committing ordinary crimes. He didn't engage in looting or burglary or rape or murder. We know that he's not charged with committing neutral conduct. For example, waging a lawful war. What he is accused of is completely characterised accurately by political speech and political activity. This is the first case to our knowledge in any International Tribunal where we have a defendant's actus reus completely based on constitutionally protected and human rights protected conduct. As my brother put it, I think, very, very well, had a state tried to prevent Mr. Krajisnik from making the speeches that formed the basis for the criminal liability here, that state itself would have been violating norms of international law. What he did was make speeches. What he did was, according to the indictment but we dispute it, helped to create a political party. And of course, this Court has recognised that it cannot under the statute make it a crime to be a member of a political party, make it a crime to be a member of a criminal organisation. That could be a basis of potential liability under a statute that set that out. This statute does not do that. It does not do what the Nuremberg trials did and that is create liability from membership in the Nazi party, member in the Gestapo, membership in, et cetera. So the membership in the SDS could not -- or even organising it could not be a basis for independent liability. And when you get a situation where the actus reus of the crime are speeches, political kills, the Court says very, very clearly one of the bases, the actus reus is he also deployed his political skills, deployed political skills. Clearly, clearly protected conduct. And stating negotiating positions, even strong negotiations positions. If one were to go back and look at the negotiating positions stated during the India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, various crises, Cyprus, various African conflicts, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, one finds as part of negotiating positions, statements very much akin to the statements that are alleged here to be the actus reuses of the crime. I must reiterate again that the defendant is not charged with having personally committed any of the actus reuses specified in Article 7(1). He is not accused of having planned, he is not accused of having instigates, he is not accused of having ordered, he is not accused of having committed except through the vehicle of joint criminal enterprise liability. The Court says defendant's contribution does not have to be substantial and that's part of the jurisprudence of this Court. Again, we think a serious error that to allow joint criminal enterprise liability without a substantial contribution. The Court says it need not be a necessary contribution. All it need be is significant. Now here's the crucial point that there is no finding on below. Significant sounds like a quantitative judgement. That is, there has to be enough. So one speech might not do, two speeches, three speeches. It has to be significant. Substantial would also suggest some quantitative contribution. What the Court never discusses is the qualitative nature of the contribution. Can the contribution be entirely political speeches? Can the contribution be entirely political negotiations? Can the contribution consist entirely of protected conduct under international law? The Trial Chamber implicitly by its verdict concludes that the answer to that question is yes, but nowhere in the decision does the Trial Chamber discuss or consider the implications of that decision, the implications of allowing protected political speech and political activity to become the actus reus for a crime of human rights violations or a war crime. For example, if one thinks about the implications of this decision, would it include lawyers? Could lawyers who provided legal services to Mr. Krajisnik during the course of the indictment or lawyers that helped formulate some of the legal presentations but who did it as part of a goal that was shared by the other members of the joint criminal enterprise, could lawyers contribute substantially? Could the activity of lawyers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sorry, can you slow down. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: I'm sorry again. I apologise to the Court. I'm not used to speaking with a translator, and I will try my best. And please don't hesitate to slow me down at any point if I go too quickly. There is a case in Canada recently where there was some suggestion that lawyers providing support for a group which ultimately was found to include terrorists could be subjected to some kind of liability. There's a case in New York where a lawyer has been imprisoned for that kind of work. What about financial contributors, people who provide financial support or religious support? What about activists who provide political support and political organising skills? The idea that without clear criteria this kind of activity could become the basis for crimes against humanity has a tremendous deterrent effect, freezing, chilling effect on legitimate political speech and political activity. People in situations of the kind that were faced by the Serbs after the declaration of independence would not be able to read this decision and decide precisely where the line was. And when you don't know where the line is, any cautious, prudent person moves further and further away from the line. Now, if the conduct is criminal conduct or even neutral conduct, there is no harm done in having people act prudently. If you don't know what your tax obligations are, big deal, Your Honours, just pay more taxes or don't go close to the line. There is no protected aspect to paying less taxes. There is no protected aspect to committing ordinary crimes like robbery or looting. But when we're talking about political activity, when we're talking about speeches, when we're talking about negotiations, when we're talking about forming political parties, we -- the law should never be in a position where it chills or deters legitimate political activities. And what is gravely lacking in the opinion of the Chamber below, the Trial Chamber, is any recognition, even acknowledgement, that it was moving into territory that is unknown and extremely dangerous. That is, moving from situations where people are beating each other up, where people are shooting each other at close range, where people are engaged in acts of the kind that were committed during the Holocaust or of the kind committed by the Japanese or others that are physical in nature to speech and to political activity. There's no recognition in the decision of the conflict. There's no recognition that this is the first case, that I know of at least, where there is a conflict between protected human rights of the defendant, speech, political skills, and of all other defendants similarly situated and the protected human rights of victims. In this case, there is a clear conflict. It has to be resolved. The Court below resolved it without recognising it, without acknowledging it, without, with due respect, understanding that it was creating a decision with broad implications for political conduct by political leaders similarly situated to our client in this case. And we believe that as the result of that, it failed to understand the implications of the decision for many current conflicts. The implications of the decision obviously for past conflicts, the implications for the war against terrorism, to use the term that is employed by many countries, are very, very grave indeed. Terrorist groups operate within many countries including this one and including my own country. They are often supported by broad networks of supporters. You have concentric circles moving all around, the actual terrorists themselves, those perhaps religious and political leaders who support the terrorism, those who provide financial support. In my country alone, based on a criminal statute, a conspiracy and RICO statute, we have had now more than a dozen criminal prosecutions which have been extremely broad in their application. Many of them have resulted in acquittals because the indictments have been too broad. Do you indict a professor from the University of Florida who has made speeches supporting terrorism and some of the speeches have been used in fundraising activities on behalf of terrorism? Do you include within the range of joint criminal enterprise rabbis or ministers or preachers or imams who might share the goals and talk from a religious perspective about the goals but don't talk about the means toward that goal? I don't mean only to include in this context current debates about terrorism but in my country you have priests talking about blocking abortion clinics and abortion centres and there have been grave issues that revolve around how far to extend the liability. During the Northern Ireland-British conflict there were grave questions about how broad and how far the issues may range for purposes of joint criminal responsibility. And I know we are coming close to the time when we have to take our recess, so I simply wanted to end this part of my presentation with the Court's approval by urging the Court, please, as my brother has done, to go back and read the citations of the Prosecution, because the Prosecution, without again making any accusations, has wrenched out of context words spoken by Mr. Krajisnik that are political in nature. And if the court were to review the actual speeches, the time that they were made, some videotapes of speeches around that period of time. Review the fact that they were made while he was in the position as a speaker where he had to accept and be polite to everybody who appeared as other speakers, I think one will find a very, very different view of the context and the political nature of the speeches that were made than appears either in the Prosecution's brief or in the arguments that are made in support of the judgement by the Court below. This case presents this Court with a remarkable opportunity to do what Professor Cassese in his capacity as professor has suggested in recent articles, what other distinguished professors from Stanford and Vanderbilt and others have said as well, and that is without necessarily reconsidering the jurisprudence of JCE to impose very clear lines, the kind that a legislature would have done had there been legislative determination, traditional legislative determination, you would have hearings, you would have reports, you would have consideration of where the line should be drawn. You'd have people testifying on one side or the other. What will this do to the political views, to the political implications? This Court has not had the benefit of that. Even in the Tadic case the issue was not briefed. The issue was really briefed on other grounds, and most of the briefs that have been submitted in subsequent cases the issues have been briefed, but in the early cases it was almost taken for granted that JCE liability is appropriate, and we think this provides the Court with a unique opportunity to draw the line and to require as actus reus crimes themselves, to require criminal conduct, independent criminal conduct where the government can point to as the actus reuses, this is a crime, this is unprotected conduct and now we move toward seeing whether or not it imposes joint criminal enterprise liability. I thank the Court very much. The time has come to take our recess, and I will continue my argument after the recess, and we will accept -- hope to hear some questions after the recess if there are any from the Chamber. Thank you very much, Your Honour. I apologise for speaking so quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Indeed it's time to break. There maybe some questions after the recess. We break for 15 minutes, and the hearing will be resumed at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So we resume our hearing. I understand that Judge Meron wants to put a question now to the Defence, please. He has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, President. This is a question to the Dershowitz brothers. As you may know from my dissent in the Media case. I am sensitive to the argument you made about protected political speech, but I will expect the Prosecutor later to deal with that, and I will direct some questions to the Prosecutor on that, not to you. At the moment I would like to raise with you, Mr. Dershowitz, a technical point regarding JCE. Assuming for the purposes of the argument this morning (a) that there was a JCE and (b), that Mr. Krajisnik was a member of the JCE, as you know, the Appeals Chamber in the Brdjanin case, the Brdjanin judgement, articulates the links that must be established between crimes committed by non-JCE members and the actual JCE members. To you what extent do you argue that such proper links have not been established, and if they have not been established, which portions of the trial judgement would be invalidated as a result? MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I would like to defer on that question to my brother who is better educated than me having attended NYU Law School.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: That's a good beginning. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: The core problem is the way this case proceeded it becomes impossible for the Prosecutor today, or improper for the Prosecutor today to retroactively seek to go through the record to try to justify the linkage.
