What I think is essential under the decision in Brdjanin is that you first start in any analysis with an indication of who are the members of the JCE. Then you have to identify, assuming you're going through linkage to those who are not perpetrators, you then have to identify the member of the JCE, and then what you have to do is demonstrate the direct, direct, connection to the action that was undertaken. And that should be the charge so that you can defend against it. What they've done here is impossible to defend against, because what happens is it's such a vague open-ended description of who are members of the JCE. Then they add members of the JCE on the basis of the activities that took place, and then they try to make the link. So it's exactly the opposite of what I think was the concern in Brdjanin if you start with actual perpetrators, because what you're doing is by definition almost you are saying a -- what they are saying is an act occurred which is a war crime. Whoever suggested it must have been a member of the JCE, therefore, you then connect it back up to the original JCE. And that is backwards, inappropriate, and, you know, also in our situation the Court -- again the Chamber's decision is somewhat inconsistent with a number of opinions by -- by this Tribunal and the positions taken by the Prosecutor is to some extent inconsistent with both of those, but the way it is described in the decision there is a need to have the JCE membership agreement or non-agreement but joining prior to, prior to, any act occurring so that the date here must be under the judgement prior to April of 1992. So it becomes very important for the Prosecutors to be able to demonstrate a joining or the JCE establishment prior to 1992. Now, maybe you can join it later, but then you have to demonstrate something to establish it, but they use the date of April 1992 as the date where there is an agreement to commit the war crimes. And the statute -- the statutory division has to be connected according to the judgement to -- there has to be a joint enterprise to commit the statutory crime that has to have occurred in April of 1992. So to answer your direct question, I think it's too late for them to do that. I think if you take the logic of where the progression has gone instead of having a logical next-step progression, they have now reached way beyond and are trying to work backwards to justify, which is inherently an inappropriate method of proceeding with a criminal charge. Anything further, or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer, Mr. Dershowitz, but my -- the focus of my question was specifically whether in your view the Trial Court established that -- found that links have been established between crimes committed by non-JCE members and actual JCE members. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: And I'm suggesting there was none. There are a couple of paragraphs, but those paragraphs are ad hoc additions that were made which is inappropriate and they still do not connect up, but that individual who is now supposed to be a member of the JCE add -- added post hoc because of something that happened without any dates, times or other things and then they make him a member of the original JCE as opposed to starting with who are the members of the JCE, identifying what he did or she did to carry out the JCE, and then seeking to get the link. I think it's paragraph 1006. I have the paragraphs that are particularly defective in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And if links have not been established, what is the impact on that, on the validity of the judgement? MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: I think the whole judgement must be set aside without any question, because there is a concession that he was not a perpetrator of any of the acts. Therefore, if he is not a perpetrator of the criminal acts and there is no link, the judgement must be set aside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I will not pursue that, but if you look at paragraphs 299, 300 of the trial judgement, you'll see there a reference to some crimes which were committed by JCE members. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: But again, Your Honour, I believe -- let me -- I would have to check, Your Honour, as to whether those provisions -- you've been receiving an indication as to deficiencies within the judgement, and I would have to examine those which they concede now are not supported, and what I would also have to do is go backwards in order to see whether those statements are connected up to the actual war crimes because they're frequently not. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour, may I add that we will supplement this, with the Court's permission, with a brief written response when we have had an opportunity to look at what the Court referred to. May I simply add one sentence about this. This is a unique case. This is not a kind of case where -- which the Court has discussed in the past where you have a firm JCE. Everybody knows who the members are, JCE, and then a stranger, for example, walks into a concentration camp and kills people or some person who is totally outside does that. Here what the Court has done is because the goal was so broad and political, that is separation, ethnic separation goal which is tragically pervasive all over the world and because the indictment says by other means, meaning lawful means as well, virtually anybody of Serbian background who lived in this area could be considered as a member of the JCE, particularly if they then participated in any of the crimes. So what the Court has done is it's mooted the question essentially. The Trial Chamber mooted the question of what happens when a non-JCE member commits a crime. They simply make him a member of the JCE retroactively, and at the very least what would be required is a linkage between that crime and the defendant. The defendant would have to, before the crime was committed, be aware of the fact that the crime was going to be committed. Now, of course in this case, we do have a conclusion of the Court that he was not in a position of authority. That he could not have prevented, and indeed many -- there's a contradiction in the lower Court's judgement, because they hold him responsible for his inactions, for failing to investigate, failing to prosecute, when they also make a finding that he didn't have the authority to do so. And I think the evidence will be very clear that Mr. Krajisnik could not investigate and could not prosecute on his own, and we have no evidence of what his opinions were as to whether there should be Prosecution or not. I'd like to -- I welcome questions so I want to make sure I'm not stopping anybody from asking questions. And please feel free to interrupt in the middle of a sentence. I would like to devote the rest of my time to considering the implications for appellate review of what this distinguished Appellate Chamber how it should look at the Trial Court's judgement in light of the fact that we're talking about political speech and political activity. Now, the Trial Chamber below did say under its paragraph 1196 of standards for making inferences that: "A finding must be more than a reasonable inference in circumstances, it must be the only reasonable inference," which is a very daunting standard. Unfortunately, the lower Court failed to apply that standard, its own standard when it came to evaluating the speeches. They may have applied that standard, I leave that to others because it's not part of my role, when we're talking about whether witnesses, as they said, lacked specificity as to the identity of the alleged perpetrators on purely factual issues of who was where and when, but when it came to interpreting speeches, I am confident that when this Chamber reviews the evaluation of the Trial Chamber they will see that it drew all inferences adverse to the defendants's political nature of his speeches. Every time there was two possible interpretations of a speech, one as posturing for political bargaining position in a negotiation or committing a crime, they would always take the inference most adverse to the defendant. For example, when they say at some point that they characterise a statement he made as a call to arms, accused call to arms, 925 paragraph, at the Assembly session of March 18, 1992. If you read that in context and look at the surrounding evidence, it is so clearly not a call to arms. It is a call to lay down arms. It is a call for political resolution of the conflict, but it's a call stated in strong terms. The same thing is true of so many of the other speeches, some of which probably many of us including myself would find disturbing as a matter of substance. For example, the statement not made by him but made by somebody else that Muslims with their birth rate will gradually stifle our territories. The accused replying to that passed over the remark. That is, he failed to correct a remark made by somebody else even though as speaker, often, he had to simply be polite. But let's assume even the worst case scenario. Let's assume that a defendant makes a speech that says that we have to worry about the birth rate of Muslims in our community or the birth rate of Hasidic Jews, or the birth rate of Catholics or the birth rate of anyone else. One all has to do is read the newspapers. That's being discussed in every country of the world today and I think if one takes everything that the defendant said and reads it in the context of what he was thinking and what his role was, one has to interpret it -- the inferences that have to be drawn, the -- if you have to conclude that it's the only inference, if you apply the Trial Chamber's own standard that it's the only inference, you certainly cannot conclude that the only inference that can be drawn is a criminal inference. I believe, actually, and I represent to this Court having read many of the speeches in context, that the most reasonable inference is an inference of political speech and not an inference of inciting violence, but I don't have to satisfy that standard. The Prosecution must satisfy the standard. There is no reasonable inference other than a criminal inference that can be drawn from those speeches. That simply cannot be done when one reads these speeches in context. If one goes through every one of the paragraphs, and obviously I'm not going to burden the Court by doing that, every one of the paragraphs which describes a speech there are always more than one way of reading the speech. Now, we know that politicians can be very good at that. Religious leaders can be very good at that too. They can talk poetically. They can talk metaphorically. They can talk in ways that posture, in ways that mean one thing to one person and one thing to another. But you simply cannot prosecute a person for war crimes based on speeches and political statements that can be read in multiple ways. And we think that although the general appellate criteria for reviewing fact findings below are to draw reasonable inferences in favour of the winning party, the Prosecution, that's the usual standard on appeal, that is not the standard when freedom of speech and political activity is involved. That is not the standard the United States Supreme Court applies. It is not the standard the House of Lords applies. I don't know that there is any jurisprudence on this issue internationally. We haven't really been able to find any specifically on what the appellate rules should be in reviewing factual determinations. But we submit that the best practice if there is no binding precedent the other way is to draw all inferences very favourably to the defendant when it comes to political speech and political activity in order not to serve to chill political speech and political activity in the future, recognising the delicate balance and the delicate conflict that exists when political speech is turned into a human rights violation. Now, I think the same thing is true when it comes to the mens rea. I focused right now up to this point on the actus reus which we think is the crucial absence in this case, the actus reus. No criminal actus reus has been alleged or proved in this case. But on the mens rea, the suggestion has been made that knowledge is enough. Now, knowledge may be enough when one is dealing with military actions done by the defendants themselves. Knowledge, for example, that there are civilians in a town when he has directed a call to the shelling of that town, knowledge would be enough. But knowledge, Your Honours, is simply not enough for mens rea when it comes to political speech. Think of the implications if that were the case. It would mean that every political figure would have to remain silent once they knew that they were making speeches and their speeches could be misinterpreted to add to the violence or contribute to the violence or could be re-interpreted after the fact. That cannot be enough. A politician must be encouraged to continue to speak even with the knowledge that there are crimes being committed. So although Mr. Krajisnik, I think, has very effectively and there will be more documentation and certainly more documentation from Dr. Karadzic about his lack of knowledge and the particular role he played and the lack of authority he had, but assuming, even for worst case scenario for purposes of Appellate review, assuming that he did know about the shelling, that he did know about this activity, he did know about the other activity which he did not, does that mean that he had to refrain from continuing to speak. His goal was, yes, to try to achieve on the ground positions, legally, that would help him in his negotiating posture. Every negotiator does that. Whenever there are cease-fires both sides want to improve their position on the ground, to increase their leverage when it comes to negotiation, and I think that everything that Mr. Krajisnik said even during the worst periods have to be read in the context of his role as a negotiator, his role as somebody who was pushing toward a peaceful resolution. Yes, he predicted war would come. Yes, he predicted that war would have horrible consequences. Yes, all of those things were said in the context of trying to avoid war. Yes, he did and others did remind the Serbs of what had happened during the Second World War when hundreds of thousands of Serbs were killed when they were exposed vulnerably to the excesses of Nazis who were working in collaboration with some of their enemies in the Croatian and Muslim community. Yes, but he told the truth. Now, it may be an ugly truth and it may be a truth that some people would then take as an invitation for action, but again unless the criteria, the very, very technical criteria for incitement had been satisfied and had they been satisfied, he wouldn't have had to be charged with joint criminal enterprise. He could have been charged with incitement. In the Rwanda situation when you have somebody getting on the radio and describing the locations of where the victims lived and why they should be killed and calling directly for incitement, that's not protected political speech. Or what Streicher did during the Second World War was held by the International Tribunal at Nuremberg not to be protected speech. But I submit that even the Prosecution would acknowledge that every one of the speeches that were made, every word uttered would be protected speech, that there was not a single speech made that in and of itself could be charged with a crime, could be charged as an incitement. So when you have a situation where we're dealing with a political speech, where we're dealing with, as the Court itself said, helping to set up, establish the SDS and other structures of government and using his political skills, even if the Court believes for the wrong purposes and the wrong ends, so long as the means, that is the actus reus, the means were not only not criminal, and here again I make this distinction very sharply there are three categories, or four, war crimes, ordinary crimes, neutral conduct, and protected conduct. And in this case we're talking about protected conduct, protected political speech, speech that could not be banned by a nation consistently with its obligation to protect free speech, that the criteria must be different. The criteria of mens rea must be different, the criteria for actus reus must be different. The criteria for complicity and joining the joint criminal enterprise must be different. After all, if one reads this indictment and the judgement, it is perfectly consistent with the indictment and the judgement that, yes, Mr. Krajisnik believed in separation. Yes, hypothetically, though we don't concede this, he even believed that a transfer of population would be desirable, as a transfer of population was done after the Second World War, in the Sudetenland, in India and Pakistan and Kashmir, Bangladesh, many, many, many other parts of the world, transfers of population - Israel, Palestine - transfers of population, that the transfer of population was a desirable thing. Even if one concedes that, that in and of itself does not create a goal, a JCE goal that is criminal and the means, the means that were identified specifically with this defendant or political speech means. And so when the goal was political and the defendant's means were political, we get a situation, and I will end with this, of the kind that occurred in the United States in perhaps its most famous conspiracy case in recent years, the case against Dr. Spock, a world famous paediatrician who strongly opposed the war in Vietnam. I was honoured to be a lawyer in that case on behalf of the defendants. What you had was six groups of people who opposed the war against Vietnam and they all opposed it in different ways. They all had a common goal; their goal was to end the war. Dr. Spock, being a Ghandian and a supporter of Martin Luther King, believed in passive resistance, including perhaps some criminal conduct, blocking of draft centres but nothing active. He would lie down and allow himself to be arrested. Other members of the conspiracy believed in different ways of ending the war in Vietnam. Some of them were more violent, some of them were more illegal, and the court threw out the entire conviction in the case on the ground that what the Trial Chamber in that case, the Trial Court had failed to do was to require not only that there be a joint goal, ending the war, but that each defendant adhered personally to means that were (a), constitutionally unprotected, and (b) that were illegal in and of themselves. They used the term bivariated or bifurcated conspiracy. When you have conspiracy that contains both lawful ways of achieving it and unlawful ways of achieving it the obligation of the indictment, the prosecution, and the Trial Chamber is to require the finders of fact in that case the jury, in this case the Judges, the finders of fact to find specifically that the particular defendant adhered to the unlawful means and personally participated and took actions that were unlawful. Now, that's not the criteria for conspiracy in general. That's not the criteria in the United States. It's only the criteria for conspiracy when the conspiracy involves politically protected speech, when the conspiracy involves activities that in the United States come within the penumbra of the First Amendment, and in all such cases, a different rule of law and a different rule of appellate interpretation must apply. And we ask this Court respectfully (a) we have not abandoning our position about the general inapplication of JCE and the fact it was not approved by the statute, but putting that aside for a minute, we ask this Court to take the opportunity to use this case to create rigid, hard, predictable, foreseeable lines that a person reading the decision of this Chamber would be able to know what speeches he could make, what speeches he couldn't make, when he could make a speech, when he couldn't make a speech, what context a speech becomes a crime, what -- in what context other political and leadership decisions become a crime. In the absence of that kind of appellate guidance, we fear terribly that speech and political activity will be chilled. Even if one disapproves of the speeches that were made in this case, and if one reads them in context I think the disapproval will be less sharp, but even if one strongly approves, the essence of freedom is freedom for those we disagree with, freedom of those to make speeches that we would wish perhaps they didn't make, freedom of those to form political parties that we would not vote for or approve of, freedom of those to advocate political solutions that we would not accept. Now, there is one paragraph in the opinion which so clearly demonstrates the political nature of the ruling below. They talked about how Mr. Krajisnik had an obligation to all the citizens of the country in which he lived and that he failed to satisfy his obligation to all the citizens of the country. That sounds like a criteria for impeachment from office perhaps, but it doesn't sound like a basis for the most serious crimes, the most serious crimes in the world, violations of human rights, murder, to be applied to a politician, a political figure who exercised his freedom of speech and his political freedom perhaps in ways that we would disagree with. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I welcome any questions now or during the rebuttal period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Shahabuddeen, you want to -- please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Dershowitz, I find your submissions and those of your brother very helpful indeed. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- and I congratulate you both. Now, I'm a little unclear about the exact parameters within which you present the right of a politician to make speeches. I think somewhere you recognised that some politicians can say one thing -- MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- knowing full well that they would be understood by their hearers to mean other thing. Now, I understand very well what you say about the protection of the right to make speeches, but is there a point at which a Court is entitled to say, Well, look here. We have some speeches of the appellant, and we will check their weight. We'll see how they were in fact understood by hearers. Is there a problem of that kind? MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour, thank you for an extremely insightful question and a very, very difficult one. I think the answer to that is yes, there is such a point but two criteria have to be met first. Number one, the defendant has to be indicted for having made the speeches. That is, it has to be an indictment based on the speeches themselves, an incitement indictment of the kind that was done in Rwanda or the kind against Streicher in the Nuremberg trials. Second, the Prosecution would have the burden, not the Defence, of setting out the criteria and the lines and indeed the statute would have the obligation to set out the criteria, what incitement constitutes. Now, there is a doctrine both under American law and international law that is very clear, the doctrine of code words. Now, we all know what that means and that's exactly what Your Honour put his finger on. If both the defendant and the hearers of the speech know that code words are being used, that when a certain phrase is uttered, a Biblical phrase, a Koranic phrase, a phrase from literature, a phrase from political speech which can only be understood as an incitement or a triggering act, plainly a defendant could be indicted for such activity, but in this case the Chamber made no such finding. The Chamber did not in any way suggest that Mr. Krajisnik intended or knew that his speech would be understood or that certain words of the speech would be understood. Instead, what the lower Court did is it used metaphors like "call to arms," or he "set the train going." That's guilt by metaphor, and when you deal with particularly political speeches precisely because of the nuance issue Your Honour so appropriately raises, it's one of the hardest questions the law ever faces, where to draw the line been protected political speech and the abuse of verbal concepts to, in effect, send out triggering messages. Now, we know that free speech does not protect a Mafia capo from saying to his associate, "Let's kill this man." We also know it wouldn't have protected King Henri VII, if I have my history correct, when he said "Will no one rid me of this meddling priest?" We also know there are other ways of communicating directly a message that would not be protected speech, though I add that it would have to be indicted separately. The idea, though, of indicting for a JCE without specifying the mens rea and the -- without specifying the actus reus and then using the speeches and using the worst interpretation of the speeches to put them all together to form a kind of totality of circumstances argument, gravely, gravely endangers free speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: As I have you on the floor. May I burden you with another little question. You have usefully presented us with a brief on JCE, and I'm referring to paragraph 30 of that brief in which you discuss a certain case or cases, and you have named a Judge of this Tribunal whom out of delicacy I wouldn't name now. The last sentence of that paragraph reads: "Perhaps politics dictated one result in one case and another elsewhere." Now, I invite you to focus on the word "perhaps." Is the appellant making an assertion in that sentence or is he speculating on what the answer might be? MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you, Your Honour, for an opportunity to clarify that. Having re-read it now in the light of question, I withdraw that sentence. I think it was an inappropriate sentence in the brief. What I really meant to say was something rather different and I put it very inartfully. What I meant to say was the potential for a political resolution of a case, subconsciously or consciously, is far greater when you have open-ended criteria like the kind of JCE involved here and in some of those other cases, and particularly when you have such horrendous acts having been committed on the ground, what the law always needs is to protect itself against at least the theoretical possibility that ideology, politics, good faith, humanitarian instincts rather than strict application of the law may somehow find itself into the mind of the Judge. To the extent there was any suggestion in the brief that any particular Judge of this Court engaged in that, I personally apologise. I withdraw the sentence and I welcome the opportunity to have made that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dershowitz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Any other question from my colleagues? Well, if it's not the case -- MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- we'll move on to the response of the Prosecution, and I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We will focus our submissions this morning on the question raised by Your Honours in the Scheduling Order, but before doing that, I'd just like to briefly address a number of points just raised. The first is the distinction between the actus reus of the crime charged and the contribution that the member of the JCE needs to make. The contribution as such doesn't necessarily need to be criminal as long as it contributes to the commission of the crime, and the criminal liability does not result from mere looking at the contribution as such but coupled with having a common purpose together with the other JCE members and sharing the intent, when these two requirements are met, the contribution as such does not need to be criminal. And also Mr. Krajisnik's contributions in this case were not limited to mere political speech, and we have addressed his -- the amount of his contributions extensively in our response to the amicus brief, paragraphs 97 through 106, and the response to Krajisnik's brief, paragraph 90 through 168. And with regard to the level of contribution, the fact that the Brdjanin Appeals Chamber said that the contribution needs to be significant, there can be no doubt that the contributions as found by the Trial Chamber are significant. The Trial Chamber referred, for example, in paragraph 1158 to the role that Krajisnik played as crucial and in 1119, it referred to his central position in the joint criminal enterprise. The other issue addressed the question of under which form Krajisnik was convicted. We've set out in our brief that liability was mainly based on JCE I except for the first incidents of the expanded crimes, those outside deportation and of forced transfer, but we will address this issue further this afternoon because this was also raised by the amicus. And second -- third, I apologise, the requirements set by the Brdjanin appeals judgement in paragraph 430 limit the responsibility of joint criminal enterprise, and as the Appeals Chamber has said, provide a safeguard against reaching into an overarching concept lapsing into guilt by association. With Your Honours' permission, I would like now to address the question that Your Honours have posed in the Scheduling Order. In a nutshell, our position is that the Trial Chamber was required and did establish that the crimes formed part of the common purpose, and this means for those crimes carried out physically by the members of the JCE the Trial Chamber had to and did establish that they were carried out in pursuance of the common purpose, and for those which were not carried out by members of the JCE, the Trial Chamber was required to establish that the JCE members used the principal perpetrators to carry out the crimes. And the Trial Chamber here was entitled to infer this link between the JCE member and the principal perpetrator, either because the principal perpetrators were members of an organisation or structure headed by a member of the JCE or because the JCE member closely cooperated with the principal perpetrators, particularly in light of the magnitude of crimes and pattern of events. On the basis of this analysis, the Trial Chamber was not required to analyse or, rather, set out in detail the specific link between each individual incident and the accused. During my submissions today, I will address how the Trial Chamber in this case directly applied the law of joint criminal enterprise in a situation where most of the crimes were carried out by principal perpetrators who were not members of the joint criminal enterprise, and I will address some legal questions regarding this form of liability. And Mr. Kremer will then later address the findings and evidence with regard to the link in more detail and discuss examples where the link may not be immediately obvious. Before the discussion on the law of JCE and the way the principal perpetrators were used, I would like to give an example of the mentioned close cooperation between the individuals involved in the implementation of the common purpose to remove non-Serbs through the commission of crimes. I will address the events in Zvornik. The references can be found in trial judgement paragraph 360 through 368. The organisations or structures in Zvornik were the Crisis Staff, the JNA, the police, the TO, paramilitary groups, and they were all headed by JCE members on different levels and the findings show that they worked closely with each other and with local Serbs. On 5 April, the Crisis Staff ordered the mobilisation of the Serb TO and around the same time, paramilitary groups including the White Eagles, the Yellow Wasps and the Red Berets began to arrive. They had been invited by the president of the Crisis Staff. Arkan's men who were in Bijeljina and who had generally been invited by the JCE member Plavsic, trial judgement 938, were also present and worked with the Serb police setting up barricades. Shortly thereafter, these groups cooperated to commit the first grave crimes in the municipality. On 8 April, the TO, the police, the JNA, and Arkan's men in a joint operation attacked Zvornik municipality murdering many civilians. Looting by Arkan's men followed two days later. This led to the first displacement of Muslims to the nearby village. And around the same time Arkan's men and the White Eagles worked together detaining Muslims in a factory where Muslims were extensively mistreated. The president of the Crisis Staff came to the facility and interrogated and beat a detainee. Arkan's men killed approximately 18 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In late April or early May, the groups working side by side in another village, another crime site, the village of Divic, Arkan's men, reserve police, and the White Eagles, those who had been invited by the Crisis Staff, attacked the village and 1.000 Muslims fled to a nearby village. Around 10 May, the police moved Muslim detainees who had been guarded by local Serbs to another detention facility. Sometime later, the prisoners were moved again and brought to a detention facility guarded by the reserve police. Armed groups including paramilitaries were frequently allowed to access and mistreated detainees. There was a densely-woven network of close cooperation between the groups in Zvornik. It shows that they functioned within the greater scheme of the common purpose that was shared by the JCE members heading and controlling the respective groups. Turning now to the question of the application of the law on JCE where the majority of crimes were not physically committed by JCE members. Before doing that, I would like to quickly remind Your Honours who the JCE members were and what the common purpose was they wanted to achieve. The Trial Chamber, in paragraphs 1086 through 1088, found that the JCE consisted of persons situated throughout the territory and distinguished between a Pale-based leadership and the rank and file. The Pale-based leadership included, in addition to Momcilo Krajisnik, Radovan Karadzic, the president of the presidency and head of the SDS party; Biljana Plavsic, a member of the Presidency; Nikola Koljevic, a member of the Presidency; Momcilo Mandic, the Minister of Justice; Velibor Ostojic, the Minister of Information; Mico Stanisic, the Minister of Interior and thus, head of the MUP; and Ratko Mladic, VRS commander as of 12 May. And the rank and file level of the JCE consisted of local politicians such as presidents of Crisis Staffs and local SDS officials, local military commanders such as JNA and VRS commanders, police commanders, and paramilitary leaders and the Trial Chamber specifically named certain members of the rank and file component. The common purpose of the JCE was the removal of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from large areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina through the commission of persecution, murder, extermination, deportation, and forcible transfer, and the Trial Chamber found that initially the common purpose of deportation and forced transfer started to include other crimes following the acceptance by JCE members and the continued contribution. While the focus was on forcibly removing Muslims and Croats, killings and ill-treatments were used as the means to achieve it and they were carried out often with the aim to instill fear and force the population to leave. Destruction and appropriation of property were seen as the measure to prevent expelled people from returning. Trial judgement 1093. On 18 March, Krajisnik called for the implementation of what we have agreed upon, the ethnic division on the ground and his call to arms benefitted from the preparation and planning of the ethnic cleansing started by the leadership in '91 where Karadzic spoke before the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly referring to possible extinction of the Muslim people. Trial judgement 1099. And during late '91 and early '92, the leadership pursued a parallel track to create a Bosnian Serb state. A peaceful political one based on negotiation and one based on the use of force. Trial judgement 1005. By keeping its options open, they were able to continue and prepare for the ethnic division on the ground by force. The leadership including the accused took active steps towards the realisation of the common objective. They consolidated Bosnian Serb central authority. Trial judgement 903 through 909. They urged to set up Crisis Staffs. Trial judgement 93 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind slowing down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: They established a Bosnian Serb police force, the MUP. Trial judgement 930. And already in spring 1991, the SDS in coordination with the JNA had started arming and mobilising the population. The implementation of the common plan started after Krajisnik's call to arms on 18 March. The Trial Chamber found a general pattern of events in the municipalities. Trial judgement 709. And the differences depended on the ethnic composition in the municipality. Where Serbs were in the minority, Serb forces took over the municipality expelling the non-Serbs. Where they were in the majority and had control over local institutions, Serb authorities and armed Serbs exercised threats, arrests, killings, destruction of religious institutions in order to compel them to leave. And as described in detail in part 4 of the judgement, the crimes were committed by the military, the police, members of the TO, paramilitaries, members of political and governmental bodies including Crisis Staffs and local Serbs. And the Trial Chamber correctly found Krajisnik liable for all these crimes based on joint criminal enterprise. How the members of the JCE implemented the common purpose which was carried out mostly by principal perpetrators which were not JCE members ties in more directly with Your Honours' question on the link between Krajisnik and principal perpetrators. Your Honours asked the question whether the Trial Chamber was required to establish a specific link between each of the crimes and Krajisnik and, if so, to identify this link, namely, to identify relevant findings in the judgement and/or the supporting evidence in the record showing that each of the crimes for which Krajisnik was found liable was committed by a JCE member or could be imputed to a JCE member. As already summarised in the beginning of my submissions, the Chamber correctly determined that crimes formed part of the common purpose either because they were carried out by JCE members or because JCE members were used by -- used the principal perpetrators, them being part of organisations or structures headed by JCE members or closely cooperating with them, particular in light of the magnitude of crime and pattern of conduct. By doing this, the Trial Chamber correctly applied the law as set out by the Appeals Chamber in Brdjanin. The Appeals Chamber in Brdjanin has determined that liability under JCE does not require that the principal perpetrators are members of the JCE. What matters, rather, is that the crime forms part of the common purpose. Appeals judgement 410. And in case the principal perpetrators are not members of this JCE, this requirement that the crime forms part of the common purpose can be inferred from a variety of circumstances including close cooperation with a JCE member. And the requisite link between the principal perpetrator and the accused is thus that a crime can be imputed to one of his fellow JCE members and that this member when using the principal perpetrator acted in accordance with the common plan. Brdjanin 410. That using can take different forms is acknowledged by the Brdjanin appeals judgement which states that the existence of the link has to be determined on a case-by-case basis, paragraph 413. That is a factual determination. And it is clear that such a case of using exists where a JCE member can make use of existing organisations or structures such as the military and the police to instruct their subordinates to implement the common purpose. In Stakic, the Appeals Chamber confirmed use of organisations or structures as the basis for convicting Stakic under JCE liability for crimes committed by the principal perpetrators who were not JCE members. The JCE members were heads of the police, the military, and the Crisis Staff who used their organisations to carry out the crimes. I refer Your Honours to the Stakic appeal judgement, paragraphs 68 through 70 and the analysis in the Brdjanin appeals judgement, paragraph 409. But as the Brdjanin appeals judgement stated, using can also be inferred from close cooperation between the JCE member and the principal perpetrator. When, for example, members of the police work closely with local Serbs to arrest or detain people, then it can be inferred that the local Serbs were also used by the head of the police. The Trial Chamber in Krajisnik correctly set out and applied the law. It recognised in paragraph 883 that it is not required that the principal perpetrator is a member of the JCE, rather, that it is sufficient that he is procured by the JCE member. Procuring means to obtain, to bring about, and describes the same concept as using and has been used in this sense by the Trial Chamber in Haradinaj to describe the requirements in Brdjanin. That's the Haradinaj trial judgement, paragraph 138. The Trial Chamber in the Krajisnik case was also conscious that to find JCE liability the members must share a common purpose, not merely have the same purpose, trial judgement 884. And the Trial Chamber understood that it had to determine whether the crime was part of the common purpose, and in trial judgement 1082, accepted indicia from which this can be incurred. This included whether the principal perpetrators were tools of the JCE, whether they cooperated with members of the JCE. The Trial Chamber explained the connections and relationships among the JCE members. They rely on each other's contributions and on the contributions of non-members who have been procured to achieve the common objective. This is consistent with the Brdjanin appeals judgement. Applying these criteria correctly to the facts of this case, the Chamber was entitled to infer that the crimes could be imputed to Krajisnik. I will address first the crimes of the JCE members and then the crimes of those who were not members of the JCE. Crimes personally committed by JCE members could be attributed to Krajisnik because of the purpose they had in common and the intent, the shared intent, for the crimes. Mr. Kremer will deal with their crimes in more detail. The common purpose and shared intent is demonstrated through the network of connections and cooperation between them. This shows that in addition to the Pale leadership also the local component, the rank and file component of the JCE had a purpose in common with Krajisnik, and the Trial Chamber identified for those rank and file members of the JCE the particular findings in -- and evidence in the footnote to trial judgement 1088. Turning to the crimes committed by principal perpetrators who were not JCE members. On the basis of the evidence, the Trial Chamber reached the own reasonable conclusion when it found Krajisnik liable also for those crimes carried out physically by people who were not members of the JCE. The Trial Chamber was allowed to infer that they were used to implement the common purpose as there were members of organisations or structures which were headed by members of the JCE, or at least closely cooperated with them. The Trial Chamber had established that the members of the JCE were either heads of structures or organisations to which the vast majority of principal perpetrators belonged such as the military, the JNA, the VRS, the MUP, the TO, paramilitary units, or political structures including the Crisis Staffs. So it could infer that the principal perpetrators were used when carried out crimes, particularly given the magnitude of crimes and the pattern of conduct, the similarities in the municipalities. For those crimes where the principal perpetrators were not part of these organisations such as armed local Serbs, the Trial Chamber was justified by the massive record to conclude and articulated sufficiently in its reasons in part 4 how they closely cooperated with members of the JCE. That these armed locals were used by members of the JCE is the only reasonable inference from the evidence of such close cooperation. The clear findings in part 4, and I have cited some in the beginning, show that the crimes committed by the principal perpetrators were directed against non-Serbs and thus furthered the common purpose. The Trial Chamber has not set out the specific link which regard to each incident in each of the individual municipalities but it was not required to do so. On the basis of the described cooperation between those groups and with others the Trial Chamber was entitled to summarise the findings on perpetrators as Bosnian Serb authorities or Bosnian Serb forces, a term used to describe armed soldiers, paramilitary units, police, and other armed persons in trial judgement 292. The Trial Chamber described in detail in parts 2, 3, and 6 of the judgement how the JCE members took over and established structures and organisations and cooperated with them. The findings in part 4 show the close cooperation among organisations and with others outside these organisations. And in light of the massive scale of the crimes committed by those in the structures which followed similar pattern, the Trial Chamber was not required to undertake an additional specific analysis with regard to the links between the principal perpetrators and the JCE members. Crimes were committed on a massive scale immediately as the takeover started. Ethnic cleansing occurred in a relatively short time period in all 35 municipalities --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: -- similar acts - I apologise - in all municipalities and the acts in all municipalities were coordinated. The mere scale of crimes, approximately 3.000 killings and the forcible removal of more than 100.000, shows the necessary participation and cooperation of various groups and shows planning at all levels. The Trial Chamber specifically found that this required the involvement of the Bosnian Serb authorities on the central, regional, and municipal level. Trial judgement 710. This leaves no other reasonable conclusion than that the JCE members used the principal perpetrators. The Trial Chamber explained further in detail how a core group of JCE members, the Bosnian Serb leadership, developed the plan to ethnically recompose the territories by expelling non-Serbs and drastically reducing their numbers and how they used the structures and organisations to do so. They used an armed population which could deploy units locally and the support and cooperation of the JNA. Trial judgement 925. They thus first relied on the JNA and then set up a Bosnian Serb army, the VRS, whose plan of action was broadly formulated by the leadership. Trial judgement 994. They created a Serbian MUP which was used in combat and for mopping up operations. Trial judgement 255. They used paramilitaries to terrorise the population. Trial judgement 979. They exerted central influence on the municipal level through the Crisis Staffs. Trial judgement 267. And the Crisis Staff functioned as a coordinating body between the leadership and the municipal level on the one hand and between the forces on the ground, the police, the military, and the paramilitaries on the other hand. And Krajisnik and Karadzic further communicated the ideas of the leadership to the Bosnian Serbs directly. Trial judgement 1001. To achieve the common purpose across the indictment municipalities, the Pale-based leadership consolidated central authority and by using these centralised structures, the Pale leadership and the local representatives on the ground could better coordinate and cooperate in carrying out the common purpose. The members of the JCE thus made sure that the purpose would be carried out by putting in place and using these organisations and structures which were, as the Trial Chamber found in paragraph 1120, instrumental for the commission of the crimes. They thus allowed -- thus allowed them to either directly through subordination or indirectly through close cooperation get the principal perpetrators to carry out the crimes in pursuance of the common purpose. Before handing over to Mr. Kremer, I would like to briefly address one legal issue with regard to joint criminal enterprise in this form. JCE is a form of committing under 7(1) even when the principal perpetrators are not members of the JCE. Only committing liability properly reflects the criminality of the JCE members. A group of people who get together with the common purpose which amounts to or involves the commission of crimes with a shared intent constitute a greater danger than people acting alone. They are able to achieve criminal results on a scale which they would never be able to realise alone, such as the ethnic cleansing of 35 municipalities in Bosnia. It is the manifestation of this greater danger which merits the designation as committing, and JCE has thus correctly and repeatedly characterised as commission by the Appeals Chamber, for example, in could Kvocka, paragraph 80, and in the Vasiljevic appeals judgement, paragraph 102. Further, the Appeals Chamber in Milutinovic considered that the high mens rea, the shared intent of the members of the JCE means that they cannot be regarded as mere aiders and abettors, rather, that JCE has to be regarded as a form of commission. That's the decision on Dragoljub Ojdanic's motion challenging jurisdiction, joint criminal enterprise, of the 21st of May, 2003, paragraph 20. And the two reasons why JCE has to be committing, the high mens rea and the manifestation of the greater danger, do not change when the principal perpetrators are not members of the JCE but, rather, used by members of the JCE. They still have to have the high mens rea, the shared intent, and the ability to commit crimes on a larger scale is even enhanced when others are used or instrumentalised to carry out the common purpose. Liability under JCE thus remains a form of committing even when the principal perpetrators are not JCE members. Unless Your Honours have questions, I would hand over to Mr. Kremer who will address the question of link in more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Goy, I have to admit that I tend to commit this sin of summarising in my head what I've listened to, and that, of course, could lead to the dangers of oversimplification, so correct me if my understanding of your position is wrong. In answer to the Appeals Chamber's questions concerning the link, you have taken the position that there are two sets of crimes, crimes committed by members of the JCE and crimes committed by non-members of the JCE. Then you would see, so I understand, no necessity to prove link where the former are concerned. You would only see a necessity to prove a link where the latter are concerned, and this link you would prove by a process of inferences. You would say, so I understand you to say, that these non-members were so closely related to the JCE that they must have acquired their instructions from the JCE, including the appellant. Well, would there be a question this way as to the relationship between an appeals court and a trial court so far as inferences are concerned? Are we at liberty here to treat the position de novo and to make our own inferences, or are we bound in any way by the inferences made by the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to answer the question in two parts. First, I'd like to address the first part with regard to whether our position is that there is no link requirement or no requirement to establish a link where a member of the joint criminal enterprise commits the crime. In order to impute liability for that crime to the accused, one has to establish a link but the link is a different type of link. The link is established through finding that this JCE member, the principal perpetrator, had a common purpose with the accused and that they shared the intent together, and when then the JCE member commits the crime in furtherance of the common purpose, the fact that they have the purpose in common and share the intent constitutes the required connection to impute the crime. With regard to the second category of cases where crimes are committed by principal perpetrators who are not members of the JCE, we agree that the -- on a -- on appeal what matters is to satisfy yourself that the inferences that the Trial Chamber drew were reasonable inferences, so that it is not for Your Honours to establish the link. The link has been established by the Trial Chamber even implicitly through the fact that they have convicted Krajisnik for those crimes, and in our opinion, these were reasonable, even the only reasonable inferences in these cases where you have the vast majority of principal perpetrators in structures headed by members of the joint criminal enterprise and for those who were not in structures on the basis of this close cooperation throughout different municipalities in light of the pattern used, that they were actually used by the members of the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I have two questions to you. The first one draws significantly on the question asked by my distinguished colleague Judge Shahabuddeen. In your argument you pointed out that the majority, perhaps the great majority of crimes in this case were committed by persons who were not members of the JCE. So my question is: Was the Trial Chamber not required under our jurisprudence, specifically Brdjanin, to systematically make findings imputing to a member of the JCE or to Mr. Krajisnik, assuming that he's a member, crimes committed by non-members? I must say that I have not been persuaded that this has been done in a systematic and specific way, and I am somewhat troubled by your statement with regard to inferences which would be adequate in that respect, inferences based primarily on close relationship with members of the JCE. My second question pertains to the question of protected speech, political speech. We have had extensive argument about it earlier today. Now, in -- with regard to political speech, it doesn't have to be established that political statements which otherwise would be protected were clearly designed to achieve an illegal purpose, and it will be helpful in that respect if the Prosecution could point to a specific statement or action by Mr. Krajisnik which would clearly reflect intent to advance common criminal purpose. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: First turning to your first question, the Trial Chamber has, though not explicitly in the findings on Krajisnik's responsibility, established the links in detail with regard to each incident, but from a -- reading the judgement as a whole, through the fact that in the parts 2 and 3 of the judgement they have established the -- said how the JCE members established the structures and who was in the JCE members, and through the fact of how these facts were then used in the implementation of the common plan. That, from our view, allows the inference and is in fact the only reasonable inference that the physical perpetrator, those in the structures and those closely cooperating with the structures were carrying out crimes in pursuance of the common purpose. And the Brdjanin appeals judgement, by setting out that the link has to be established on a case-by-case basis and that it can be established, inferred from the circumstances of the case such as close cooperation allows for such an approach. Turning to your second question, the protected speech. As mentioned in the beginning of my submissions, one has to distinguish between the actus reus of the crime as such and the contribution of the JCE member, and once that is made with the shared intent, with the high mens rea, that would be sufficient as a contribution as long as it is significant. And we have addressed in our response to Mr. Krajisnik and in the response to amicus the -- our submissions why the Trial Chamber's findings on Krajisnik's shared intent were reasonable findings, and I'm not in a position at the moment to point Your Honours to something specific. I can just refer you to the arguments that we have made in our brief with regard to the mens rea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Before you take the floor, Mr. Kremer, I see we are approaching the pause at 12.00. Probably it's inappropriate for you, unless you want to start for five minutes. It will probably be more beneficial for you to start -- to have the pause now, the break now, and start immediately afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: That would be very helpful. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Not to break too early your submission. So we can break now for 15 minutes and reconvene at 10 past 12.00 for the continued response of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I will now give the floor to the Prosecution, to Mr. Kremer for the submission of the Prosecution in response, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going to continue on the answer to the links question which was posed by Your Honours in the Scheduling Order, and I will follow up on what Ms. Goy has stated in terms of the legal structure and give it some factual substance. Our analysis of the factual findings in part 4 and the legal findings in part 5 of the judgement revealed that the crimes are linked to Krajisnik and other JCE members by direct commission by JCE members, as Ms. Goy has commented, and through the JCE use of the principal perpetrators to commit the crimes. Our analysis did reveal a few errors and ambiguities in the judgement. None involved the question of link and we filed with the Chamber yesterday a list of explanations. Our analysis showed that the crimes were committed either by JCE members or by persons used by JCE members. I will discuss both links to crimes committed by JCE members and principal perpetrators used by JCE members but will spend most of my time on principal perpetrators used by JCE members. The final part of my submission will address three persecutory acts committed within the general framework of the common purpose where the link is implicit. First, there are multiple examples where a JCE member personally committed crimes. All these crimes can be imputed to Krajisnik because Krajisnik and the JCE members who participated in the crimes shared the common objective. Their crimes became his crimes. Ljubisa Mauzer Savic, leading SDS figure in Bijeljina and commander of the Serb National Guard paramilitary unit, on May 7, 1992, at least six Muslim men who had been hiding in Mucici, a part of Brcko town, were shot dead by Mauzer and soldiers presenting themselves as Seselj's men. Paragraph 327. For other crimes committed by Mauzer, go to paragraph 305 and paragraph 325. Mirko Blagojevic, leader of the Serb radicals paramilitary group, 326 of the judgement. On May 4th, 1992, Muslim firemen who had been detained at the fire station by JNA soldiers were beaten by Blagojevic. Branko Grujic, president of Zvornik SDS and Crisis Staff, paragraph 367. On April 9th, 1992, Witness 674 was interrogated and beaten by Branko Grujic. Brothers Dusan Repic Vukovic and Vojin Zuco Vukovic, leaders of the Yellow Wasps paramilitary unit, paragraph 372. The Yellow Wasps headed by the Vukovic brothers Repic and Zuco arrived at the Dom Kulture on 11 June and killed at least five detainees. One man had his ear cut off. Others had their fingers cut off, and at least two men were sexually mutilated. Repic's men forced detainees to eat the severed body parts, killing two detainees who could not bring themselves to do so. On June 27th, Repic returned to Dom Kulture alone and shot 20 detainees dead and wounded 22 others. Vlado Vrkes, president of the local Banja Luka SDS. Paragraph 509. On 3 April, the Crisis Staff imposed discriminatory measures on Muslims in Banja Luka. SDS president Vrkes, accompanied by SOS members and the Serb police, forced out the Croat director of the municipal SDK appointing a Serb in her place. Ratko Radic, SDS municipal president of Hadzici. Paragraph 547. In mid-July 1992, Ratko Radic transferred Witness 141 and her sister to the premises of the factory outside Hadzici and were forced to work. At the factory, Radic raped the sister regularly. Jovan Tintor, member of the SDS board -- Main Board and president of Vogosca Crisis Staff. Paragraph 598. On 1 May 1992, a Muslim police officer in Sarajevo and his colleague were arrested by Serb TO. They were taken to the police station in Vogosca town where Jovan Tintor interrogated and beat them. Dragan Gagovic, Foca police chief and Dragoljub Kunarac, commander of a reconnaissance group within the local Foca Tactical Group. Paragraph 640 of the trial judgement. Here Muslim civilians were detained at Foca High School and Partizan Hall which was guarded by police officers. Serb soldiers or policemen, including the chief of police Dragan Gagovic, would come to these detention centres, select one or more women, take them out and rape them. Some of these women were also taken out of these two detention centres by Serb soldiers, including Dragoljub Kunarac, and subjected to sexual assaults. During one rape, Kunarac expressed the verbal and physical aggression, his view that rapes against women were one of the many ways which the Serbs could assert their superiority and victory over the Muslims. Krsto Savic, commissioner for the SAO Eastern Herzegovina. Paragraph 669 of the trial judgement. On 16 June 1992, soldiers in camouflage uniform led by Krsto Savic entered the house of a Muslim resident in Nevesinje municipality. During this operation, Savic shot Redzep Trebovic in the leg. The Serb soldiers held his wife back from helping him. When the family was allowed to bring him to the hospital four hours later, he had died from the injury. His house was burnt down. Gojko Klickovic, president of the Bosanska Krupa War Presidency. Paragraph 398 of the judgement. On 28 April 1992, Klickovic ordered the commanders of three battalions, of the 1st Podgrmec Brigade to immediately evacuate Muslim population from the territory under their control. Pursuant to his order on 1 May 1992, the Executive Committee of Arapusa commune jointly with the local refugee committee and the battalion command issued instructions resulting in the unlawful detention of the 460 to the village of Fajtovici in Sanski Most municipality where 1.200 persons were already detained. These examples of JCE members committing crimes not only establish the connection between the JCE members' crime and Krajisnik but also show the JCE members used non-members to commit crimes to further the common purpose. They also show the type and style of leader who joined the JCE and who played key roles in implementing the common objective on the ground. Let us now look at principal perpetrators who are not JCE members. They fall into two groups, those who were members of an organisation headed by a JCE member and those who were not. I will first review principal perpetrators who were not [sic] JCE members but belonged to an organisation through which the JCE member used them to commit crimes within the common purpose. Then I will discuss how the various organisations work to achieve the common purpose before finally discussing those non-JCE members who were not part of an organisation but were used by JCE members to commit crimes within the common purpose. Ms. Goy has already raised the names of the organisations that were used headed by JCE members; Crisis Staffs, the JNA, the VRS, the MUP, the TO, and paramilitaries at the republican, regional and local levels. The local politicians and the organisations of the TO, military, police, and paramilitary through their commanders used their men to commit crimes pursuant to the common objective. Our position is, as Ms. Goy has stated, that the Trial Chamber was entitled to find that the JCE used them through this straightforward organisation -- organisational and structural link. From our analysis of parts 4 and 5 of the judgement and the evidence underlining the crime findings, I have prepared a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina showing in a different colour each organisation; the TO, the paramilitaries, the JNA, VRS, MUP, and the Crisis Staffs. If you could turn on your monitors. The first -- first group of -- the first group to be entered is the TO, and this shows the range of TO criminal activity during -- during the period. The low population on the map is due in part to the fact that the TO was incorporated in some municipalities into the JNA and in -- and later once the VRS was formed into the VRS. Secondly, we'll add paramilitaries. You'll see that the paramilitaries were more active than the TO in committing crimes. The paramilitaries, like the TO, when the VRS was established also became part of the VRS. The MUP is the next one to be added -- I'm sorry, the JNA. These are the JNA or the VRS are carrying out activities throughout the regions. If we add the MUP, you will see that their population is also in virtually all of the municipalities. And finally the Crisis Staffs that were the glue between or behind the fabric of ethnic cleansing in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The map illustrates that all of these groups were involved in crimes in the indictment municipalities as shown on the map, and it also serves to illustrate, the kind of intra- and inter-organisational cooperation that was taking place during the indictment period, in particular at the time when the municipalities were being taken over. The Prijedor municipality, which Your Honours know well from the Stakic case, also shows how JCE members used non-JCE who were not members of the organisation. First let me start with -- refer you to paragraph 470, and I'm just summarising very quickly the events to show the scale and system which is typical of not only Prijedor but the other municipalities. The JNA and the police took control of Prijedor town on 30 April 1992. Check-points were set up, important buildings were occupied, important organs and companies were taken over. Non-Serb police were dismissed. SDS removed the SDA from functions in the municipality. 471, the Crisis Staff assisted by soldiers or paramilitaries then expanded the restrictive measures imposed on the non-Serb population. The SDS controlled the propaganda machinery and how searches of the non-Serb houses were conducted. 474, the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS and the MUP continued mopping up operations from late May 1992 onwards. Paramilitaries fought alongside the VRS. Another JCE member appears here, Slobodan Kuruzovic, member of the SDS Muncipal Board and the local TO commander was in charge of Trnopolje camp. He announced to his prisoners that the Serb plan was to reduce the Muslim population to 10 per cent, then 2 per cent of the population. 478, on 26 May 1992, Kuruzovic commanding a special unit from Prijedor surrounded the village of Trnopolje while a detachment of the military police placed the remaining local residents in the elementary school. 487, in three large detention facilities, Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje guarded by soldiers, police forces, TO, or a combination thereof, teams of military and civilian authorities screened detainees. The detainees were abused, beaten and killed. Detainees -- I'm sorry, the detainees were abused, beaten and killed by the guards and members of local organisations and local Serbs who were routinely allowed into the camps. Thousands of people were detained there in cramped conditions between May and November 1992 by armed soldiers under the control of Kuruzovic. From Trnopolje detainees were transported out of the municipality. That's 492. 493, camp authorities in Trnopolje did not distribute food, and on occasion Serb soldiers beat and killed Muslim and Croat detainees. In one such incident, Serb soldiers took 11 detainees to a maize field and shot them dead. Moreover, soldiers coming from outside the camp and Kuruzovic, the camp commander, raped the female detainees. And finally 494, on 21 August, 154 detainees from Trnopolje were placed on buses and taken to Koricanske Stijene in Skender Vakuf municipality where they were executed by police and uniformed soldiers. That is the extent of the cooperation between the structures. That is the extent of the cooperation and coordinated effort between the leaders of the various structures to ethnically cleanse Prijedor of its Bosnian Serb -- or Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat minorities. Coordinated and cooperated -- cooperative action typified the method of operation to achieve the common purpose. Not only did these organisations work together within municipalities, they also worked together across several municipalities. Deportations and forcible transfers frequently required coordination between organisations operating in several municipalities to ensure a successful expulsion of the minorities. One brief example of this at the state and municipal levels will suffice. More than 400 detainees at the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac operated by the MUP were transferred to a detention facility in Pale to be exchanged for Serb prisoners. Paragraph 315. On 15 May 1992, Prime Minister Deric ordered that the Pale detainees from Bratunac be transferred to Visoko in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina outside Bosnian Serb control. Deric ordered the Sokolac Crisis Staff to provide three trucks for their transportation, the Pale Crisis Staff to arrange their escort, and the Ilijas Crisis Staff to allow the convoy to pass. The Bosnian Serb Central Exchange Commission processed their transfer. Trial judgement 151, 1035, 156, and 244. This is a cooperation at the state and local level involving the prime minister and the Central Exchange Commission as well as local municipality leaders through which this convoy would have passed. Before I turn to the second type of principal perpetrators, those non-JCE members who are not part of the organisations, I propose briefly to discuss how the JCE members used their organisations and their connections of the -- with structures to the Pale-based leadership. The Pale-based leadership component directed and controlled the JNA, the VRS, the TO, the MUP, and the paramilitaries at the republican level, and at the local level control rested with individual politicians, military and police commanders, and paramilitary leaders and others which the Trial Chamber called the JCE rank and file. I will discuss each organisation briefly, but before I do so, I want to stress that the main findings on structures are found in part 3 and part 6 of the judgement and are useful in understanding just how tightly controlled these structures were by the state and used by the state in order to achieve the common purpose that was defined and communicated and eventually implemented through the use of the structures and the people who worked within them and who cooperated with them. I'll start with the TO. The TO as the municipal defence force had close links with Crisis Staffs. Crisis Staffs appointed and dismissed TO commanders and received reports from TO units. Crisis Staffs issued orders to the TO units on military matters. Crisis Staffs, or their members, assumed a very direct military role and got involved in military activities. Crisis Staffs also provided various forms of general assistance to the TO, calling for mobilisation within their municipalities and providing financial and other assistance. Paragraph 285. Already on 15 April 1992, a JNA colonel had been appointed commander of the Bosnian Serb TO to supervise and control local TOs as an interim measure pending the creation of a Bosnian Serb army. Paragraph 946. When the JNA formally withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina, the TO units became part of the VRS. Local Crisis Staffs often remained responsible for logistical support to the TO. Paragraphs 285 and 186. TO commanders who were JCE members implemented the common objective by using members of their organisation. Take, for example, Marko Pavlovic, Serb TO commander in Zvornik. Working together with other JCE members, Branko Grujic, president of Zvornik SDS and Crisis Staff, and Jovan Mijatovic, member of the Zvornik Crisis Staff and deputy to the Bosnian Serb Assembly, to displace the Muslims of Kozluk. On the night of 20 June, the Serb TO under the command of Marko Pavlovic attacked Kozluk. On 26 June, a large number of Serb soldiers, TO, and paramilitaries entered Kozluk in tanks and other military vehicles. Among the group were Branko Grujic, Pavlovic, and Jovan Mijatovic. They informed the Muslims that they had one hour to leave or they would be killed. On the same day, a convoy of vehicles organised by the Serbs who had attacked and taken over Kozluk, transported approximately 1.800 persons out of the municipality to Serbia. Another example involving destruction of property involves Nedeljko Davidovic, Serb captain of the TO at Banja Luka working together with JCE member Dragan Djuric, deputy to the Bosnia-Herzegovina and Bosnian Serb Assemblies. I won't get into it but it's found at paragraph 503. Let me move to paramilitaries. Members of the Bosnian Serb leadership invited paramilitaries and appreciated their services. Plavsic sent letters to Seselj, Arkan and Jovic, together all who wanted to fight for Serbianhood. Paragraph 938. Military leaders are members of the JCE -- or paramilitary leaders are members of the JCE. Individual paramilitary leaders are identified by name in trial judgement 1088. Arkan, Blagojevic, Kusic, Mauzer, Milankovic, and Vukovic, as -- and many of those names you heard as people who committed crimes themselves. The Bosnian Serb leadership used paramilitaries opportunistically to terrorise the Muslims and Croats in order to achieve the common objective. Notwithstanding their awareness of the serious problems posed by the paramilitary formations in various municipalities as well as their unruly behaviour. Judgement 979. But instead of suppressing these groups, they incorporated them into the regular VRS units. Some groups invited by the SDS local boards, Crisis Staffs, and regional governments were accepted as fighters for the Serbian cause despite their record of lawlessness and ruthless efficiency. Others were tolerated as long as they did not pose too much trouble for the Bosnian Serb legitimate authorities. Paragraph 215 and 979. Local SDS boards, Crisis Staffs, and regional SAO governments also invited and assisted paramilitary groups, for example, the Yellow Wasps, the Red Berets, Mauzer's men, and Arkan's men operating in North-eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina, Bijeljina, Brcko, and Zvornik. Trial judgement 215. Local paramilitary groups also formed within municipalities. They participated in the takeover crimes and later crimes in a number of municipalities and worked closely with police, political and/or military police organisations. For example, in furthering the common objective, local politicians and the Crisis Staff in Cajnice worked in close cooperation with the police, the military, and local paramilitary units like the Blue Eagles which had clear links to the local Serbian authorities. Trial judgement 618. When the JNA withdrew from Visegrad on May 19th, the town was under the control of the local Serb authorities which had an exclusively Serb police. The local Serb authorities permitted paramilitaries to operate within the town. Paragraph 696. Their use to further the common objective is demonstrated by their actions. Paramilitaries subjected the Muslims to mistreatment and humiliation, to rapes and beatings. Serb forces, which included paramilitaries, killed more than 266 non-Serb civilians, mostly Muslims in Visegrad in June 1992 and the following months. Trial judgement 701. More than 200 are categorised as disappearances by the adjudicated facts which the Trial Chamber inferred was committed by Serb forces. Trial judgement 698 and 701. JCE member and military leader Milan Lukic's local paramilitary unit -- local paramilitary leader used his unit to kill approximately 66 people by locking them in a house and setting it on fire and shooting those who tried to escape. Paragraph 699. They were also used to appropriate property. 696. Their crimes fit the pattern and advanced the common plan to terrorise the population into leaving. The police participated in expulsions. The cooperation between the local authorities in the municipality with the paramilitaries was so efficient that within a few weeks Visegrad was almost completely cleansed of its Muslim civilians. Paragraph 700. I've discussed earlier the crimes committed by JCE members and paramilitary leaders like Mauzer, Blagojevic, the Vukovic brothers, and I refer Your Honours to the paragraphs that I've cited concerning their crimes because it also shows how they used their paramilitary units to commit crimes. Turning to the army. With regard to the crimes committed by members of the army, the Trial Chamber distinguished before the period -- or the period before and after the establishment of the VRS on 12 May 1992. When the takeover started in April 1992, the JNA, together with the non-enlisted Bosnian Serb men of fighting age, were the Serbian army on the ground. Judgement 925. The cooperation between the JNA and the Bosnian Serb leadership was not a closely guarded secret. Paragraph 946. Krajisnik knew of the JNA's cooperation in the takeover of power. Paragraph 947. The Trial Chamber explicitly rejected Krajisnik's claim that the JNA was neutral prior to 12 May 1992. Paragraph 192. As stated in March 1992 by the JNA 2nd Military District commander, the leadership of the Serb people and all Serbs are ready for war. Paragraph 42. JNA commanders, JCE members used soldiers, non-JCE members under their control to further the common objective. Take, for example, JCE member Lieutenant Colonel Tadija Manojlovic, a JCE officer who at the end of April 1992 ordered JNA heavy artillery, rocket launchers, anti-aircraft guns and tanks to be fired every evening on targets in Sarajevo neighbourhoods. The Serb SJB also took part in the attacks. By early May 1992, Serb forces controlled Ilidza. Paragraph 553. JCE member General Jankovic, commander of the 17th Corps of the JNA, was involved in the takeover of Bijeljina and the unlawful detention of about 3.000 civilians, mainly Muslims, at the Bijeljina barracks and Patkovaca barracks. That's in paragraph 301. Another JCE member, Captain Reljic, JNA commander, participated in the takeover of Bratunac municipality.
