On 16 April, the TO in Bratunac was mobilised and in the following days, Arkan's and Seselj's paramilitary units and the JNA unit under the command of Captain Reljic arrived in the municipality. While the JNA and the TO began disarming Muslim villagers throughout the municipality, the paramilitaries harassed locals and pillaged abandoned Muslim homes. Most of the Muslim leadership left Bratunac municipality for Srebrenica after receiving threats from these Serb paramilitary units. This effectively surrendered Bratunac to Serb control. Paragraph 311. The VRS was established, as I've already said, on 12 May 1992, at a session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. Krajisnik promoted the creation of the VRS. Ratko Mladic was appointed as commander of the VRS Main Staff. Paragraph 194. Mladic was directly subordinated to the Presidency. The same paragraph. Mladic as commander of the Main Staff was a member of the JCE. His military commanders on the ground were also found to be members of the JCE. The VRS Main Staff kept members of the Presidency well briefed on the military situation throughout the Bosnian Serb republic. The political leadership passed orders to the military officers, including oral orders and orders given to military officials attending Presidency sessions. Paragraph 206. The VRS was involved in the full range of crimes committed during attacks and detention. Soon after its establishment, the VRS issued written orders for the detention of all Muslim men fit for military service. Paragraph 1038. The use by a JCE member of the VRS to implement the common purpose is illustrated by the actions of JCE member Major Svetozar Andric, commander of the VRS 1st Birac Brigade, whose brigade was active in Zvornik in April and May 1992. Around 28 May, between 400 and 500 Muslims in Divic village, including women, children, and elderly persons, were forced under -- onto buses by members of the Yellow Wasps and told that they would be taken to Muslim territory. Andric issued an order on 28 May 1992, from the command of the VRS 1st Birac Brigade to the Zvornik TO: "The moving out of the Muslim population must be organised and coordinated with the municipalities through which the moving is carried out. Only women and children can move out while men fit for military service are to be placed in camps for exchange." Paragraph 1043. Another VRS Commander Marko Adamovic, a commander of the VRS military police unit operating in the Kljuic region, around 1 June 1992, Adamovic with approximately 100 armed Serb police officers arrived in the Muslim village of Provo. 40 unarmed villagers including women and children were ordered to line up facing the wall of a house. Several residents were beaten and between five and eight men were killed. Adamovic ordered the soldiers, through a megaphone, to set the village on fire and to kill the women and children. When the male residents were led out of the village in the direction of Peci, an explosion and gunshots were heard coming from the village and the Serb soldiers opened fire on the civilians who remained. A soldier threw a grenade into the crowd killing several women. As a result of the shooting, about 38 people were killed, including children and at least one house was burned town. Paragraph 450. Another brief example, General Momir Talic, commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, controlled Manjaca camp in Banja Luka. The crimes in Manjaca camp which held from several hundred to 3.000 detainees were made possible only through using his VRS soldiers and others including local Serbs willing to assist. 383 to 384. The other VRS-controlled detention camps described in the judgement were no different. Moving to the police and the scene repeats itself again and again and again. There is complete control by JCE members over what is going on and they are using their members, their police officers, their soldiers to commit the crimes to further the common purpose. Mico Stanisic, minister of interior and head of the police, was a named member of the Pale-based leadership component of the JCE. 1087. Under Stanisic were regional CSBs and municipal SJB police commanders. Local police commanders are included as JCE members and Simo Drljaca and Stojan Zupljanin are specifically named. The Trial Chamber found in paragraph 255 that MUP forces were involved in criminal activities in the indictment municipalities ranging from mere war profiteering to the running of detention centres where Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats were subjected to ill-treatment. In the course of 1992, the Bosnian Serb MUP became heavily involved in the operation of detention centres. Paragraph 249. Units also participating in forcing non-Serbs to leave municipalities that ought to become Serb territory from April to December 1992, MUP police officers were also extensively engaged in combat under the VRS. The MUP leadership also participated in the common criminal purpose. JCE member Vitomir Popic, the police commander of Gacko, used his officers and local Serbs to commit unlawful imprisonment, murder, rape and torture. In late May and early June 1992, the local police under commander Popic together with local leader of the White Eagles began arresting Muslims and taking them to a detention camp in Bjelica municipality. In early June, there were around 120 Muslim detainees at the Gacko police station. Some of the detainees were beaten frequently. The conditions of detention were harsh. On 3 July 1992, five Muslim men were executed by seven local Serb men led by police commander Popic. On 4 July 1992, in the same police station, Popic forced a detainee to watch the rape of his own wife by a Serb man from the Munja unit of the Red Berets assisted by two other Red Berets. Paragraph 656. Those are the military groups but the political structures or the political people in the Crisis Staffs and in the SDS party were no different in terms of their conduct. They, too, were connected from -- to the Bosnian Serb leadership through the various members placed there by the Bosnian Serb leadership. SDS policies and SDS members played an important role in the implementation of the common plan. The Pale-based leadership were all senior SDS politicians. Krajisnik was a member of the SDS Main Board and president of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. Radovan Karadzic was president of the SDS. Local politicians were to be -- were found to be members of the JCE. Many were specifically named in trial judgement 1088. Many of them were SDS deputies or SDS Main Board members. One of Krajisnik's contributions to the JCE was formulating, initiating, promoting, participating in and/or encouraging the development and implementation of SDS policies intended to advance the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. The SDS Crisis Staffs were transformed into republican organs on 4 April when the SNB ordered their activation and instructed that the TO and the reserve police officers be put in readiness. Paragraph 263. The SDS's coordinating role of and dominant influence over municipal Crisis Staffs is reflected by the fact that almost every Crisis Staff in the municipalities covered by the indictment included at least one deputy from the Bosnian Serb Assembly or a member of the SDS Main Board. Paragraph 265 and 266. The Crisis Staffs reported via the SDS Main Board, via the Bosnian Serb Assembly, and individual leaders such as Karadzic and Krajisnik and directly to the Bosnian Serb Presidency. Paragraph 270. Municipal Crisis Staff actions were Pale-based leadership actions. Paragraph 267 summarises it best by ensuring that at least one Assembly deputy was a member of the municipal staff allowed the Bosnian Serb leadership to exert a substantial amount of control and central influence over them. The president of the Ilidza Crisis Staff perceived this system as one of organisational subordination of the Crisis Staffs to the president of the Assembly himself. I needn't remind you that this was Krajisnik. The Bosnian Serb leadership through party or republican organs issued direct orders or instructions to Crisis Staffs which were received and acted upon. Crisis Staffs in turn would cite orders and decisions from regional and central organs as the basis for their actions. The central republican authorities also supported Crisis Staffs materially through loans, direct funding, and material including weapons and ammunition. Judgement 140, 268, and 270. The Bosnian Serb leadership further tightened its grip over the municipalities on 10 June 1992 when the Presidency replaced War Presidencies with War Commissions consisting of four members including a state commissioner appointed by the Presidency. The state commissioner would appoint the other members who would have to be confirmed by the Presidency. From July 1992, Krajisnik was the Presidency member in charge of and its contact person for the war commissioners. Paragraphs 271, 274, 276, 182, and 277. The Crisis Staffs were the glue that held together the machinery working to achieve the common purpose. Under the dominant influence of the SDS, they were the coordinating body between political, military, and other forces in the municipality. Paragraph 266. They took control over the takeover of municipality with the assistance of the TO, the paramilitaries, the army, and/or the MUP. Taking control meant using them to set up check-points, disarm the non-Serb population, establish and enforce curfews, and a whole myriad of other discriminatory measures against the non-Serb population to force them to leave the territory. How the actions of political leaders furthered the common purpose is illustrated by Nedjeljko Rasula, president of the Sanski Most Municipal Assembly and deputy to the Bosnian Serb Assembly. On 22 June, around 20 detainees from Betonirka prison camp were taken to nearby Kriva Cesta where they were ordered at gunpoint by soldiers in olive-grey uniforms to dig their own graves. A group of 10 persons, among them Rasula, sat at a picnic table nearby watching the digging. When the detainees had finished, a soldier slit the throats of all but three detainees who were taken back to the camp. Then there is Dusko Kornjaca, SDS Crisis Staff president of Cajnice, SAO Herzegovina deputy minister. "In June 1992, Serb authorities destroyed the mosques." I am quoting from judgement 620. "Serb authorities destroyed the mosques in the town of Cajnice using artillery and explosives. The SDS Crisis Staff president Kornjaca was reported to be publicly enthusiastic about this action. Later in 1992, he ordered the destruction of all other Muslim religious sites in order to eradicate traces of the Muslim presence in Cajnice." Paragraph 620. I also remind you of the other local and state political leaders I mentioned under the people who committed JCE-member crimes, and what this demonstrates is that Krajisnik had and was in the company of SDS Main Board members, SDS Assembly deputies or Assembly deputies all who were involved personally in the commission of crimes across the municipalities. We're not focused on one municipality as an example. These are representative of what was happening in every municipality and the Trial Chamber chose to specifically name some of the JCE members and name others more generally like a commander of a -- of the JNA or a commander -- a local commander of the police as the person responsible for the crimes. But what is clear from all of these examples is that all of these leaders used their men to either personally commit crimes or to commit crimes that furthered the common objective. Let me now turn to the second type of principal perpetrator, not a member of the organisation. As has already been alluded to, JCE members sometimes used persons who were not members of their structure to commit crimes. These persons worked for, in concert, or in close cooperation with the organisations. Ms. Goy referred to them as local Serbs, and so will I. For example, Serb locals working as guards in and Serb locals allowed into detention camps committed crimes against detainees. We've seen several examples already. The Trial Chamber was entitled from the evidence to infer that they were used by the JCE members responsible for the camps. As discussed earlier in the Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje camps run by the MUP and the VRS, detainees were executed and subjected to severe mistreatment which included psychological abuse, beatings, sexual assaults, and torture. The crimes were also committed by Serb locals who were routinely allowed to enter the camps to abuse, beat, and kill prisoners. Paragraph 487. Another example of armed Serb locals supporting the JNA, VRS and takeover mopping operations and committing crimes of murders, destruction of property, et cetera, is found in paragraph 630. Outside the town of Foca, Serb forces took over Muslim -- took over or destroyed Muslim villages in the Foca municipality. The attacks continued until early June 1992. The Serb forces consisted of military, police, paramilitary, and sometimes Serb villagers. During attacks, Muslim houses and apartments were systematically ransacked and burnt down. Muslim villagers were rounded up or captured and sometimes beaten or killed in the process. This is one of several examples of JCE members using non-JCE members, Serb locals, to achieve the common purpose. They weren't within the structure but they worked closely in cooperation with the structure to achieve the goal of the common purpose. Sometimes the connection between the JCE member and the Serb locals is not so clear in the judgement paragraph where the reference is found. As Ms. Goy has explained, the Trial Chamber was entitled to draw inferences from the evidence underlying the entire paragraph, the entire section on the municipality, or the other parts of the judgement to find the link. The Trial Chamber did not need to specify every link for every crime. In any case, the links between the crimes and the JCE members become clear upon looking at the evidence that's cited in the judgement. Let me provide an illustration from the Bratunac municipality, paragraph 315. On May 10, 1992, Serb paramilitaries also attacked Krasan Polje in the Vitkovici -- or near Vitkovici in Bratunac municipality. On that day, over 500 Muslim men from villages in Bratunac were detained in the Vuk Karadzic school. Detainees were severely mistreated and beaten repeatedly. Dozens were killed by armed Serb locals and members of paramilitary groups. Three guards forced all detainees in a huddle in the section of the sports hall resulting in seven or eight suffocating to death. Several men were taken off by the guards and killed. About 50 detainees were beaten or shot to death by the guards in the sports hall. This paragraph identifies the principal perpetrators as armed Serb locals, members of the paramilitary groups and guards. You may ask: How was the Trial Chamber entitled to infer that they were used by JCE members? The evidence footnoted provides the answer. Exhibit P485 establishes that the head of the MUP was in charge of the Vuk Karadzic school. Part of the school building was headquarters for the Serb military forces. An armed soldier guarded the gym or sports hall. P72 establishes that JNA reservists guarded the school. The link is through the camp commander, the head of the MUP and the local commander of the JNA. The Serb locals in this example acted in concert or close cooperation with the members of the army and police when they committed the crimes furthering the common purpose. The JCE member heading the organisation would have to authorise or permit their use. Neither they nor the members of the organisation were punished or disciplined for committing the crimes. In fact, they and the members of the organisation committed these crimes again and again. They acted and were treated just like the members of the organisation. Thus when they committed crimes, the JCE member used them like members of his organisation. My answer to your question applies to all of the crimes committed by non-members. Our analysis shows that there is an answer and a link through a structure, either directly or working with a structure for every one of the crimes. There is a single factual finding, however, where the inference is attenuated. An example is contained in a lengthy paragraph in judgement paragraph 670. The paragraph describes many crimes committed against a group of Muslims who fled Presjeka village in Nevesinje municipality to the Velez mountains on 22 June 1992 after Serb forces shelled their village. The finding in question is: "Sixteen elderly persons who could not keep pace were left behind and were later killed by a local Serb." The evidence cited in the judgement does not provide more information as to the link to a JCE member. The paragraph does not find that the attacking and detaining forces -- or does find that the attacking and detaining forces surrounding this event to be Serb forces, including the VRS. Under the circumstances in light of the evidence, it was inferred, I believe, that the Trial Chamber held that the local Serb was part of the attacking Serb forces. That is an inference -- that is the only inference that is capable in light of the scantiness of the evidentiary record, but that is the single problematic link that we were able -- that we identified during the course of our review of every crime. Let me just very quickly deal with the final part of my remarks, which is the way in which acts of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Meron would like to put to you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I just would like to make sure that you address the argument made earlier by the counsel suggesting that Mr. Krajisnik, as head of parliament and not of an executive organ, could not be considered a member of a properly defined JCE because he, it was argued, was involved only in local diplomatic and political efforts. I think we sort of owe it to the counsel to -- for the Prosecutor to relate to that too. It would have been helpful, for example, if the Prosecution could point to specific speeches by the appellant establishing beyond a reasonable doubt that he shared unlawful common purpose of a JCE. Thank you, President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: First of all, I would remind the Chamber that this case is not about hate speech, that this case is about contributing -- or joining a JCE which had as its common purpose the commission of crimes, in this case the commission of serious crimes over a large, large area, crimes involving murder, extermination, persecution, deportation, and unlawful transfer. The decision on mens rea was not formed only on the speeches that Mr. Krajisnik made. It's made on the basis of all of the evidence, all of the evidence involving the participation of the Bosnian Serb leadership in the implementation and carrying out of the common purpose. Specifically on Krajisnik's mens rea, I should point Your Honour Judge Meron and the Chamber to paragraph -- or to P292, which is at tab 21, particularly at page 4 where Mr. Krajisnik says the following: "Everything we do in this parliament, everything I do personally I do exclusively for pure areas." It makes no -- there's no ambiguity with what he says. It is not a political speech said to all of the parliamentarians, this is what we're doing, and the people who are doing it are the parliamentarians who were present there. They knew what he was talking about and he knew what he was talking about. Given the mass of evidence that the Trial Chamber had before it about who was involved in these crimes, SDS members, SDS deputies, the leadership, the instrumentalisation of structures, it was -- the only conclusion that they could draw was that Mr. Krajisnik was in it as deep as everyone else. And in fact, they found as a result of the evidence that they heard he was at the top of it. He was the person, together with Karadzic, who was implementing it. They worked together to make sure that his vision of a pure area, a pure Serbia, free of Muslims and free of Croats was achievable, and they achieved it by using structures of the state in a criminal way to make sure that it was achieved. And it was achieved nine months later at the cost of 3.000 lives and at the destruction of over a hundred thousand lives of people who had lived in the region for centuries. Yes, as Mr. Dershowitz says, you've got to look at the history, but don't look at it from the perspective of the Serbs. Look at it from the perspective of the people that they drove out. If I could have five minutes, I promise to finish. Thank you. The judgement did not in most cases make an individual specific factual finding with regard to the links for three acts of persecution, unlawful detention, destruction of personal property and cultural and sacred sites. What the Trial Chamber did is it expressly dealt with the more significant examples from each municipality based on the overwhelming evidence of systematic pattern of unlawful detention, destruction of property across the indictment municipalities. This evidence allowed the inference that the acts were part of the common objective and were carried out using organisations under the control of the JCE, otherwise Serb forces. And I'll just deal with one example and then wrap up. For example, the Trial Chamber found unlawful detention in 33 municipalities, in more than 350 detention facilities. Paragraph 810. An example from Prijedor municipality illustrates how they dealt with it for detentions, 483. Serb authorities detained mostly Croat and Muslim civilians in 58 detention and collection centres in Prijedor municipality in 1992. Five of them were considered long-term detention centres, Keraterm, Trnopolje, Omarska. The police station in Prijedor town and the command posts of Miska Glava. The other 53 locations mentioned in schedule C of the indictment were places of short-term detention. Most of the Muslims and Croats in Prijedor were detained for some period of time at one of those detention or collection centres in 1992. The five detention centres mentioned are discussed in detail. The 52 others, or 53 others, are not. Although the Trial Chamber finding does not contain further details regarding who established and operated the additional unlawful detention facilities, it is our submission that the Chamber was entitled to infer these -- that these acts were part of the common objective and were operated by Serb forces or Serb authorities acting in pursuit of it. Why? Because all of the evidence demonstrated a system and pattern of detention facilities operated and used by the JCE members to carry out the common objective in their relevant municipalities. Detention was part of the pattern of attack of the non-Serb -- against the non-Serb population. Paragraph 708. The civilian detention centres were an instrument as much as they were an intermediate step in the logic of dislocation and expulsion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Paragraph 1055. Detention of civilians was used as a method of pressuring non-Serbs to leave the territory. Paragraph 1043. The same approach was used for destruction. Destruction, when you look at it carefully, was through or with the cooperation of the organisations used by the JCE members. The Serb forces used heavy artillery, mortars and tanks as well as explosives or incendiary devices to destroy non-Serb property. Paragraphs 830, 837, and 838. Destruction was part of the pattern of the attack on the non-Serb population described by the Chamber in paragraph 707 to 709. Destruction of houses rendered it impossible for the villagers to return. Paragraph 708. With regard to the destruction of cultural property, Predrag Radic testified that in 1992, Serbs destroyed mosques in various parts of the ARK in order to wipe out traces of the Muslims' existence. Paragraph 378. That the Bosnian Serb leadership accepted and approved of this systematic destruction of non-Serb private property comes from the minister of justice himself. On May 5th, 1992, Momcilo Mandic in a telephone conversation with Brano Kvesic said: "We are holding Turks under siege in Sarajevo." He added that: "We want to build a new and nice Sarajevo. We don't like this old synagogues and mosques. We have to change architecture and everything." And by April 23rd, Mandic would level a Sarajevo municipality to the ground. The Bosnian Serb leadership accepted the destruction of civilian settlements would be swift and vast. Trifko Radic reported to the Bosnian Serb Assembly on 12 May 1992 that "we have no other solution but to shell and destroy towns. We have destroyed one third of Visoko, maybe tonight another third will go." Paragraph 974. Our position is that using a descriptive approach was justified giving the consistent pattern of recurring detentions, recurring destructions during attacks and takeovers which were all directed to drive out the non-Serb population from the indictment municipalities. The Trial Chamber reasonably concluded that the acts of detention and destruction were committed by Serb authorities or Serb forces and that they could be linked to JCE members carrying out the common objective. Each of these facilities and each of these acts were commanded by a leader on the ground, whether it's a local police leader, a local military leader, a Crisis Staff member, the link is there. The link is a structural link and the link is a human link. The human link is the JCE member whether he is defined or not, whether he was found to have committed crimes or not. And our position is that it was not necessary for the Trial Chamber to look to each and every crime committed throughout the nine years or the -- I'm sorry, the nine months from -- in the indictment period and link the actual physical perpetrator to a JCE member specifically by name. That is not required. The evidence showed clearly that the leaders of the structures were controlled and -- by JCE members who shared the common plan, and the crimes that they committed were a part of the common objective. There could be no doubt that all of the crimes committed by the Serb forces in the takeovers and following the takeovers, particularly in respect of detention and destruction crimes, were committed by them and were part of the common objective and, therefore, properly linked. Unless you have some questions, those are my submissions.

MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: [Microphone not activated] ... Either is acceptable. I would prefer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We resume the hearing, and I will give the floor to the Defence for the reply of the appellant as scheduled. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Again, I'd like to thank the Tribunal for both allowing me the opportunity to make the presentation and also for your arranging to have lunch before it was necessary for me to present our reply, and particularly because it gave me an opportunity to look at the document that the Prosecutor had made reference to about the pure area, a reference we had never seen, a reference which is not contained anywhere in the decision. There is a discussion, however, on paragraph 905, excuse me, 905 in the decision which explains that reference, and it's very interesting. It starts off -- in the decision it says: "The accused deftly handled the political fracture at the February 28, 1992, meeting of the Deputies Club." And if you read the five pages of notes, you will see that Mr. Krajisnik did deftly handle the problem. What was happening is he was pushing for a vote and a constitutional determination to be made following the Cutileiro recommendations which had been made and that if you read the minutes, what happened was a separate group from Krajina was looking to expand Serbia into Muslim areas. They wanted a much wider Serbia, and he was looking for a more limited Serbia covering the sections that had extensive populations of Serbians and not wanting to expand in as the other group, the more radical group, wanted. And if you review the four or five pages, they are so reflective of everything that we have been saying from the beginning. He talks about: "Therefore, it is good for us to all understand, to forgive one another if something we say sometimes without a solid basis," he's referring to the other side, "we must find a way to solve the problem. I think we can find a solution." He goes on to say, "I don't think they're bad people." He's referring now to those who want to expand, and he's talking about, "As far as the constitutional -- constitution is concerned, gentlemen, we need this constitution, and I hope at that God willing we will finish in a month or two. We need a democracy of Bosnia." He goes -- it's a full reflection in every sense of a political position. The quote that was referred to is also interesting. It goes on and it starts discussing, "Tomorrow let them adopt the constitution." He was talking about having the Serbian people, by its constitution, make a determination as to whether they wanted to adopt the more limited Cutileiro Plan or to allow others who are looking for a more expansive view to adopt their more expansive view, and he was pushing for the more limited view at that time. And it goes: "We don't have to fear that much. They are Serbs -- we are Serbs. We cannot understand reality. God help the Serbian people. No one has the right to do that, bypassing our unity. I tell you, everything we do in this parliament, everything I do personally I do exclusively through pure areas of [unintelligible] Herzegovina [unintelligible]. I will not yield that right to tell the people of Krajina that they are not right." What he is saying is, we want the section that had been discussed earlier by the international community, a section that was primarily Serbian and not expanding to territories which were not Serbian, and therefore the other group which wanted to expand, he was saying no, let the constitution apply. In response to Judge Meron's question of Ms. Goy, she said that they had previously filed documents stating their position as to which were the critical paragraphs which showed that Mr. Krajisnik joined the -- the JCE, and I have pulled out five or six of the critical paragraphs that they rely upon and I'd like to read some of them. Paragraph 115 is referred to in their answer in paragraph 23. "During the session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly held on February 25, 1992, the accused told the deputies that the Serb people had two options before them; namely, to fight by political means or make the most out of the present time as a first phase or to break off the talks and go for what we have done over the centuries, win our own territory by force." That's a reflection of his so-called agreeing to allow the Muslims and the Croats to be forcibly removed. All he is talking about is, "We want to do it democratically or we should do it -- or we may be stuck doing it by force." The next references are on page -- it's paragraph 910. As Mr. Krajisnik recalled in his 1994 speech. We're talking about after. The battle of the republic began on 18 March 1992, the day on which the Bosnian Serb leadership in the person of the accused made known to the Assembly deputies its wish to pre-emptively take over territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina while separating the Bosnian Serbs from the other two ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down. Thank you. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: There's no citation to that. And the next section says: "The essence of the accused's message to the representatives of the Bosnian Serb people was that he wanted new facts created on the ground in order to strengthen the hand of the Bosnian Serb negotiators of whom himself and Karadzic were the most prominent. The accused acknowledged that strengthening a negotiating position through the creation of facts which were the very subject of the negotiations was not a fair method yet he insinuated better that the Serbs be unfair to the Muslims than vice versa. The government says the March 18th speech was a call to arms." It was not a call to arms. What it was was an indication that what you do is if you want to set up a plan, it had been proposed internationally, the Muslims had rejected it at that point. He wanted to implement that plan at that point in time by having municipal governments in place so that they can run that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When Bosnia and Herzegovina announced publicly and was -- that it was withdrawing from Yugoslavia, and it was determined that it would be recognised, the desire was to have an area as had been negotiated and discussed, an area within the larger Bosnia-Herzegovina which had -- which was mostly Serbian, which had a government in place to address the concerns of the Serbians, and then what you do is you have the entities as they had had and as they now have, the different entities joining together in a constitutional format in order to proceed. Page -- paragraph 923 is the same. Paragraphs 1003 -- I'd like to read all of them, but I don't think that that's a valuable use of time. They cite at 1003 which to some extent is viewed as the most critical of their paragraphs and it says: "At the Assembly session of July 25, 1992, the accused asserted that the takeover of the territory to date had been insufficient. The people created the borders and we have to agree here today on territory that are not under our control right now but to which we claim rights due to them being ethnic territories. We then stretch the desired extent," and then it gives the boundaries as to which they are seeking. Again, it's a political assertion of what is desirable under the circumstances. And the final cite is to paragraph 1015. "Other events also drew the accused away from Pale," and then it goes on to describe a statement that he made that all Serb patriots will have the same emblem, the Serb tricolours, as if that is a call to arms. Now, what I think is significant is that at least as the Chamber made the determination, and this Chamber has used similar language too, in the Brdjanin decision, this Court said: "Where convictions under the first category of JCE are concerned, the accused must both intend the commission of the crime and intend to participate in a common plan aimed at its commission." With all due respect, I think this Chamber said it backwards. What I mean by that is first you have to have the joint criminal enterprise intending to carry out the acts to further the joint criminal enterprise. So first you have the joint criminal enterprise, and then you have the acts in furtherance of the joint criminal enterprise. Having said that, a decision -- the court below said we first have to find out when we had the joint criminal enterprise and when he was a party to that joint criminal enterprise. The date that was selected was an April of 1992 date, and the only things that occurred prior to that are all of these political statements. To the extent that the government -- the Prosecutors are suggesting that he gained knowledge later, which we both reject factual and legally, whether simply having gained knowledge is sufficient. But assuming for the moment that he gained the knowledge and therefore at that point he joined the JCE, the question is when? He would then not be responsible for the implementation of the plan prior to his joining. You do not apply it retroactively. So that, for example, if an event occurred in April but he didn't have knowledge of the JCE until July, he would not be under the JCE doctrine responsible for what occurred in April, May, June prior to the time when he became a member. So you have a decision here that April is the critical date, and I suggest there is nothing on the April date of -- there's nothing by the date when the claim and the decision was made that he was a member which supports that conclusion, and the knowledge later is insufficient. And even if that works, you still need a determination of when, and then what acts he's responsible for thereafter. The decision is blank on that because it decided the April date, which I suggest is inappropriate. Let me just touch for one minute on some of the questions with respect to linkage. Two points I wanted to make. The first is that the Prosecutor makes it sound as if Chambers below followed Brdjanin. As you know, the Brdjanin came down well after the decision below, so it clearly was not following and intending to comply with this Court's decision, which I know is over at least one Justice's dissent. The second is that I tried, and I have not been able to do this as thoroughly as I would have liked over the break, but having listened to the listing provided by the Prosecutor, I don't believe any of those people by name are listed in the indictment. You have such a vast array of entities listed in the indictment that it then becomes easy for them to say anyone who we can show committed the war crimes, since we said it's the army or we said it's the municipal governments or we said it's the Crisis Committee, whatever they say it was since they've listed that in the indictment, they simply pluck that name out. They say this person committed a war crime. Therefore, this person was a member of the JCE. If they cannot find the name to pluck out, they simply say that person was acting pursuant to the military, pursuant to the -- you know, the gangs that were roving, pursuant to anything they want. It all gets lumped in, and therefore they have satisfied the linkage. And I've just re-read parts of Brdjanin, and I don't believe for one second that the decision intended that result. It was being quite specific in talking about, sure, you can retain someone as your instrument to carry out the -- your objective as part of the JCE, not working the other way of saying anyone who committed a war crime, now we have to do -- trace it backwards, which is what they are attempting do now. And with all due respect, it's a backward process. They shouldn't be coming in here today trying to justify the decision and the indictment by looking through the mass of evidence to see if they can support and then scratching out some that they can't support and doing it that way. Thank you. Let me turn over the floor. Thank you. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: I would like to respond to first Ms. Goy and then Mr. Kremer. Ms. Goy correctly points out a distinction between the actus reus on the one hand and the contribution on the other, but that distinction disappears in this case, because all of the evidence that goes to proving or trying to prove that he was a member of the JCE is exactly the same evidence as his contribution. They are his political activities and his speech. There is no separate activity that is evidence of joining and not evidence of his significant contribution or vice versa. In other words, what they're doing is they're counting twice, and what they're essentially arguing is that political speech can be both the only evidence that he joined a JCE and also the only evidence of his substantial contribution, and they can't point to a single instance of a speech pursuant to the question of Judges that would be a criminal speech or a speech involving crime. In fact, the fact that they had to invoke one speech that's not even referred to in the transcript, in the judgement itself, shows that there are no speeches that they can really find, no speeches that are referred to, and there are dozens and dozens and dozens of speeches referred to in the judgement, and they don't point to a single speech referred to in the judgement as evidence of criminal conduct and the only one they find is taken out of context, was never seen by the defendant and is only in an appendix to the opinion. They acknowledge that the vast majority of crimes were committed by non-members, which is really a response to the question put by one of the justices. In the event that there isn't sufficient linkage, it really means the whole conviction has to go. If the vast majority of the crimes were committed by non-members, you can't save the conviction because of spill-over jurisprudence just because there were some crimes perhaps committed by members. And as my brother pointed out, members who became members only upon committing the crimes. They were not named as members previously which really goes to the essence of what Kremer's argument was. Mr. Kremer very poignantly, with tears in my eyes and I'm sure in the Court's eyes, went over these horrible cases of rape and of rape in front of family members and killing of children and all these incredibly horrible acts that took place but never pointed to whether or not any of those acts were intended by the defendant, whether they were part of a later agreement by the defendant, whether they were predictable, foreseeable under stage 3. There's simply no evidence that the defendant here ever learned of these acts until after he heard the transcript of the trial itself. So the catalogue of terrible acts may help to explain why there is a prosecution here and why there are so many people who would like to see this prosecution affirmed, but it bears no relationship, because what's missing -- the missing link in this case is any linkage between the defendant himself and the acts committed by the people in the field. What conceivable benefit -- let's assume there's a goal to have some kind of separation or ethnic purity. How is that served by, just to be brutal and gruesome to quote from the government, having somebody have to eat the body parts of somebody else or somebody engage in the rape of children, all these kinds of activities? They are plainly not intended or foreseeable. Yes, every war, almost every war has brutality that goes with it. That doesn't make every waging of a war a war crime. Mr. Kremer describes the group as something that Mr. Krajisnik joined, and he should have known what he was joining because of the other members of the group. You know, it sounds almost as if he's applying for membership in a club. That's not the way it worked. He didn't join. He didn't come in one day and get initiated into the Mafia by having a pinprick in his finger. He didn't join the Ku Klux Klan. He didn't join the Nazi party or the Gestapo. He didn't join anything. The Court imposed on him a conceptual framework saying that over time, without specifying exactly when, he should be deemed to have been part of, not that he joined. And it also makes it sound, when you here the government's presentation or the Prosecution's presentation, like he exercised control over those who committed the crimes. But there is an explicit finding by the Court on page 402 that he did not exercise effective control at any point in time over these activities. Now, the Prosecution cites some reference to some War Commissions that were appointed late in the process, but if one goes and reads the description of the War Commissions, one finds they were a one-way process; that is, their only task was to report the work to other members of the Presidency. Put another way, the information all came back to them. They had no authority to direct activities. At worst, this would go to the issue of knowledge and mens rea. It doesn't in any way go to the issue of actus reus, because according to the judgement itself, it was a one-way information flow. The other point cited by the Prosecution is that the defendant here may have appointed one or two commissioners, but without any further information, who were these commissioners, would he have known in advance, did these commissioners in fact commit any crimes, the very fact that he may have had some responsibility for appointing commissioners in no way, again, goes to the actus reus, particularly in light of the finding of the Court that he exercised no control. Therefore, the Prosecution is led, finally, to conclude that the defendant, and I'm quoting from them, "was in the company of," "in the company of," and then it points to members of SDS. Not even in the company of any of the criminals. And if that's not guilt by association, I don't know what is. In the company of. Not even a description of what happened while they were in the company of. And then: "These leaders use their men to commit crimes." But there's into evidence linking this defendant to any of the people who committed any of the crimes. He didn't know these people. He had no association with them. Mr. Kremer correctly points out this is not a case about hate speech, but speech is the central evidence, and it doesn't even rise to the level of hate speech. We're talking about political speech. We're talking about what the Court acknowledges as political deftness, of using his political savvy, all in the interest of trying to get the best possible deal he could for his constituency. And he did get that deal. Ultimately, he got a deal through the Dayton Accords and that's what he is responsible for. He is responsible for the negotiation. Does his negotiation position strengthen with developments on the ground? Of course, every negotiator understands that. And the point about pure areas as was explained bears no relationship. Not only that, but it couldn't be an incitement speech because as the Prosecution concedes it was stated only in front of a small number of people as part of a speech relating to why the constitution should be ratified and why the extremist Bosnian view should be rejected. The pure areas were eventually achieved by diplomacy. Finally, because I know because I'm running out of time and I would hope to invite any further questions, Mr. Kremer after a brilliantly evocative statement of all the crimes again which caused tremendous compassion, then said that these things must be "looked at from the point of view of the victims." And the mens rea and the actus reus have to be looked at not from the point of view of the defendant but the point of view of the victims. With all due respect, I beg to differ. This is a criminal case. Now, obviously the victims' perspective helped frame the jurisdiction of this court and explained the reasons why this court has been set up to do its very important duty, but when it comes to deciding the guilt of the defendant, it must be viewed from the perspective of what the defendant knew, when he knew it, what did he do, when did he do it, what is the evidence of an agreement. It must be looked at through the prism of the defendant's actions and through the prism of the defendant's state of mind. And when looked at that way, these horrible, horrible crimes must be punished and have been punished and will be punished, but they must be punished by punishing the right person in the right proportion to what that person did. And the idea that, as Ms. Goy put it, his role may have been central, those are quotes, his role may have been crucial, but they were political: "His role was political. It may have been crucial and central to achieving the overall political result that was sought in this case by political means." But if one goes through all of the speeches as we have gone through, there is never a call to arms. There is a call to disarmament. There is never a call to violence. There is a call to constitutionalism. There is never a call for ethnic cleansing. There is a call for compromise. There is never a call for a war crime. There is a call to avoid war. And the implications of an affirmance of this conviction would be that if a political figure seeking peace is in a troubled world where there is war and where there are war crimes being committed, he may not remain on and engage in his political activities, political activities which may be essential to resolving the dispute peacefully. Mr. Krajisnik could have been a man of lack courage and have left the country, as many did. He could have remained silent in the face of what was going on. He did not do that. He continued his political activities and it's for continuing his political activities that he has been prosecuted and sentenced to life imprisonment, essentially, for a man his age. So what we urge the Court to do and we know the Court will do it, is to please read as thoroughly as possible all the speeches, all the allegations and to make its own conclusion and draw its own inferences and to apply the standards that we have suggested that when there are doubts they must be resolved in favour of political aspects of speech and that without a finding of criminal conduct, without a finding of criminal actions this defendant cannot stand convicted of these serious war crimes. Thank you, Your Honours. If there are any questions, I'd be happy to respond to them now or at any time during the proceedings. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. No questions. So this concludes Mr. Krajisnik's appeal. We move on now to the amicus curiae appeal, and I will give the floor to the amicus curiae for half an hour for his submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just ask the Tribunal to go into private session for a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. President, you will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, please, you may go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this morning you ordered that there should be no reference to the evidence of two witnesses who I believe are witnesses on the issue of a fair trial. We have no intention at all of referring to that evidence, but what we do wish you to know is and, as you know, our brief is highly critical of who of the counsel for Mr. Krajisnik at the trial, and it's our intention to refer to what is in our public brief. We are not going to refer directly in any event to any of the matters in our --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask that all microphones that are not used to be switched off. Thank you. We have difficulties following the speaker. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I do propose is that when I reach any matter that relates to anything in the confidential brief, I shall refer the Chamber to the paragraphs in that brief, and I shall ask the Chamber to read those paragraphs at the appropriate time. I hope that that accords with the Chamber's wishes. The matters that we refer to are obviously of public importance. They do not involve issues of protection of witnesses or indeed matters of public order.

utterances.text: I believe you can proceed that way if you so wish. The important is that no confidential matter is brought to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. May the Chamber then please go into public session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I propose firstly to address the issue of fair trial on which I expect to spend about 20 minutes and then to follow shortly on the issue of JCE for approximately 10 minutes. Because of time constraints, I shall not be addressing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: President, since the time of amicus is going to be fairly limited, with your permission could I pose what for me is a critical issue so that he would be able to address it in his argument? Thank you, President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You will discuss, I know from what we said, the competency claims. In your brief you asserted regarding trial counsel to Mr. Krajisnik, especially in light of the additional evidence and I will not refer to that. The specific point I have is this one: In your brief you noted that Mr. Stewart, in February 2005, readily admitted in court that he had read no more than 15 per cent of the relevant documents. Nonetheless, the Trial Chamber denied the motion for adjournment and the Appeals Chamber affirmed. In light of those decisions, is your argument about Mr. Stewart's level of preparations in a way settled or not, and is it your argument that taken together the totality of Defence counsel's actions and the Trial Chamber decisions in essence deprived the appellant of effective legal assistance? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say straight away that the answer to your second question is yes, that the Chamber has to look at the totality of the evidence, and it has to look at the evidence as it is at the end of the trial. The Chamber can look at the matter with hindsight and, as in all manners of this kind, should look at the evidence as a whole. I hope shortly that answers the question at this stage. As I was saying, I propose to speak about fair trial for a period of about 20 minutes, then 10 minutes on JCE, and then subsequently in reply, Mr. Jones will be able to take up other matters on JCE and there's an issue of deportation about which we have informed the Prosecution. I turn then firstly to fair trial. As a defendant before the Tribunal and as a participant in the Tribunal's legal aid programme, Mr. Krajisnik had a right to fair trial, which includes the right to the effective assistance of counsel. Although the right of counsel is only one of a defendant's minimum guarantees, it is perhaps the clearest illustration of their interdependence, because where a defendant exercises the right to counsel, counsel becomes, in effect, the facilitator of all other guarantees. The right to disclosure, to cross-examine, to present evidence, the right to adequate time and resources are rendered worthless if counsel does not exercise his functions effectively. Regrettably, in our submission, that is what happened to Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik was originally represented at the pre-trial stage by Mr. Brashich, an attorney from New York, and later, mainly in trial, by Mr. Stewart, a Queen's Counsel from England. It is our submission that both of them, individually and cumulatively, provided grossly ineffective assistance and the trial was rendered systemically unfair. I deal first with Mr. Brashich. Mr. Brashich was Mr. Krajisnik's lead counsel for just over two years. He was removed by the Registry ten days before the trial was due to commence for failing to disclose that he'd been suspended from practice. He had eight prior admonitions for professional misconduct, mainly for charging excessive fees. In the 25 months that he was lead counsel, his team billed 26.500 hours of legal work, the equivalent of one person working a 40-hour week for 13 years, and it cost the Tribunal $1.5 million. In spite of this, he produced no useful work product. On the 12th of May, 2003, following his removal as counsel, he had the audacity to tell Judge Orie that most of the preparation he had done was, unfortunately, locked in his brain. Mr. Stewart was assigned as lead counsel in July 2003, and a target trial date was fixed for the 2nd of February, 2004. When Mr. Stewart asked Mr. Brashich for his work product, Mr. Brashich pretended not to understand what he meant. When two and a half months before the trial Mr. Stewart finally received the full case papers, many of them had the seals intact. They were, according to Mr. Stewart, a complete shambles and an absolute mess. Such work product as emerged was, according to Mr. Stewart, trivial in amount and made no significant contribution to the preparation for trial. It is axiomatic that the main work of an advocate, especially in complex cases, is undertaken before the trial commences. Pre-trial preparation is critical to an effective defence. There can be no doubt that Mr. Brashich's failures to disclose his suspension, hand over the case papers promptly, provide a well-ordered work product violated his duties of competence and diligence under the Tribunal's Code of Professional Conduct. The Prosecution has, as I understand it, not disputed that conclusion. The result of Mr. Brashich's misconduct created -- as a result of Mr. Brashich's misconduct, a situation of unparalleled seriousness had arisen in what was until then, barring Milosevic, the Tribunal's most complex trial. Unless Mr. Stewart promptly and fully informed the Trial Chamber of the gravity of the situation and the Chamber allowed his team sufficient pre-trial time to prepare a defence, Mr. Krajisnik had no prospect of a fair trial. It is manifestly clear that neither happened. Mr. Stewart failed to apply for a pre-trial adjournment in spite of advice from experienced co-counsel referred to in our brief at paragraph 35. When five months into the trial and struggling for survival Mr. Stewart applied for a substantial adjournment, it was too late. His team was drowning in a pile of papers he'd still not been able to sort out, let alone adequately review, let alone read. In desperation he confessed, "I should have brought this very specifically to the attention of the Chamber a long time ago, and I wish I had, but I've done today, and the Chamber has to look at it now, in the circumstances now, and we do need time." As amicus, with a duty to protect Mr. Krajisnik's interest, we have considered carefully whether Mr. Stewart was grossly ineffective as counsel. Such allegations are not easily made, especially against advocates of his standing. The Appeals Chamber laid down in November last year in the Barayagwiza case the test to be applied where an appellant alleges ineffective assistance of counsel. At paragraph 131 of the judgement it said: "An appellant must establish that his counsel's incompetence was so manifest as to oblige the trial to act -- Chamber to act. He must further demonstrate that the Trial Chamber's failure to intervene occasioned a miscarriage of justice." There are thus three requirements, manifest incompetence, the Chamber's failure to act, a miscarriage of justice. We have argued in our brief that as a matter of human rights law it should be enough for an appellant to show that he was denied effective assistance of counsel and thus denied his right to fair trial. We submit that all three requirements laid down in Barayagwiza are met. The incompetence of the Stewart team is manifest. The Trial Chamber failed to act, or at least act effectively, and it caused a miscarriage of justice. In our appeal brief, we set out in detail the reasons why we submit Mr. Stewart's stewardship was manifestly incompetent. He commenced a trial grossly unprepared, not having read the papers, taken adequate instructions, or conducted sufficient investigations in the field. He failed promptly to bring the severity of the situation to the Trial Chamber's attention by not fully acknowledging its seriousness and by failing to apply for a pre-trial adjournment. He failed to utilise his pre-trial resources properly by employing insufficient staff and failing to give the case his full attention. He systematically failed to appeal significant decisions which impacted significantly on the fairness of the trial. It should go without saying that counsel who commences a trial without reviewing the bulk of the disclosed papers, developing an effective defence strategy, being in a position to cross-examine witnesses adequately or adduce effective evidence is bound to be ineffective. If that is correct, a trial conducted in such circumstances is unfair. The fact that any case, let alone one of this complexity, should come on for trial when there had been no effective trial -- pre-trial preparation was bound to raise grave questions for the Trial Chamber. Should it have given Mr. Stewart more time before the trial commenced? Should it adjourn the trial until Mr. Stewart was properly prepared? Should it try to salvage the trial by granting adjournments piecemeal when Mr. Stewart requested? More significantly, could mid-trial adjournments ever make up for a lack of pre-trial preparation? The Chamber was aware four days before the trial of Mr. Stewart's difficulties on disclosure as set out in paragraphs 24 and 72 of our brief which we urge the Chamber to read. With the advantage of hindsight, as I answered Judge Meron a moment or two ago, with the advantage of hindsight and reviewing the fairness of the trial as a whole as required on appeal, it is our submission that the Trial Chamber failed in its responsibilities for ensuring a fair trial by failing to adjourn the trial at that stage. On the first day of the trial, the Chamber granted Mr. Stewart a month's adjournment so he could prepare cross-examination of the first Prosecution witness. In the following 12 months, there were five more short adjournments. The Chamber refused two motions for substantial adjournments, one of which was upheld on appeal. Thirteen months into the trial, however, referring to the tens of thousands of pages of documents in his office, Mr. Stewart told the Chamber that his team had read no more than 15 per cent of them. "I haven't read many of them. I don't even know what they are. I don't have enough B/C/S resources to find out what they are. It is absolutely impossible. The position is hopeless." His case manager had left. His counsel had -- co-counsel had given notice because her cross-examination was hampered by not having the time and resources to read and analyse Prosecution documents. Finally, she left because, as she said, they could not provide an effective defence in the time that has been available and all the implications that that carries for a fair trial for Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik was remarkably patient. Eventually he requested equivocally, not without surprise, to self-represent, because he said, self-representation could not make it any worse. The Chamber allowed him to supplement Mr. Stewart's cross-examination by his own efforts with, as Mr. Stewart said, disastrous results. Mr. Stewart and his team definitely thought Mr. Krajisnik was prejudiced. At the defence stage, Judge Orie, though originally not doubting Mr. Stewart's competence, castigated him for failing to meet deadlines, described his team's work product as seriously deficient and expressed grave concern at their failure to identify expert witnesses. The Trial Chamber, though doing its best to salvage a trial which should never have commenced, failed in our submission in its responsibility for ensuring fair trial by granting only periodic adjournments when it was obvious to everyone that the Stewart team was manifestly incompetent. Its lack of preparation had affected the whole trial process. The Prosecution claim that Mr. Krajisnik has failed to establish he was prejudiced. The Chamber will recall that I requested that my remit as amicus should be expanded to include the appointment of an independent investigator into the deficiencies of Mr. Stewart's team. The request was denied. The burden of establishing prejudice has therefore fallen on Mr. Krajisnik himself, and he has filed a notice to admit additional evidence which he believes would have assisted his defence. The Chamber will ask whether Mr. Stewart's refusal was a responsible strategic decision or, as Mr. Stewart said, because of lack of time. If it was for lack of time, was the Trial Chamber failing in its duty to ensure a fair trial? In a leadership case of this scale, it was essential to identify and utilise expert testimony on relevant military, political, demographic, and constitutional issues. In direct contradiction to Mr. Krajisnik's entreaties, Mr. Stewart called no expert witnesses to rebut the evidence of the experts on whom the Prosecution replied to establish that Mr. Krajisnik, alongside Mr. Karadzic, was at the apex of power in the Bosnian Serb republic. The wrongful omission of expert evidence in those circumstances deprived Mr. Krajisnik of an opportunity to establish the parameters of his constitutional role and authority in day-to-day political and military affairs. The Trial Chamber's findings on Mr. Krajisnik's individual responsibility may well have been very different if he'd been able to present expert evidence on this issue. I referred when I began to the interdependence of fair trial guarantees, that the minimal rights to disclosure, to cross-examine, to give evidence and obtain the attendance of witnesses are worthless if counsel cannot exercise his functions effectively. In our submission, it was manifest that the Stewart team's lack of pre-trial preparation not only placed the trial at risk but on examining its history, as the Chamber will examine it now, made a fair trial impossible. Justice Robert Jackson said of the Nuremberg trials, "We must never forget that the record on which we judge these defendants today is the record on which history will judge us tomorrow. To pass these defendants a poison chalice is to put it to our own lips as well." The Brashich scandal, the ensuing ineffective representation of the Stewart team, and the failure of the Trial Chamber to act effectively, in our submission denied Mr. Krajisnik a fair trial. Your Honours, those are my submissions on that first issue. I pass very, very shortly to what I have to say about JCE. Firstly, contrary to the Prosecution's submission, we submit it's clear from the last sentence at paragraph 1098 of the judgement that the Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Krajisnik of JCE I, not JCE III. Secondly, as to JCE III, the Trial Chamber never explicitly found Mr. Krajisnik guilty of that, nor did it specifically find that the new crimes were foreseeable consequences of the original crimes. The mere fact that a person in a leadership position knows that if war comes it will lead to bloodshed is insufficient to establish JCE III liability. Unfortunately, all wars entail bloodshed. The Chamber's findings on JCE I are flawed in our submission because they acquaint knowledge of the new crimes with acceptance and acceptance with intent. This dilutes the requirement of mens rea. The Chamber said at paragraph 1098: "With acceptance of the actual commission of new types of crime and continued contribution to the objective comes intent. On this basis, if Mr. Krajisnik became informed of the new crimes, for example unlawful detention, sexual violence, murder of civilians, and nonetheless continued with the common plan, then he accepted those crimes and with acceptance comes intent." In our submission that is not good enough. For example, two men agree to burgle a house. During the course of the burglary one of them, unknown to the other, shoots the householder. If the other burglar, knowing of the shooting carries on with the burglary, the fact that he knew of the shooting and continued with the common plan means that he intended the killing. That can't be correct. Another reason why the Chamber's finding on JCE I is flawed is it imputes crimes to Mr. Krajisnik without, as the Chamber has recognised, establishing a link between the perpetrators and Mr. Krajisnik or another member of the JCE. In our submission, the Chamber failed to make crucial findings on imputation of crimes committed by JCE members because it failed to go through the required process of applying the law to the evidence and satisfying itself that each of the crimes of which Mr. Krajisnik was convicted could be imputed to at least one member of the JCE. On the Trial Chamber's analysis, the link was established by the accused or the Bosnian Serb leadership being informed of crimes committed by the direct perpetrators, but the Appeals Chamber has made it clear in Brdjanin the link has to flow the other way, not from direct perpetrators to a JCE member but from a JCE member to the direct perpetrators with a JCE member using the direct perpetrators as tools or instruments to carry out the common plan or ordering or instigating them to commit crimes. We illustrated this in our brief at paragraph 152 with a diagram showing how the Trial Chamber turned the correct JCE model on its head. It's wrong, we say, because it creates too open-ended form of liability whereby an accused becomes responsible for crimes committed by those with whom he has no connection by virtue of him being -- becoming informed of their crimes. The Tribunal has repeatedly emphasised the injustice of holding an accused responsible for a crime where the link is too remote or tenuous both in the context of JCE and in the context of command responsibility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. I see there are no questions. I will give now the floor to the Prosecution for their response.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon. Ms. Goy and I will now present arguments in response to amicus curiae's appeal. First, I will address ground 1, subgrounds (a), (b), and (c), relating to fair trial and then Ms. Goy will argue ground 3 with respect to joint criminal enterprise. With respect to any grounds of appeal or arguments not addressed today, of course we are relying on our written submissions set out in the response brief and I now turn to ground 1. This ground of appeal must fail because Mr. Krajisnik had a fair trial. The Trial Chamber at all times had a close eye on the proceedings and ensured that the trial as a whole was fair. The specific fair trial guarantees set out in Article 21 of the statute were afforded to Mr. Krajisnik. In particular, he was represented by counsel at all times and effectively communicated with his Defence. He had a reasonable opportunity to answer the charges against him. He cross-examined Prosecution witnesses through counsel and was allowed to put questions himself. He was able to put all relevant defence arguments before the Court and to influence the outcome of the proceedings. In particular, he testified himself for 40 days, presenting his entire defence and explaining his version of events. He called 24 witnesses. He filed a detailed final trial brief and presented closing arguments through counsel. In addition, the Chamber ensured that Mr. Krajisnik had adequate time and facilities to prepare his defence. The Chamber granted the Defence numerous adjournments throughout trial. Thus the trial was fair. The sub-grounds (a), (b) and(c) must be dismissed because none of the alleged failings of former counsel constitute gross incompetence and Krajisnik was afforded a practical and effective defence. He had adequate time and facilities and any restrictions imposed by the Trial Chamber were within its discretion under its trial management duties. None of the alleged violations constitute a breach of Krajisnik's fair trial rights resulting in actual prejudice. I will now turn to subground (a) with respect to ineffective assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can you please slow down a bit for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I apologise. As has been held by the Appeals Chamber in the Blagojevic case, paragraph 23 of the appeals judgement, there is a strong presumption of competence of counsel which can only be rebutted by evidence to the contrary. An appellant must among other things demonstrate gross incompetence. This has not been done. As I have described to Your Honours, Krajisnik had a practical and effective defence, had the opportunity to answer the charges and present his defence through cross-examination, through his witnesses and his testimony. The Trial Chamber, after 18 months of trial, in its self-representation decision concluded that the Defence team was competent, dedicated, functioning and working with the accused. This is paragraph 35 of the decision. The three individual examples of Chamber's criticism of counsel, which are listed in paragraph of amicus curiae reply, cannot undermine this overall evaluation of competence. Indeed, the first example is a reference to Prosecution's submissions and the other two relate to inadequate 65 ter witness summaries. Insufficient summaries do not establish incompetence of counsel. This issue was moreover resolved by the Trial Chamber which instead of determining relevant evidence on the basis of the summaries gave the Defence a general time-frame for its case enabling them to choose their witnesses freely. This can be found on transcript page 18802. Thus there was no prejudice. Amicus curiae's other arguments equally cannot rebut the presumption of competence. The ineffective assistance claim against Mr. Brashich failed. Amicus curiae argues that Mr. Brashich's failures contributed to inadequate time and facilities for the preparation of the defence. However, the Appeals Chamber already considered the impact of Mr. Brashich's removal on adequate time of -- and facilities, including his failure to hand over materials and his failure to provide work product to new counsel. Despite these failures, the Appeals Chamber found no error in the Trial Chamber's conclusion that overall Krajisnik had adequate time and facilities to prepare his defence. Thus there can be no impact of Brashich's failures on Krajisnik's fair trial. There's also no reason to revisit this decision, because it was not established that replacement counsel, Mr. Stewart, was grossly incompetent. With respect to former counsel Mr. Stewart, amicus curiae simply disagrees with strategic decisions made at trial and attempts to show how in retrospect they may have been proven wrong. As established by the Appeals Chamber in the Nikolic Rule 115 decision of 9 December 2004 in paragraph 37, this is insufficient to show gross negligence. I'd like to comment on some specific examples raised. First, Krajisnik was able to challenge Trial Chamber decisions before the Appeals Chamber. Counsel indeed appealed the Chamber's second adjournment decision and failed. The mere listing of procedural and discretionary decisions which counsel allegedly failed to appeal cannot establish misconduct. There is no indication of any potential error in the Trial Chamber's decisions that could support the allegation that counsel should have appealed them. Second, Krajisnik called 24 witnesses in his defence and testified for 40 days himself. Now, no examples of alleged failures in the selection of witnesses, save for the reference to expert testimony, nor has it been shown how these failures contributed to the Chamber's assessment of Krajisnik's low credibility. The decision not to call experts does not per se render the trial unfair. Mr. Stewart was reasonable to weigh the value of expert testimony against that of other evidence. Also, the evidence of the Prosecution experts was tested in cross-examination and through witnesses called by Mr. Krajisnik. For example, government witnesses, Assembly witnesses, and army witnesses. There's further no specific example of the alleged failure to test the Prosecution evidence adequately. For these reasons, the presumption of competence was not rebutted. And before I move to the next subground I would like to briefly go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to briefly comment on the two statements admitted by Your Honours as additional evidence. Since the decision came out last night, we've been unable so far to look further into the matter, but our primary position at this point is threefold. First, the statements should not be relied upon because they're largely subjective and entirely untested assessments by persons who were at some point in time members of the Defence team. They cannot rebut, either individually or cumulatively with the other allegations, the presumption of competence of senior counsel. Second, some of these allegations, albeit not in the form of written evidence, were indeed brought to the attention of the Chamber by former counsel Mr. Stewart who described them as untruthful and scurrilous attacks. And I refer you to transcript page 9599 to 9602. The Chamber in response stated that it was willing to accept that counsel was hard-working and spending time on the case. Transcript page 9601. Despite these allegations, the Chamber did not consider that counsel's competence was an issue and did not act under Rule 46 of the Rules. Third, the Trial Chamber in its self-representation decision in August 2005 acknowledged that problems existed but that such problems had now largely been solved. That is in paragraph 35 of the decision. No gross incompetence or prejudice has been established. However, given that these statements have now been admitted, it may now be appropriate should the Appeals Chamber consider relying on those statements to give former counsel a chance to respond to these allegations. Also, since the evidence is untested, the Prosecution would like to reserve its right to investigate this matter further with a view of filing rebuttal evidence. This concludes my submissions on this issue, and we can go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you. I now move to subground 1(b), relating to adequate time and facilities. Mr. Krajisnik was afforded the right to adequate time and facilities. Amicus curiae has not established that the time available was inadequate nor that the alleged violations resulted in prejudice. As I have mentioned, the Chamber allowed the Defence numerous adjournments right from the outset of trial and throughout. The Trial Chamber sat only 18 out of 48 days right after commencement of trial, and amicus curiae has not explained why this additional time was manifestly inadequate due to the fact that it was allowed immediately after instead of before the beginning of trial. There were 141 non-sitting days. This time-frame excluded recesses and holidays. There was a block of seven free weeks when the Chamber was reconstituted. Considering these adjournments detailed in the second adjournment decision, the Appeals Chamber found there was no error in the Chamber's conclusion that there was adequate time and facilities. There's nothing subsequently that could call this decision into question. After the decision, the Chamber granted several adjournments in the Defence case. For example, in November 2005, the Trial Chamber allowed the Defence an extra seven weeks to prepare and present its case. This is on trial transcript 18801. Extra time was also given for preparation and conduct of Krajisnik's testimony. Pages 18803 to 18804 and transcript page 24601. Amicus curiae's argument under this subground must be dismissed for these reasons, and I will now turn to subground 1(c), restrictions. Amicus curiae alleges violations of the right to cross-examination and to call witnesses which fall under the equality of arms principle. However, the requirements for such a challenge have not been met because any restrictions imposed did not disadvantage Mr. Krajisnik vis-a-vis the Prosecution, and he had a fair opportunity to present his case.
