The restrictions imposed were within the Chamber's discretion and did not cause any prejudice. I will now go through some of them. The frequent adjournments indicate the Chamber's flexibility in time management. The imposition of time limits such as the 60 per cent guideline for cross-examination was not strict and within the Chamber's discretion. No error has been shown in the exercise of that discretion. Indeed the Chamber was flexible in responding to Defence requests. Cross-examination, for example, of witness Treanor was only started after a month. This is transcript page 1833. Amicus curiae also complains about the time allocated for the Defence case but does not show any error in the exercise of the discretion or how the allocated time caused prejudice. The discretion of the Trial Chamber is detailed in its decision of 16 August 2006. Another issue, while the Chamber admitted municipality binders across the bar table, it expressly restricted their size to a maximum of ten documents. This is on transcript pages 13386 to 13390. Most of these dossiers were even smaller. Complaints regarding their volume must fail. There was also sufficient time for cross-examination of Mrs. Plavsic. Krajisnik was not at any disadvantage vis-a-vis the Prosecution, who was allowed only half of the time for cross-examination. Moreover, the need for cross-examination was reduced because Mrs. Plavsic testified about very limited issues which were indicated to the parties in advance. Finally, under the subground, the Chamber did not commit any error in denying Krajisnik's request for self-representation. The Chamber was correct to consider a change from Defence counsel to self-representation in the middle of trial as a basis for restriction. It was held by the Appeals Chamber in the Seselj case on 20th of October, 2006, that there may be circumstances justifying restrictions to be assessed on a case-by-case basis. Your Honours, in this case, in footnote 22 of the self-representation decision of 1st May 2007 acknowledged that timing of the request is a relevant factor. Overall, no error has been shown, and the trial as a whole was fair. And this concludes my submissions on fair trial unless Your Honours have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Counsel, I don't remember very well the details, but sometime in 2005 Defence counsel applied for a six-month adjournment, and one of the grounds he gave was that he had read only 15 per cent of the documentation. Now, the Trial Chamber dismissed his application, and he appealed to the Appeals Chamber, which in turn upheld the decision of the Trial Chamber. Is it competent for this Appeals Chamber to go behind the decision of that Bench of the Appeals Chamber on the 15 per cent reading of the relevant documentation?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours, no. There is -- in the Blagojevic appeal it has been held that interlocutory appeals decisions address issues with finality unless there are circumstances that would call this decision into question subsequently are not considered or if there were any manifest errors that were not apparent at the time. Your Honours, in our submission there are no such circumstances that would allow for reconsideration of this appeals decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I thank you for your answer to my distinguished colleague Judge Shahabuddeen. I have some problems with your answer. The decision of the Trial Chamber of 4th March 2005, I believe it was, found that the level of preparation might have been higher, and then the Appeals Chamber affirmed that decision, applying, as it was proper, a very forgiving standard of review. Namely, we were looking for abuse of discretion. But I would suggest to you that today we have quite a different situation. We reviewed the total corpus of evidence to determine whether there was a violation of the appellant's fundamental right to counsel. So the situation is quite different before us. Now you have argued, counsel, that it was incumbent on Mr. Krajisnik to point to a prejudice to him that would have resulted from questions pertaining to representation. Now, I have some problems there too. It seems to me that a conduct by counsel can be so egregious that it would be presumptively grossly negligent, and that in such cases the burden would shift to the Prosecution to demonstrate otherwise. Thank you, President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in response to the first issue, our position would be that, nevertheless, it has to be shown that these issues, these alleged violations, while even if they were considered of some -- of problematic or of some negligence, in hindsight they do not amount to gross incompetence. And overall, having a look at the conduct of the trial overall and the Trial Chamber being in the best position to determine and having constantly acknowledged that it had a fair trial at its foremost consideration was in the best position to determine whether adequate time was given and whether counsel was sufficiently prepared to conduct his defence. And we submit that it has been done, and there's no reason to consider these individual violations, because overall the trial was fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, thank you. You may go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will be addressing the question that I've already spoken about this morning very briefly, the question under which form of joint criminal enterprise Mr. Krajisnik was convicted, JCE I or JCE III. And I was wondering whether in light of the questions Your Honours have posed, I would be allowed to get a couple of more minutes to address this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Certainly a couple of minutes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll try to be brief. The Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Krajisnik on the basis of JCE I and JCE III. Initially, only discriminatory forced transfer and deportation were part of the common plan, whereas Krajisnik's liability arose for JCE III under all the other crimes, extermination, murder, persecution, based on the other acts than forced displacement. And soon thereafter, these other crimes which the Chamber refers to as expanded crimes became part of the common purpose and thus the conviction arose under JCE I. And although we agree that the Chamber could have been more explicit, I suggest to take Your Honours through the parts of the judgement that show that the Chamber did in fact make the necessary findings. And I will address the two periods distinguished by the Chamber, the beginning of the implementation of the common purpose and the period thereafter. Turning to the first period, the Trial Chamber found in paragraphs 1097 and 1118 that initially discriminatory deportation and forced transfer were included in the common purpose. And for the expanded crimes, liability arose under JCE III. They were in this initial period at least foreseeable consequences of the implementation of the common plan and Krajisnik was aware of this possibility and willingly took that risk. Trial judgment paragraph 1099 confirms this. And although there is no explicit finding of his responsibility under JCE III in this initial period, a reading of the paragraphs 1096 through 1099, together with 1124 confirm this. In 1124, the Trial Chamber finds that the accused's responsibility arose with the crimes in Bijeljina, which includes schedule incident A1.1, the killing of at least 48 civilians. This means that the Chamber found Krajisnik responsible for these killings although it had determined that initially the common purpose was only deportation and forced transfer. And that the Trial Chamber considered the expanded crimes initially as JCE III crimes is confirmed when one reads the sequence of paragraphs 1096 through 1099 together. In 1096, the Chamber raises the question of liability under JCE III and then determines in the following paragraph that initially the common purpose was limited to deportation and forced transfer, followed by trial judgement 98, which explains, as amicus curiae has just pointed out, the Trial Chamber saw that the common purpose expanded over time to include other crimes. 1099 can then only mean that the other crimes initially fell under JCE III. 1099 says, and I quote: "Notwithstanding the above, even before the Bosnian Serb takeovers began in April, the accused and Karadzic were aware that the armed conflict would have devastating consequences." This paragraph thus includes the requirements for JCE liability under the category 3, the awareness that the crimes including killing were a foreseeable consequence and the -- of the implementation of deportation and forced transfer and that the accused willingly took that risk. Turning to the second period after the initial phase. During the indictment period, all of the expanded crimes became JCE I crimes. The Trial Chamber found that in paragraph 1118. And this happened very soon, and I will explain in a minute our position that due to the reporting practice, incidents that occurred a few days after the first of the expanded crimes were part of the common purpose. At the very least, however, on the 12th of May when the strategic goals were proclaimed, all of the crimes formed part of the common purpose. That all of the crimes became part of the common purpose is confirmed at the end of trial judgement 1119 when the Chamber said that Krajisnik had the mens rea for the crimes which the Chamber found to be committed. And they became so due to the expansion of criminal means, through the commission of new types of crimes, no effective measures being taken, and the persistence of the implementation of the common plan. And the Trial Chamber was entitled to infer the intent for JCE I crimes through these circumstances as the Appeals Chamber has frequently confirmed, for example, in the Kvocka appeal judgement, paragraph 243, that intent can be inferred from the circumstances. The Chamber did not give specific dates when a particular crime became a JCE I crime. It referred to very soon. The findings made in trial judgement 996 support that at least 12 May, they were included in the common plan. And I quote from 996, the second sentence: "Takeovers, killings, detention, abuse, expulsion, and appropriation and destruction of property had begun in the territories claimed by the Bosnian Serbs well before the pronouncement of the strategic goals on 12 May." And the paragraph ends with: "This was the Bosnian leadership's goal and if there was any goal needed on 12 May, it was the continued pursuit of the very same goal." That in our position they can be JCE I crimes even earlier is a few days after the first incident occurred. Results from the fact that the trial judgement, as obvious from footnote 2223, relied on the reporting practice it had detailed in other parts of the judgement. So liability under JCE I arose for each type of these expanded crimes that happened a few days later. For the gravest crime like murder, this included already the second incident. And we have referred to this information flow in our brief in paragraphs 92 to 93 of the Prosecution response to amicus and the Prosecution response to Krajisnik, paragraphs 213 through 228. I would therefore just like to highlight the information about the first killings which occurred in Bijeljina on the 1st or 2nd of April, 1992. Krajisnik and the rest of the leadership were informed already on the 3rd of April. I refer Your Honours to witness Bozidar Antic, transcript page 18186 through 18187 and 18219. The people in Zvornik knew about them on 8 April, trial judgement 926. And on 10 April, the information was published in the newspaper. P584 referred to in trial judgement footnote 692. These examples also show that the information flow was not limited to the Pale leadership but also reached the rank and file of the JCE component and the public at large. Therefore, to conclude, the Trial Chamber correctly convicted Krajisnik under JCE I and JCE III. This concludes my submission and I thank Your Honour for the additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now give the floor to the amicus curiae for his reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm taking the next part of our submissions. I just did wonder whether there was the possibility of a break at this stage. I know there's something to do with tapes being changed and interpreters. I'm perfectly content to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: If you remain within the time as scheduled, that is 15 minutes, we have the time to do it now before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged and that's certainly my intention. Well, in the brief time remaining to me, I'm going to deal first with four short points on fair trial, then deportation, one short point, and then one or two points in rebuttal on JCE. Firstly with regard to fair trial, I would start by respectfully adopting the observation made by His Honour Judge Meron that the issue has not been settled by the Trial Chamber or the Appeals Chamber's decision of 2005. Certainly the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber did not have all the facts before them that you have now, and therefore in our submission you can revisit the issue. You have vastly more information now, for example, with respect to the lack of pre-trial preparation and the Brashich team, and so if it's a question of applying the Blagojevic test, then we say certainly there are circumstances which call into question the 2005 decision. Now, with respect to the Prosecution's response, they provide initially at least, if you like, a litany of the fair trial guarantees which Mr. Krajisnik enjoys. He was able to cross-examine witnesses, et cetera. But if you can't adequately prepare, then it's something of a charade. It's like if you go to play a game of tennis and you find that someone's removed the strings to your racket. It still may be a game of tennis but it will be a pretty poor spectacle. And that's why the human rights case law to which we referred in our brief emphasises that the fair trial guarantees must be effective and that's what's key. In terms of strategic or tactical decisions, it's not a strategic decision to be hopelessly underprepared. Mr. Stewart himself admitted that many of his decisions were not strategic or tactical. It was simply because he did not have time, including the decision with respect to expert evidence. And thirdly I would observe, again by way of a metaphor, the difficulty of fixing a leaky boat at sea. So adjournments during a trial can only afford so much relief and you can't fix a leaky boat when you're in the middle of the ocean. Now on deportation, as I said, we alerted the Prosecution that we would make this point so I apologise for it not being a reply so much as a point which we're making. In ground 4 of our brief, we submit that the Chamber erred when it convicted Mr. Krajisnik of deportation as a crime against humanity under count 7. Now the Prosecution partly concede the point, or to a large extent they concede it, by saying yes, the Trial Chamber did not carry out the case-by-case analysis of whether a de facto border was crossed by those displaced. So they concede that the Chamber's findings on deportation were in error for a number of municipalities. But they seek to keep the conviction alive with respect to one municipality, and that's Bijeljina, and ask you to affirm Mr. Krajisnik's conviction on that basis. Now, it relates solely to one piece of evidence of Mr. Milorad Davidovic, and that's T14235 which is cited at footnote 700 of the Trial Chamber judgement. Now, if you look at what Davidovic said on that page, he referred to displacements of Bosnian Muslims to "Hungary and the West," after he'd referred to displacement to Muslim controlled territory. And this is all he said: "Or else there were organised departures through Serbia to take people to Hungary and the West, and I can give you detailed information about that as well." And that's all he said. So we'd ask you to note a number of points about this very meager piece of evidence. First, Davidovic volunteered this information, and he volunteered to elaborate on it, but he wasn't asked to do so. Second, you'll note the vagueness of this response, and particularly the reference to "the West." What is encompassed in the West, and more importantly, if by the West we're talking about Western Europe, perhaps even the USA, it's obvious that the Bosnian Serb authorities would not be physically able to deport people to those countries because, of course, they'd have to pass through lots of other countries first. And so there's a very important distinction to be made. Refugees from the war in Bosnia ended up in all sorts of countries around the world. That doesn't mean they were deported to those countries any more than during the Second World War refugees from Nazi Germany fled to many countries but they weren't deported to those countries. That's a misconception. Fourth, Davidovic referred to organised departures through Serbia, but he didn't say who organised it or how. And he certainly didn't say that Mr. Krajisnik or anyone linked to him organised those departures. And finally, for deportation through Serbia, the Serbian authorities would have had to be complicit in the deportation. It's their territory after all. But the Trial Chamber didn't make any finding to that effect. And in fact the Chamber confined the JCE to persons within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you'll find that at paragraph 1087. "The Chamber finds that the JCE, of which the accused was a member, consisted of persons situated throughout the territories of the Bosnian Serb republic." So the JCE, anyway, territorially doesn't extend to Serbia. And finally while the Trial Chamber did refer to the transcript of Davidovic, the page relied on by the Prosecution also refers to internal displacements of Bosniaks to Brcko and other places. So in our submission, that one throwaway line of Davidovic is simply not enough to form the sole basis for conviction of crimes against humanity, deportation as a crime against humanity, and if that's right and if you're with us on that, then the conviction under count 7 should be quashed in its entirety, indeed has to be quashed in its entirety. Now I recognise I probably have two minutes left, so on JCE I would really just make a full bullet points. There are really two concerns for you, the Chamber, to address. First, this linkage which is required and the fact that the Trial Chamber -- the Trial Chamber's approach is insufficient. And secondly, you may feel that the Appeals Chamber is not in a position to draw inferences from the Trial record, and that's -- certainly those concerns have been raised by at least two members of the Bench. Now, we say the Prosecution response to both those concerns is unconvincing, especially the assertion that parts 2 and 3 of the judgement provide the necessary linkage. If I could summarise our response to Mr. Kremer's point this way: First, and we agree here with the submissions of Mr. Dershowitz, Mr. Kremer's repeated graphic evidence of the crime base and then simply asserts that those crimes were connected or controlled by the Bosnian Serb leadership or the Pale-based leadership component, but he fails to substantiate that latter point. Secondly, this reference to paramilitary leaders, Arkan, Mauzer, others, the so-called rank and file JCE members, who undoubtedly were involved in terrible crimes doesn't provide that there was a common plan between Mr. Krajisnik and them. And I'd also adopt what the Dershowitz brothers said about the need to independently identify who is a member of the JCE without reference to any crimes committed by them. Otherwise, there's a circularity or a double counting. The Prosecution and the Chamber should be able to pluck someone from Bosnia, if you like, and say is this person in the JCE or not? And the answer to that question shouldn't depend on whether they committed any crimes, otherwise you have that circularity and we say the Chamber fell into that trap of having no independent notion of a JCE member independent from the question of whether they committed crimes, and there is that double counting. And references to organisations and paramilitaries being under the complete control of the Bosnian Serb leadership doesn't deal with the Trial Chamber's finding at paragraph 1121 that Mr. Krajisnik didn't have effective control over such people. So we -- we do agree -- adopt the submissions of Mr. Dershowitz that you take these crimes, a man being forced to watch his wife being raped, terrible crimes, but that illustrates in fact the over-broadness of JCE, because there's no suggestion that Mr. Krajisnik incited or instigated police officers or Red Berets to commit rape in a police station, and yet he's fixed with that terrible crime among many, many others, murders of people made to dig their own graves. And doesn't that show how the JCE notion has become completely overextended. And if I might just finally end on a point about JCE III. The Prosecution invites you to find that implicitly the Chamber found a JCE III, but why on earth would they only do so implicitly. The Trial Chamber had only to say, "We find Mr. Krajisnik guilty in terms of JCE III," or they could have used the catch phrase, if you like, "these crimes were the natural and foreseeable consequence of the common plan." That's all they had to do, and they didn't do it. And so in our submission, paragraph 1099 is far too broad to contain that implicit finding as my learned friend, my learned colleague Mr. Nicholls pointed out all war crimes -- sorry, all war entails terrible crimes. But unless you're confusing the crime of aggression with JCE, you can't simply say that that foreseeability entails foreseeability and liability under JCE III. So unless I can assist you further, that would be our reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. This concludes the amicus curiae appeal. We break now for 15 minutes and reconvene at 5 past 5.00 to hear the Prosecution's appeal. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We had a slightly longer break, and we resume the hearing with the Prosecution's appeal. I give the floor to the Prosecution for their submissions for 20 minutes. You have the floor, Mr. Kremer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution appeals the 27-year sentence imposed on Mr. Krajisnik as a result of his conviction for the crimes that we've been talking about this morning and part of the afternoon. The Prosecution submits that the sentence is entirely outside the proper range of discretion for a Trial Chamber having regard to both the gravity of the crimes and the degree of participation of the accused in the crimes and that the sentence cannot be reconciled with the principles governing sentencing as expressed in the Gacumbitsi Appeals Chamber judgement, paragraph 205. We know from the discussions this morning that this case is about a massive, widespread and systematic ethnic cleansing of a large part of Bosnia-Herzegovina where 3.000 Muslims and Croats approximately were killed through murder and extermination, where 100.000 Muslims and Croats at least were forcibly displaced from a large part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and where these Muslims before they were displaced or before they were killed and even some Muslims and Croats who still remained were subject to a persecutory campaign that was part of a systematic and widespread attack on this civilian population involving underlying acts of killing, cruel and inhumane treatment, physical or psychological abuse, sexual violence, unlawful detention, forced transfer and deportation, forced labour, intentional and wanton destruction of property and plunder. The Trial Chamber found at 1146 that: "Countless stories of brutality and violence and deprivation resulted from these crimes. These stories would not have been necessary if racial hatred and nationalism had not consumed Mr. Krajisnik and the other JCE members. The Bosnian Serb leadership and the rest of the JCE members commenced a persecutory campaign that resembled how criminal states implement their campaigns of terror. First, Mr. Krajisnik and the Bosnian Serb leadership engendered in the Bosnian Serbs fear and hate of others using a propaganda machine. Fear and hate against the Muslims and Croats in order to win their support and to create the condition to implement the criminal purpose." Trial judgement 1121C. Muslims and Croats were prevented from moving freely. Their houses were searched and their privacy violated. Paragraph 784. People were fired from their jobs. 785. And denied access to schools and public services on the basis of their ethnicity. 786. The persecutory campaign as affecting the individual Muslim or Croat in a town, even not in detention, was striking. Ahmed Hidic described the situation in Bosanski Petrovac before he was driven out and deprived of his properties. He said: "I was never in a detention camp but the whole town of Bosanski Petrovac was like a big detention camp. We could not leave and we were always afraid to go out. There was so much killing going on around us and destruction of our houses and businesses. The town was completely sealed off with check-points, and there was a curfew from sunset to sunrise. There were night patrols, and we could not get food. The electricity was cut and sometimes water was also disrupted." P87, page 8. And it's cited in footnote 953. Second, there was the takeover of the municipalities by force, and during the attack Muslims and Croats were killed and ill-treated. In the end, the Bosnian Serb leadership held 35 municipalities in their control. Third, the persecutory campaign was expanded and more efficiently implemented. Muslims and Croats were arrested, beaten and killed. Private houses, mosques and Catholic churches destroyed. The goal was to extinguish any memory of the Muslim and Croat presence. The unbearable living conditions imposed on Muslims and Croats made it impossible for them to remain. 729. They fled the region in huge numbers. Their exodus was often regulated and organised by a resettlement agency run by the Bosnian Serb authorities. In Banja Luka, a resettlement agency managed all aspects of relocation. Paragraph 392. The Crisis Staff set the procedures for departure and used public institutions to implement them. Those who wanted to flee had to file about 15 different documents to obtain what they described as permission for resettlement. The final insult to the people being persecuted was that this ethnic cleansing bureaucracy required each of them to pay a fee for every certificate. To efficiently implement the ethnic cleansing, or as Mr. Krajisnik said "ethnic division," trial judgment 911 and 1097, thousands of Muslims and Croats were detained in more than 350 detention centres, often within public facilities. Paragraph 810. Adil Draganovic describes his detention at Manjaca camp in Banja Luka. "Every night, every day we were beaten, and that beating would then last for a half an hour, 45 minutes or an hour. One was using a cable to beat, another a baton. Two were using their boots, kicking us in the stomach, in the chest, in the mouth, and the others were beating me at the same time. Once you fall down, then they beat you in an even worse way. They would be kicking with the boots. I don't know how I survived that night." Reference P519B and trial transcript 5009 to 510 cited in trial judgement 386, footnote 871. He goes on to say: "And then I can also remember permanent verbal humiliation, so to speak. They told us that we weren't a people of any kind. They said, 'What do you want? Do you want a state? You're not going to have one. You'll be like the Palestinians. Look we Serbs, we got our state. We've got the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina. You're going to be killed, all of you here in the camp are going to be killed.'" And how they made the people feel is best expressed in the paragraph that follows. "The humiliations took place in these barns where we stayed and in which the conditions were totally inhumane. We were smaller than mice. Our lives were not worth the life of a mouse." P519C, transcript 5450 to 5452, trial judgement 386, footnote 871. And he does say that this -- these conditions were so severe that in the first month he lost 26 kilos. But this is just the tip of the iceberg, as it were, as to how brutal the conditions were. Women, pregnant women, young girls, even as young as 13 years old, were raped on a regular basis while men were forced to engage in degrading sexual acts with each other. Trial judgement 800 and 304. Around -- and just in terms of Mr. Krajisnik and his knowledge about what was going on, I refer you to paragraphs 1041, 1046 and 1047 as examples of Mandic's communications with -- Mandic, who is the Minister of Justice and responsible for detention facilities, and his communications with Mr. Krajisnik about really what was going on in the detention facilities. Around 3.000 Muslims and Croats were killed. Large numbers while in detention. These killings took many forms, from shooting, beating to death, suffocating, burning alive, being forced to jump off a bridge and being shot in the water, digging one's grave before being shot or having one's throat slit, being shot while performing forced labour or acting as human shields, dying of heatstroke through lack of water. Mass executions and exterminations took place in 14 municipalities. I refer you to paragraph 663 and Exhibit P285A which is the -- a statement by a witness describing the sheer horror of being shot and luckily not being killed, then being put into a building which was set alight by accelerant poured over the bodies, and he was the only fortunate person to escape. The last person who was asked to set the bodies alight when he refused was killed and his recollection of the pleading of this man not to be shot was the following: "The sound of his voice will stick in my mind forever. They just shot him dead and added him to the pile of bodies." The Bosnian Serb campaign of terror and death caused the killing of 3.000 and the expulsion of more than a hundred thousand. By the end of 1992, Krajisnik had achieved his personal and political goals through criminal means. The region was cleansed of Muslims and Croats. His obsession had become reality. Paragraph 950. The ethnic composition of the region had been changed over the course of one year not through peaceful negotiation but through a massive and systematic ethnic cleansing campaign. Krajisnik could finally and proudly explain on public television that what was being said, that we are possessing the territories ethnically populated by other national communities, that is not true. Paragraph 1076. At the time he said that, he was right, but he omitted to say that only nine months before the same territories were ethnically populated by the other national communities. Krajisnik and his fellow JCE members implemented a massive criminal campaign using state structures. They mobilised thousands of Serbs serving within these structures to commit the crimes on the ground. For the results of this ethnic cleansing campaign Krajisnik deserves a life sentence. This brings me to the second point and that is the role Krajisnik played in the crimes. Krajisnik was a key member of the joint criminal enterprise. He was, as the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 1119, one of the driving forces behind it. He was one of the leaders at the centre of power. Paragraph 180. He wanted the land ethnically pure so that he could finally claim that it belonged to his people. Paragraph 1076. He did not want to share land or power with other ethnic groups, and in order to achieve total Serb domination and statehood Krajisnik knew that it was necessary to push Muslims and Croats out by force. Paragraph 1119. He accepted heavy human cost to achieve his political dream, the death and the destruction of thousands of lives and unfathomable human suffering. 111 -- 1119. He intend the horror to take place and formulated, initiated, promoted, and developed this policy to advance the criminal plan. 1121A. While an ordinary human might expect a man of his power and authority to prevent the crimes against the population, he proceeded without pause. Paragraph 1160. Never did he express regret. Paragraph 1115. Krajisnik and Karadzic, two bodies and one soul. Trobajevic, former deputy minister under Krajisnik, trial transcript 11422, used that description to talk about how they ran the Republika Srpska as a personal fief exercising direct influence at all levels of Bosnian Serb affairs, paragraph 987, is how the Trial Chamber summed up the evidence. From this position, Krajisnik participated and promoted the implementation of his plan. 1121A. And the plan was implemented in all its steps. He directed the Bosnian Serb government and forces to implement the criminal plan. 1121D. As a senior political leader he denied the reality and even provided misleading information about the crimes to mislead the international community. 1121K. He was at the apex of power, at the apex of a state pyramid. From his position he directed, encouraged, instigated the lower levels down to the bottom to implement the criminal plan. Krajisnik did not experience the horror he caused others. Krajisnik made the others experience the horror he wanted, horror that could have been avoided but horror that was undertaken in order to achieve an ethnically pure Bosnian Serb state. Twenty-seven years of imprisonment is unreasonable for being one of the driving forces behind catastrophic events that resulted in so many killings and so many expulsions. The Prosecution accepts that the Trial Chamber took notice of the principles governing sentencing and acknowledged that the gravity of the crime is the primary factor to be taken into account. However the question is whether it gave them sufficient attention in determining the sentence. I refer you to Galic appeal judgement 442. The contrast between the facts as found and sentence imposed is striking and gives us the answer to this question. The sentence imposed cannot be reconciled with the principles. It cannot be reconciled with the principles of retribution because it does not make plain the condemnation of the international community for this conduct. It cannot be reconciled with the principles of deterrence either. Twenty-seven years for a man who abused his position of power to implement a prosecutorial campaign that changed the ethnic composition of Bosnia-Herzegovina undermines respect for the international legal order. In light of the fact as found by the Trial Chamber the sentence -- or facts as found by the Trial Chamber, the sentence is manifestly inadequate. If falls outside the range that was available to the Trial Chamber or to use the Appeals Chamber's words in Galic, it was taken from the wrong shelf. I refer you to paragraph 455. In conclusion, it's our respectful submission that in light of the massive nature and gravity of the crimes and the crucial role played by Krajisnik, the only sentence that can be reconciled with the sentencing principles is life imprisonment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Kremer. I will now give the floor to the Defence for the response. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour, I will respond only --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: -- to the joint criminal enterprise. I plan to respond only to the points relating to the joint criminal enterprise in five minutes and then have the defendant himself respond to the general sentencing points, with the permission of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I leave it up to the Court, but I understood from Mr. Dershowitz's role, it was in respect of the legal point this morning on joint criminal enterprise. We've had two discussions on it. We're in the matter of sentencing where I don't think I even used the word joint criminal enterprise. I'm not sure what Mr. Dershowitz can add to my submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour, I think I can add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, we are on the Prosecution appeal. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: I understand, Your Honour. I wanted to limit my remarks simply to the effect of JCE on the sentencing. That's the only issue I would like to address in three to five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's fine. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: With the permission of the Court, Your Honour. Thank you very much. The Prosecution mentions that they did not mention JCE. Of course not, but the whole thrust of their sentencing approach is through the vehicle of JCE, that is, there would be no way if you looked from the beginning on and you looked only at Mr. Krajisnik's conduct that you could claim that a sentence in excess of even a small number of years would be excessive. The only way they get to their sentencing argument is by working backwards, by looking at the crimes on the ground and holding him responsible for all of those crimes and then leaving a very, very brief time in their argument for showing what his responsibility was and they cite particularly paragraph 1041 to show Mr. Krajisnik's responsibility. If you look at 1041, Mr. Krajisnik is performing his function. He is trying to exchange prisoners. There is no mention of civilian prisoners. There is mention of prisoners of war and the whole focus of that conversation with the Minister of Justice is to exchange prisoners of war on one side with prisoners of war on the other side. The claim is that Mr. Krajisnik directed, encouraged, I'm quoting from them. If they could prove that, they could have their case decided under section 7(a). They wouldn't have to use joint criminal enterprise. It's precisely because they cannot prove that he directed, encouraged, because the Court made a ruling that there was no effective control. And then they point to several other political points, that he provided misleading information. Misleading information is the job of diplomats to provide all over the world, and you don't expect a diplomat to provide information that journalists or people in the international community would find to be absolutely accurate. And he says that they, they, putting together Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, of course there's an enormous difference. One was the commander-in-chief and the other was in a legislative function. And finally, just one brief point. One of the reasons why the Trial Court was so mislead and misunderstood so greatly the political nature of Mr. Krajisnik's rule -- role was precisely there was ineffective assistance of counsel. The two are directly and closely related. A decent lawyer would have put on expert witnesses, would have studied the history, would have learned this case, and if there had been a decent lawyer who understood the need for expert witnesses, Your Honours, we would not be here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dershowitz. I now turn to Mr. Krajisnik to continue the response. Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I must say that after the presentation like this by the Prosecutor I remain speechless. The Prosecutor seems to have done something that was not an appeal. There were no arguments. There was no response. There was no evidence. He's repeating everything that he stated to me eight years ago. I really cannot understand that today again he's repeating that on the 18th of March, Mr. Krajisnik called to arms. Your Honours, you have the video footage. I called for us to go on the field and draw maps in accordance with an agreement by the three ethnic communities. The Prosecutor, who I commended in the beginning for good cooperation, today is trying to mislead in order to show how Krajisnik has not been punished enough because all of this information is correct. Mr. Dershowitz said it well. I'm just going to repeat that had I had an adequate defence -- I'm a man who doesn't blame anyone. And had there been 150 witnesses here and had someone interpreted this statement of the 28th of February, they would have seen that Momcilo Krajisnik spoke to a group of deputies who said, "We don't want a Serbian Republic, which we got under Cutileiro's plan. We would like a Krajina state to divide both Bosnia and Herzegovina." I said we can't do that. Let's ask these people. Do we want Republika Srpska, which Mr. Cutileiro gave to us, or are we going to create bedlam in the whole international community and have two independent states being divided? On the 28th of February, we had the first version of the Cutileiro Plan where it says, and you can see it there, that I, in my activities, am committed to that. My activities are one thing, and negotiations are something else. In the negotiations I urge pure Serbian ethnic territories. We spoke about Serbian territories where there was an absolute and a relative Serbian majority, and then we had Muslim and Croatian communities. This was a benign statement, and that is why I believe that it is a shame had we had the experts -- well, I told Mr. Stewart, and I'm not going to say anything bad now. I told him the Prosecution has nine experts. If we don't know what is well, we know what is expensive. If the Prosecutor can have nine, let us at least have one. So, Your Honours, they say that there was a transfer of the population and there is information that you have on that and I pointed out to that a lot and the Prosecutor saw that. 480.000 Serbs left the federation, and 420.000 Muslim left Republika Srpska. So now the Prosecution should have said out of those 420.000 Muslims how many of them were expelled and how many left because people were fleeing from the war. I indicated that 380.000 Muslims left the federation. They were running away from war, while 400 .000 Serbs ran from Republika Srpska, fleeing from the war again. This is my objection to the Prosecutor. They should have said Mr. Krajisnik issued two statements against ethnic cleansing. In December, I made two statements where I opposed ethnic cleansing. In July, there was a call to all members of the SDS. It was issued that other ethnic groups must be respected. There was such orders. People in the field did all kinds of things. I'm not saying that they didn't. Now from what I understand, the Trial Chamber here, because they saw that the two sides were not equal enough, they wanted to make a compromise, and they said because of lack of evidence they convicted Krajisnik, and now the Prosecution insists that this is not enough because all of this is correct. I would just like to remind you the Prosecution today said that on the 3rd of April Mr. Antic testified in connection with the crimes in Bijeljina trying to impute that Krajisnik was aware of them. You also have the testimony of Mrs. Plavsic. She testified here that she was sent by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina to Bijeljina by Izetbegovic, and when she was asked, "Did you inform Krajisnik," she said, "No, I did not. It was not my obligation to do so." I testified here. I said that I tried to receive information by telephone and that I was cut off by Mauzer, who is also being implicated in this JCE. Also discussed here is how Mandic said that he informed Krajisnik about the crimes. I stated this in my appeal. You will see. Mr. Mandic, when he was questioned by the Prosecutor said, "I informed Krajisnik about everything that I knew," but when the lawyer asked him, "What did you know?" "I knew what was going on in the Kula prison." "Were there any crimes there?" "No." You will find that there. Now simply we're substituting ideas in order to disregard everything that is positive. I am the only politician who publicly before 100.000 people in Banja Luka in 1993 or 1994 stated, "We don't hate Muslims and we don't hate Croats." I didn't state that before The Hague Tribunal. I didn't say that thinking that I would be held responsible for anything. All I said was that it is wrong for any man to hate another man on the basis of his ethnicity. I love my own people. All I wanted was to implement the agreement that we had in early 1992. Your Honours, that agreement was -- well, on the 28th they said he said cleanse territories, and then on the 18th of March there was a different version of Cutileiro's plan, and you can see what I was committed to. I urged the support of those principles, and I supported that. You cannot advocate the exchange of territories, ethnically pure territories. That's a pejorative idea and no sensible person would advocate that. This is a consequence of war. I would just like to mention one more thing. There was a nexus between the things on the ground and the leadership. If we look at the municipality of Bosanski Novi, we have Mr. Pasic who testified here where 7.000 Muslims were relocated. When he was asked, "Did you inform the Pale leadership," he said, "I did not." Why did the Muslims leave? They left because "there were special units from Croatia, some paramilitaries who were disturbing these people." When those people came to see me, I didn't have any communication with Pale. Then I went to UNPROFOR upon their request and helped them to leave. We have the same case with Petrovac, the same case with Prnjavor, Kljuic, Kotor Varos, and all the rest. I would like to say one more thing in connection with Bijeljina. I stated in my appeal brief precisely, and this is what I object in Mr. Kremer's presentation, that in Bijeljina the Serbs had majority rule in the entire municipality. There was a majority of the population and all the deputies were in a majority. So there was no reason for the Serb side to begin the war there in order to take over power. You will see that there was an Assembly session of ours on the 7th of March when it was publicly said that the Serb side -- peace suits them. What happened in Bijeljina? In Bijeljina local people and outsiders got into a fight. Somebody came on horseback. Somebody threw a bomb, and the war began and there was no discussion who did what then, and especially because before that, there was a crime that occurred in Brod and in Kupres. I'm going to end with this, with a request, Your Honours. Please, all I would like you to do is to review all the arguments. If what Mr. Kremer says were true, I would be an unhappy man. I'm unhappy that the war had taken place, but this is not correct. The Trial Chamber did not take into account many elements just because I didn't present evidence on that. I testified here for 40 days in order to cover the holes that were not covered in my defence. And once again, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. I give the Prosecution the floor for their reply. You have five minutes to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I have nothing to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, this concludes then the Prosecution's appeal. According to the Scheduling Order --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: There would be room now for -- sorry. According to the Scheduling Order of 18 July, there will be room now for a personal statement of Mr. Krajisnik if he wants to do so. It's up to him to decide whether to take the floor for a maximum of 10 minutes on a personal basis. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a rule in life that everything that begins lasts for a certain amount of time and then has an end. So, Your Honours, after more than eight years, I hope that this will mark the end of these proceedings in my case. I have listened to all the arguments presented in the course of the trial, and for the first time I experienced something that I never believed before. I heard the suffering of the other side. During the war all I heard was what happened to the Serbs. And I'm unhappy because of that suffering. No one had the right, in the name of my people, to do anything harmful to somebody else, never mind kill them. I even told the lawyers, please, do not cross-examine these witnesses. I don't want -- even if they could help me a lot, because it's difficult when you see a young woman who lost her husband and a child and now she's wandering all over the world thinking about the revenge she could take on someone. And of course she would see a criminal in me who, in her eyes, is guilty of all the evil deeds. I did not want the war. I didn't want the war in spite of all the charges, because war doesn't bring any good to anyone. My parents taught me that, and it's an old saying, that if a person wishes for war, may war find them in their own house. It's like a curse. But when the war began, I did everything in order to achieve peace. A little bit earlier I heard that many went through misfortunes that Krajisnik did not experience. Gentlemen, during the war I lost my wife, and I had three underaged children living with me at Pale. My wife was suffering from lupus systematicus and until August, because of her, because she was sick, I had to stay with her, and then because of the Muslim shelling her situation deteriorated and she had to go to Belgrade where she died. And throughout the war I was doing my work and trying to take care of my three underaged children. I lost my uncle. I lost my cousins. I lost my place of birth. I lost my place of residency. I lost my property, and I know what it means for each person to be in the midst of war. Of course I did not suffer as much as many others did. They suffered much more than I did. And of course, I believe that it is a great misfortune that happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And once I stated this historical truth, and that is that people always said that in Bosnia it's very dangerous. It's like playing with petrol. If you smoke close to a source of oil or petrol, because this is a region that maintained peace only on the basis of compromise and tolerance and the life together among the three people, but at the moment in time when these people begin to quarrel, that conflict lasts for years and ill deeds are remembered for a long time. I followed the testimony here. Nobody ever presented a positive example. I took part in positive examples. I'm not going to mention them because I don't want to have the merit of that, but now when I watch television and when I see what is happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I'm unhappy from where I am. There is no true reconciliation that has taken root there. There they are now calculating how many of ours are in The Hague, how many of theirs, how many were convicted, how many were not, and then they applaud their own and scold the others. So there is no reconciliation. The reconciliation does not occur just with the punishment. There has to be forgiveness as well. So that is the way to approach the person who is deemed guilty. And crimes have not been forgiven. I have here witnessed people who have admitted that they were guilty of crimes, and hundreds of times they were stopped from committing suicide because it's difficult to live with the crimes one committed and to recall those whom you did wrong. If it means anything, I forgave all of those who I could consider guilty or I could blame in my life. I believe that a solution is in forgiveness, and I think that forgiveness cannot be attained through punishment alone, especially because there is one trial going on here and another one in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I hope that this message will also be a message to people to stop counting of how many of their people are at an advantage and how many are not. All the people are equal here, especially when we think of those who believe in God, because we know that before God we all must be the same. By nature I'm a patriot, and in spite of people who believe that there is no justice, I hope that you will correct the decisions of the Trial Chamber, because being an optimist, I feel unfortunate but I do not believe that I am guilty. And excuse me, just one moment. I forgot to say something. I would like to thank the Mr. Karganovic and Mr. Dershowitz team, and I'm very grateful that they are here, and I'm very pleased with the objective approach of Mr. Nicholls, which reminds me in a way of the things that I was against, that -- and now when I see how much he has done in order to secure some justice for me, I would just like to express my gratitude to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. This brings us to the conclusion of this appeal hearing. Before closing, I would like to express our gratitude to the parties and their counsel for the submissions and their constructive approach, notwithstanding today's heavy schedule. I would like also to thank all those who gave their assistance in the holding on this appeals hearing, and a special thanks to the interpreters who, as usual, contributed efficiently to facilitate the consideration of -- of the appeal and facilitate our discussions. The Appeals Chamber will now rise. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: adjourned at 5.52 p.m. 23 24
